The first word explains the means; the latter two explain its essential nature. He explains the middle word: "all mental modifications" (*sarvavṛtti*). He explains the first word: "of that, the higher" (*tasya param*).

"Cessation" (*virāma*) is the absence of mental modifications (*vṛtti*). Its "cause" (*pratyaya*) is the means for that [cessation]. "Practice" (*abhyāsa*) is its performance; "repetition" (*paunaḥpunya*) is that very thing. He who has that as his priority is described as such. Now, why does the other kind of detachment (*vairāgya*) not become the cause of cessation? To this he says: "For it is with an object" (*sālambano hi*). It is logical that a cause should be similar in nature to its effect, not dissimilar. And the other detachment is with an object, whereas the effect—namely, concentration (*samādhi*)—is without an object.

Therefore, its arising is logical from that very state which is without objective support (*nirālambana*), consisting merely of the clarity of knowledge. For it is the *dharmamegha* (cloud of dharma) samādhi itself—arisen from the *sattva* of the intellect when the stains of *rajas* and *tamas* have utterly dissolved—which, proceeding by transcending various objects, perceives the defects in all objects; and being established in its own nature through the abandonment of all objects, it becomes the cause of the objectless samādhi in which only residual impressions remain, because of their similarity.

Taking as its object means taking it as a support; it is "as if having reached non-existence" because it does not perform its functional activity in the form of a manifestation. Thus, it is seedless and without an object. Alternatively, the "seeds" are the afflictions, karma, and latent dispositions; that from which these have departed is thus [described]. (1.18)
For those who are merged into the bodyless state and those merged into primordial nature, existence is the condition. 1.19.

He demonstrates the factors for the relinquishment and acquisition of the internal distinctions within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamādhi*): "Indeed, this meditative absorption of cessation is of two kinds: that which has means as its condition (*upāyapratyaya*) and that which has existence as its condition (*bhavapratyaya*). That meditative absorption of cessation whose condition—meaning its cause—is the means to be described hereafter, such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, is called 'that which has means as its condition'."

"Bhava" (existence) is ignorance (*avidyā*), so called because living beings are born from it; or it is the perception of a self in what is not-self—namely, in the elements, the senses, or the modifications and primal natures, such as the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the great principle (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*)—as held by the "pleasure-seekers" (*tauṣṭika*) who are devoid of dispassion. This very existence is the condition or cause of that cessation-concentration (*nirodha-samādhi*); thus, it is "conditioned by existence. Between those two, the one conditioned by means (*upāya-pratyaya*) belongs to the yogins who are about to be liberated.

By means of this specific rule, he negates the connection of the remainder with one who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*). To the question, "For whom, then, does [samādhi] arise through the condition of existence (*bhava-pratyaya*)?", he provides the answer in the sūtra: "The condition of existence pertains to those who are merged in the bodyless and those merged in primordial nature (*prakṛti*). The meaning is: for those who are both bodyless (*videha*) and merged in primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*). He explains that: "For the bodyless gods, there is the condition of existence."

Those who have realized one of the elements or the senses as the Self, and whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) have been permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of that [realization] through its worship, become "bodiless" (*videha*) upon the fall of the physical body. Having dissolved into the senses or the elements, their minds remain as mere residual impressions (*saṃskāra-mātra-avaśeṣa-manas*), devoid of the six-sheathed body (*ṣāṭkauśika-śarīra*). Indeed, by means of a mind occupied solely with its own residual impressions, these bodiless ones experience and attain a state similar to isolation (*kaivalya*).

The state of being without activity (*avṛttikatva*) constitutes its similarity (*sārūpya*) with isolation (*kaivalya*), while the presence of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) along with their functional capacity (*sādhikāra*) constitutes its dissimilarity (*vairūpya*). There is a variant reading in some places: *saṃskāramātropabhogena*. Its meaning is as follows: that for which there is experience consisting solely of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) and not of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*). Having reached their limit, they exhaust and pass beyond the ripening of their own respective impressions of that kind, yet they enter into saṃsāra once again. And thus it is stated in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*: "Those who contemplate the senses remain here for ten *manvantaras*; but those who contemplate the elements remain for a full hundred."

Likewise, those who are absorbed in primordial nature (*prakṛtilayas*)—having realized one among the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the great principle (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), or the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) as the Self, and whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) have been permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of that practice—become dissolved in one of those [states] such as the unmanifest after the fall of the body, provided their office (*adhikāra*) has not yet been fulfilled.

For the mind would thus have fulfilled its purpose only if it were to produce discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). However, for a mind that has not produced the discernment of the difference between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa, its purpose remains unfulfilled, and thus it possesses further functions. When the mind, still possessing these functions, has dissolved into *prakṛti*, they experience a state as if it were isolation (*kaivalya*), until the mind returns again by virtue of its remaining functions. Although it has reached equilibrium with *prakṛti*, once the limit is reached, it manifests once more and is then separated [from *prakṛti*].

Just as the body of a frog that has entered the state of earth during excessive rain returns to the state of a frog's body through the drenching of showers from the clouds, so too it is stated in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*: "But those who possess self-conceit [the devotees of the gods] remain for a thousand years; the Buddhists, free from fever, remain for ten thousand years; those who contemplate the Unmanifest remain for a full hundred thousand years; but having attained the Attributeless Puruṣa, no calculation of time exists."
Thus, its status as something to be abandoned is established by virtue of its being the cause for the attainment of renewed existence. ||1.19||
For others, it is preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. 1.20.

He states the sequence of means for the concentration of yogins: "For others, it is preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. [An objection: But surely even those who contemplate the sense-faculties and so forth possess faith; therefore, he says: "Faith is the clarity of the mind."

Furthermore, that clarity of mind (*cetasaḥ saṃprasādaḥ*), which is an inclination, a longing, and a faith (*śraddhā*) directed toward the reality attained through scripture, inference, and the instruction of a teacher, does not belong to those who possess the conceit of self (*ātmābhimānin*) regarding the senses and so forth; for such lack of clarity is rooted in delusion—this is the meaning. Why is this alone considered faith? To this he says: "For she protects the yogin like a virtuous mother from the misfortune born of falling onto a wrong path."

This specific desire produces an effort directed toward the object of desire; thus he says: "For that person who possesses faith. Its explanation is: "In one who seeks discrimination, vigor arises. "Mindfulness" is meditation (*dhyāna*) that is untroubled and undistracted; it becomes concentrated (*samādhīyate*), meaning it is joined with the concentration that is a limb of yoga (*yogāṅga-samādhi*). And by the presentation of concentration as being inseparable from restraint (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and so forth, restraint, observances, and the rest are also indicated.

Thus, he says that for one endowed with all the limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*), cognitive concentration (*saṃprajñāta*) arises: "of one whose mind is concentrated" (*samāhitacittasya*). An excellence of discernment (*viveka*) regarding wisdom (*prajñā*) is produced. He speaks of the arising of non-cognitive concentration (*asaṃprajñāta*) preceded by cognitive concentration: "From the practice of that [wisdom], upon reaching each successive stage therein, and through detachment from each respective object, non-cognitive concentration occurs. For that is the cause of liberation (*kaivalya*); indeed, cessation (*nirodha*) preceded by the discriminative discernment (*khyāti*) of the difference between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa brings the mind to rest, having fulfilled its purpose through the performance of all its functions and duties. (YS 1.20)
It is near for those with intense spiritual urgency. 1.21.

Now, if faith and the other [qualities] are the means to yoga, then would not both samādhi and its fruit accrue to everyone without distinction? Yet it is observed that for some there is success, for some failure; for some success after a long time, for some after a longer time, and for some quickly. To this he says: "Those indeed are nine types of yogins. The means—faith and the rest—are mild, middling, or intense, according to the force of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) from previous births; those who possess these are so described.

The intensity—whether mild, moderate, or intense—of that spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*) arises solely through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and experiences from previous lives. The Sūtra shows which among these possess the most rapid attainment: "For those of intense spiritual urgency, [success] is near" (Sūtra 1.21). The rest is commentary. The fruit of cognitive concentration (*saṃprajñāta-samādhi*) is non-cognitive concentration (*asaṃprajñāta*); the fruit of that, too, is isolation (*kaivalya*). (1.21)
There is a further distinction [of degrees] because of their being weak, medium, or intense. ||1.22||
There is a further distinction because of their being weak, middling, and intense; this has been explained by the commentary through a literal exposition (nigada-vyākhyāta). ||1.22||
Or [samādhi is attained] through devotion to the Lord. 1.23.

He reflects in order to cite another sūtra: "Is it from this alone? The word *vā* (or) does not indicate doubt. [The sūtra says: "Or from devotion to Īśvara. He explains: through *praṇidhāna*—that is, from a particular kind of devotion (*bhakti*) whether mental, vocal, or physical—the Lord, being drawn forth and made present, bestows grace upon him. *Abhidhyāna* is the desire for a future object—the thought, "May this desired thing be his"—and by that alone, and not by any other activity. The rest is easy to understand. 1.23.
The Lord (Īśvara) is a distinct soul, untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, or latent dispositions. 1.24.

Now, if the universe is indeed composed only of the conscious and the unconscious and nothing else, then if God is unconscious, He is merely the Pradhāna, since the modifications of the Pradhāna are included within the Pradhāna itself; and thus there can be no "turning toward" (āvarjana) Him because of His unconsciousness. Or, if He is conscious, even so, because the power of consciousness is indifferent, because He is not subject to transmigratory existence, and because He is devoid of egoism (asmitā) and the like, how could there be "turning toward"? And how could there be "meditative intent" (abhidhyāna)? With this intention, he says: "Now, the Pradhāna... and so forth.

To this, he gives the answer in the Sūtra: "The Lord (Īśvara) is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions (kleśa), actions (karman), their ripening (vipāka), or latent dispositions (āśaya). Afflictions such as ignorance (avidyā) and the rest indeed afflict the transmigrating Puruṣa with the blows of manifold sufferings. Virtuous and non-virtuous [actions] are dharma and adharma; they are metaphorically called "actions" because they are produced by action. Ripening (vipāka) consists of birth, lifespan, and experience. Latent dispositions (vāsanās) that conform to the ripening reside upon the ground of the mind (cittabhūmi); thus they are called "dispositions" (āśayas).

For the karma that brings about the birth as a camel is not capable of producing the experience appropriate for a camel until it manifests the latent impression (bhāvanā) cultivated by the experience of being a camel in a previous life. Therefore, the impression born from the experience of the camel-birth is conducive to the maturation (vipāka) of being a camel.

Now, one might object: "These afflictions and so forth are attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*) and do not touch the *puruṣa* in any way whatsoever. Therefore, since it is established that the *puruṣa* is untouched by them simply by virtue of being called 'the *puruṣa*,' what is the use of mentioning 'afflictions, karma,' and so on? To this he replies: "And these, while residing in the mind, are attributed to the transmigrating *puruṣa*. Why? Because he is the experiencer and the conscious agent of their fruit."

Therefore, since the Lord also possesses that [bond] because of his being a *puruṣa*, the negation of it is appropriate; thus he says: "For that particular *puruṣa* who is untouched by this experience—which, though residing in the intellect (*buddhi*), is common to all *puruṣas*—is the Lord. He is called a "particular" (*viśeṣa*) because he is distinguished, that is, he is set apart from other *puruṣas*. Wishing to show what is excluded by the word "particular," he offers a rebuttal preceded by an objection: "In that case, have those who have attained isolation (*kaivalya*) [also attained it]?"

The bondage of those absorbed in *prakṛti* is *prākṛta*; the bondage of the bodiless (*videha*) is *vaikārika*; and the bondage of those who enjoy objects of divine and non-divine experience consists of *dakṣiṇā* and the rest. These are the three types of bondage. For those whose minds are refined by the contemplation of *prakṛti*, the state of absorption in *prakṛti* occurs immediately upon the fall of the body; thus, for others, a prior limit of bondage is recognized. Therefore, in this context, there is merely the prescription of the subsequent limit, while the prior and subsequent limits are negated.

He shows the distinction by summarizing it: "But he is always liberated and always the Lord. Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is the perfection of the powers of knowledge and action. Here he asks: "Who is this? For since knowledge and action are not possible for the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which is unchanging, they must be said to reside in the pure *sattva* of the mind (*citta-sattva*) that is free from *rajas* and *tamas*.

Since a relationship of ownership between Īśvara—who is eternally liberated—and the existence of the mind arising from ignorance is not possible, it is therefore said: "Because of the assumption of an exalted *sattva*. For Īśvara’s relationship of ownership with the mental *sattva* is not based on ignorance as it is for ordinary beings; rather, [it is motivated by the thought]: "I shall rescue living beings, who are overwhelmed by the threefold suffering, from the great ocean of rebirth through the instruction of knowledge and dharma."

Nor can there be instruction in that [liberation] without the attainment of an excellence in the capacity for knowledge and action; nor can this [capacity] exist without the assumption of a *sattva* (pure quality) from which the stains of *rajas* and *tamas* have been removed. Having reflected on this, the Blessed One assumes the preeminence of *sattva*, even though he is untouched by ignorance (*avidyā*). One who identifies with ignorance becomes ignorant of the true nature of ignorance, but not one who cultivates ignorance while recognizing it as ignorance. Indeed, an actor who assumes the role of Rāma and displays various gestures does not thereby become deluded.

Thus, this nature of his is adventitious (*āhārya*) and not real (*tāttvika*). This might be argued: "The Blessed One would have to accept existence (*sattva*) out of a desire to uplift [beings], and that desire for upliftment would depend upon the acceptance of existence; since this desire is also natural (*prākṛta*), there is thus a circular dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). To this, it is said: "eternal" (*śāśvatika*).

This would indeed be so if there were a first creation; however, in the beginningless succession of creations and dissolutions, at the time when the period for the desire to dissolve the world—arisen during another creation—had reached its end, the Blessed One made a vow, thinking, "I shall take up the excellence of being," and then dissolved the world.

Then, although the sentient being of the Lord’s mind—which has been perfumed by its vow—has reached a state of equilibrium with *pradhāna*, it transforms back into that very nature of the sentient being of the Lord’s mind at the conclusion of the great dissolution, due to the force of the latent impressions of the vow. Just as Caitra, having made a vow that he must rise early tomorrow morning and then falling asleep, rises at that very time due to the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of his vow; therefore, because the beginninglessness of the Lord’s vow and the sentient being’s material cause (*upādāna*) is eternal, there is no circular dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Nor should it be said that the Lord possesses the quality of consciousness and yet does not attain equilibrium with *prakṛti* even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). For if something never attains equilibrium with the primary cause (*pradhāna*), it cannot be a product of *pradhāna*, nor can it be the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) because it would then lack sentience; thus, another [unwarranted] conclusion would follow that lacks scriptural authority. And that is untenable, because there is no entity other than *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. Such is this eternal excellence of the Lord.

Is it with a cause and with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or rather without a cause and without a means of valid cognition? The answer is: its cause is the scripture (*śāstra*). Scripture consists of the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Itihāsa*, and *Purāṇa*. An objection is raised: but what is the cause of the scripture? For scripture is preceded by perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). And there is no perception or inference of anyone regarding the excellence of God’s existence. Nor is it logical that scripture originates from the perception of God.

The sense is that even if he were to say this after having fabricated it, it would be for the purpose of manifesting his own sovereignty. He refutes [this objection] by stating: "It has as its cause an excellence of being" (*prakṛṣṭasattvanimitta*). This is the intended meaning: first of all, the validity of the Mantras and the Āyurveda, which were composed by the Lord, is established because their application is effective and because there is certainty regarding their non-deviation from the actual state of things.

Nor is it possible for one who operates within the scope of worldly means of knowledge to establish positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) regarding the various medicinal herbs, their specific combinations, and mantras—by adding or removing particular syllables—even throughout a thousand human lifetimes. Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that these concomitances are established through scripture (*āgama*), and that scripture is established by them, because both that [scripture] and its lineage would be beginningless. For during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), those lineages are interrupted. Nor is there a lack of evidence for the existence of such a dissolution.

For it will be demonstrated that the world is a non-differentiated modification of the Pradhāna. Furthermore, a transformation into a dissimilar state is observed in the case of a similar transformation, just as milk, sugarcane juice, and the like take the form of curd, jaggery, and so forth. Likewise, a prior state of similar transformation is observed in the case of a dissimilar transformation; therefore, here too, the Pradhāna, while existing as a dissimilar transformation in the form of the Mahat, the Ahaṃkāra, and so on, must at some time also exist as a similar transformation. And its similar transformation is the state of equilibrium (sāmyāvasthā).

And that is the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). Therefore, from the composition of the Mantras and the Ayurveda, it must be accepted that the Lord’s *buddhi-sattva* was shining forth on all sides due to his being entirely free from the stains of the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas*. Likewise, even the mass of the Vedas, which is intent upon teaching worldly prosperity and the supreme good, must have been composed by the Lord precisely because of the excellence of His *buddhi-sattva*. And when there is such an excellence of *sattva*, errors and deceptions arising from *rajas* and *tamas* are impossible.

Thus, it is established that the treatise (*śāstra*) has as its cause the excellence of the constituent nature (*sattva*). This might be argued: "If the treatise makes known excellence by virtue of being an effect of that excellence, then it would be an inference *śeṣavat* (inference from the effect), and not scripture (*āgama*). To this he says: "Of these two. The meaning is that it does not make [excellence] known as an effect, but rather makes it known through the beginningless relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*). For excellence resides in the *sattva* of the intellect of the Lord (*īśvara*), and the treatise also resides therein by virtue of being its signifier.

He summarizes: From this scripture, which expresses the excellence of the *buddhi-sattva* of Īśvara, it follows—that is, it is known—through the characterization of the subject by means of the object, that "Īśvara is always [so] and always liberated. Thus, having distinguished him from other *puruṣas*, he distinguishes him even from other Īśvaras with the words "and that belongs to him. He states his freedom from all degrees of excellence with the words "not, first of all," and asks "Why? with the words "Because whatever..."

Why is that sovereignty said to be "free from all excellence"? To this he says: "Therefore, where... The meaning is that for those who have not reached the culmination of excellence, sovereignty is merely figurative. He states its freedom from equality: "And there is nothing equal to that."

*Prākāmya* is the state of having one's will unimpeded; *ūnatva* (deficiency) arises from its obstruction. Alternatively, if there were no deficiency, then for both [deities], there would be an obstruction of their *prākāmya*; for either the effect would not arise, or if it did arise, the effect would be perceived at once as being embraced by contradictory properties. Bearing this intention in mind, he says: "And if there were two [lords]. Or, if their intentions were not contradictory, then since lordship (*īśanā*) would be exercised by each individually, the role of others would be redundant, as the governance would have been accomplished by just one.

Or, if they were to act in concert, there would be no single Lord, as in the case of an assembly; furthermore, for those whose lordship is eternal, successive stages (paryāya) would be impossible, which would entail the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (kalpanā-gaurava). This is how it should be understood. Therefore, everything is clear. 1.24.
In that [state], there exists the unsurpassed seed of omniscience. (1.25)

Having thus stated that scripture is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding his power of action and knowledge, he establishes inference as the means of valid cognition regarding his power of knowledge—furthermore: "In that regard, there exists the seed of omniscience which is unsurpassed. He explains this with the words: "That which... and so forth.

The degree to which the darkness obscuring the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi*) is removed is the cause—the seed of omniscience—characterized by the apprehension of past, future, and present objects, both individually and collectively, including those that transcend the senses. This apprehension is qualified as "small" or "great": one person perceives only a little of the past and so forth, another perceives much, another perceives more, and another perceives the most; thus, the smallness or greatness of the apprehension is determined in relation to the object to be grasped.

That [capacity] which, increasing in this manner, reaches its limit (*niṣkrānta*) through excellence, is the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*). By this, the mere object of knowledge (*prameya*) has been stated. Here he provides the proof: "There is the attainment of the limit of the seed of omniscience. This is the statement of the thesis (*sādhyanirdeśa*). The "limit" (*kāṣṭhā*) is the state of being beyond excellence (*niratiśayatva*), because there is no further degree of excellence beyond it. Therefore, the proof is not a case of proving what is already established merely by means of a boundary. "Because it possesses excellence" (*sātiśayatvāt*) is the logical reason (*hetu*).

"Whatever possesses gradation, all that reaches a state beyond gradation; just as magnitude, which is gradated among the *kuvala*, *āmalaka*, and *bilva* fruits, becomes non-gradated in the Self—thus he demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*), like [the property of] dimension (*parimāṇavat*). Nor is it correct to argue that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from this rule due to qualities such as weight (*garima*) and so forth."

Indeed, the weight of the whole is not greater than the sum of the weights of its parts; rather, by collecting the weights residing in each of all things from the atoms up to the ultimate wholes, there arises the notion of an increasing weight. Knowledge, however, is not something that can be accumulated in this way; thus, it is appropriate that it possesses degrees of excellence according to whether it has one, two, or many objects, and therefore there is no deviation [from the rule]. He concludes: "Where there is a limit... and so forth.

[Objection: Surely there are many founders of religious systems (*tīrthakara*), such as the Buddha, the Arhat, and the sage Kapila; why then, on the basis of this inference, are they not all omniscient? To this he says: "In general... [and so forth]. [Question: Then from what source is the knowledge of their specific qualities obtained? To this he says: "Of that... [and so forth]. The meaning is that the scriptures composed by the Buddha and others are mere semblances of scripture (*āgamābhāsa*) and not true scripture, because they are deceptive, teaching paths such as momentariness and selflessness (*nairātmya*) which are contradicted by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

*Āgama* is so called because from it—characterized by the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Itihāsa*, and *Purāṇa*—the means to worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) come forth and enter the intellect; from that [source], there is the comprehension of specific designations and so forth. Specific designations such as Śiva, Īśvara, and others are well-known in the *Śruti* and other scriptures. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), being possessed of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgatā*) and the ten imperishable qualities (*daśāvyayatā*) are included. As it is stated in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:

"Omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, eternally unimpaired power, and infinite power—those who know the ordinances say these are the six limbs of the all-pervading Maheśvara."
Likewise:

"Knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, austerity, truth, forbearance, fortitude, the power of creation, self-awareness, and indeed the power of presiding—these ten imperishable qualities abide eternally in Śaṅkara."

It might be argued as follows: since the Blessed One is eternally satisfied and endowed with the highest degree of dispassion (*vairāgya*), thirst for his own self-interest is impossible; and since he is compassionate and intent on creating beings who are solely focused on happiness, it is illogical for him to create a world of living beings filled with much suffering; furthermore, because it is illogical for a discerning being (*prekṣāvat*) to act without a purpose, and thus even though he possesses the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), there can be no activity of creating the world—therefore, [the author] says: "Even in the absence of benefit to himself... [and so forth].

The purpose [of the Lord] is the favor toward living beings (*bhūta*). Indeed, once the mind has accomplished its task—consisting of the experience of sound and other objects and the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*)—it ceases to function. Thereupon, the *puruṣa* becomes isolated (*kevalī*). Therefore, for that purpose, the Compassionate One teaches the means to discriminative discernment. Because the mind has not yet fulfilled its purpose, the Lord, though causing living beings to experience pleasure and pain with the aid of merit and demerit, is not lacking in compassion.

To explain the means for the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), he states the door [to liberation], which is favoring living beings (*bhūtānugraha*): "by the instruction of knowledge and virtue" (*jñānadharmopadeśena*). Knowledge and virtue are "knowledge-virtues" (*jñānadharmau*); by the instruction of these two, through the ripening of the discriminative discernment obtained from the combined practice of knowledge and virtue, at the dissolution of the eon (*kalpapralaya*)—at the end of a day of Brahmā—wherein the entire world, with the exception of Satyaloka, comes to its cessation.

At the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), when even Brahmā, together with the world of Satyaloka, comes to an end, transmigrating beings return to their own causes and thus partake in the suffering of death. The term "kalpa" is illustrative; the meaning is that having attained isolation (*kaivalya*), I shall rescue those persons who—even at other times—undergo birth, death, and so forth by the power of the ripening of their own accumulated karma, so that those persons become truly rescued.

And since this instruction in the knowledge of the Dharma by one impelled by compassion is established even for the followers of Kapila (the Sāṃkhyas), he says: "And so it was said by the teacher Pañcaśikha: 'The first knower is Kapila. Regarding the statement "the first knower," the words of the teacher Pañcaśikha refer to the original liberated teacher at the beginning of one's own lineage (*svasaṃtāna*), and not to the primordial, eternally liberated supreme teacher (*paramaguru*). Among those who were liberated at the beginning—that is, among the wise who were liberated at some point in time—Kapila is our first knower, liberated one, and he alone is the teacher.

It is heard that even for Kapila, upon his birth, the attainment of knowledge occurred solely through the grace of Maheśvara. Kapila is well known as a specific incarnation of Viṣṇu; however, Svayaṃbhū is Hiraṇyagarbha. It is also heard in the Veda that he attained Sāṃkhya and Yoga. The sense is that this very Īśvara, the primordial knower, is Kapila and Viṣṇu, and not Svayaṃbhū. But for those who follow the tradition of Svayaṃbhū, the sense is that he is the Īśvara. (1.25)
He is also the teacher of the ancients, because he is not limited by time. (1.26)

Now he states the distinction of the Blessed One from Brahmā and the others: "He is this very one. The introductory transition (*pātanikā*): "He is this very one. The aphorism (*sūtra*): "He is the teacher even of the ancients, because He is not limited by time. He explains: "For the ancients... Time—consisting of a hundred years and so forth—does not apply, that is, does not function, for the purpose of limitation (*avaccheda*). The "attainment" (*gati*) of excellence is to be understood from scripture (*āgama*). ||1.26||
The syllable Om is its designator. 1.27.

Thus, by this continuous exposition, the Blessed Lord Īśvara has been shown. Now, in order to show His designative symbol (*praṇidhāna*), he states its designator: "The *praṇava* is its designator. He explains: "the designatum" (*vācya*). Therein, he introduces the opinion of others by way of inquiry: "What is this? The meaning is that "being a designator" (*vācakatva*) is the state of being a communicator.

For others [hold that] if the relationship between word and meaning were intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), it would be manifested by a convention (*saṃketa*) of the nature: "this meaning is to be understood from this word. In that case, where that [intrinsic] relationship does not exist, it could not be manifested even by a hundred conventions. Indeed, a jar that is to be manifested by a lamp cannot be manifested there by even a thousand lamps if it is not present. However, the word "karabha," once a convention has been established for it, is seen to convey the meaning "elephant" when applied to an elephant.

Therefore, the capacity to denote is established solely by convention (*saṃketa*). Having reflected on this, he determines his own position: "It remains as such" (*sthito 'sya*). This is the intended meaning: all words are capable of denoting objects in all their forms. Their natural relationship with objects of every form is indeed ever-present. However, the convention of God (*īśvara*) serves both to manifest and to restrict [this capacity]. Furthermore, the distinction between a word that denotes and a corrupt form (*apabhraṃśa*) is produced by the presence or absence of that divine convention.

This is what he says: "But the convention belongs to God. He provides an illustration with the word "just as. Now, an objection might be raised: at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), the power of the Word, which consists of *pradhāna* and has entered into the state of *pradhāna*, is also dissolved. Consequently, when [the world] arises again through the sequence beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), how could the expressive power—which was previously non-existent—be manifested by the convention of Maheśvara? For its power would have been destroyed. To this he replies: "Even in other creations."

Although the word has attained a state of equality with the primary object by being accompanied by its power (*śakti*), nevertheless, when it manifests again, it manifests as endowed with that very power—just as a plant born from a seed that has reached the state of earth during the failure of rain re-emerges through the sprinkling of streams of water released from the clouds. Therefore, the Blessed One establishes the convention (*saṃketa*) in accordance with the previous connection and convention.

Therefore, because the continuity of similar linguistic usage (*sadṛśavyavahāraparamparā*) is eternal, the followers of the Āgamas maintain that the relationship between word and meaning is eternal, though not eternally immutable (*kūṭasthanitya*). The sense is that those who do not rely on the Āgamas are not capable of realizing that the convention (*saṃketa*) remains exactly the same even in other cycles of creation (*sargāntara*). ||1.27||
The repetition of that [mantra] and the contemplation of its meaning. (1.28)

Having stated the name [of the Lord], he states the application (*praṇidhāna*): "The repetition of that [mantra] and the meditation upon its meaning. He explains: "Of the *praṇava*," etc. Meditation (*bhāvana*) is the repeated fixing [of the mind] upon the object in the consciousness. To the question, "What is accomplished by that?", he says: "The *praṇava*," etc. The mind rests upon the one Blessed One. Here he cites a verse from Vyāsa: "And thus," etc. Thereupon, the Lord favors him by granting the attainment of the fruit of that concentration (*samādhi*). 1.28.
Thence follows the attainment of knowledge of the inward-turned consciousness, as well as the absence of obstacles. 1.29.

Furthermore, what follows from this? "From that [comes] the realization of the inward-turned consciousness and the absence of obstacles. That which moves toward (*añcati*) or perceives (*vijānāti*) in a contrary or opposite direction (*pratīpam*) is "inward-turned" (*pratyak*); it is both that and consciousness (*cetana*), thus "the inward-turned consciousness" (*pratyak-cetana*), referring to the person (*puruṣa*) possessed of ignorance (*avidyā*). By this term, he distinguishes him from the Lord (*īśvara*), who is endowed with the eternal excellence of *sattva* and is possessed of knowledge (*vidyā*). The "realization" (*adhigama*)—that is, the knowledge—of this inward-turned consciousness occurs in its own essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), as well as the absence of the obstacles (*antarāya*) which will be described hereafter.

The commentary on this is as follows: "Those who... [and so forth]. "Its own" means its self; "its form" refers to that. By the mention of "form," he negates those attributes superimposed by ignorance (*avidyā*). Now, one might object: "How can devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*), which has the Lord as its object, bring about the direct realization of one's own conscious self? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*. To this he says: "Just as the Lord... He is pure because, being immutable and eternal, he is devoid of arising and passing away; he is serene because he is free from afflictions (*kleśa*); he is solitary because he is devoid of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*); and for that very reason, he is free from calamities (*anupasarga*).

The "afflictions" (upasarga) consist of birth, lifespan, and experience. Because it possesses some degree of difference from similarity, [the text] distinguishes [the self] from God by stating, "the experiencer of the intellect. By this, the term "inner" (pratyak) is explained. The contemplation of one of two objects that are absolutely dissimilar is not conducive to the direct perception of the other. However, the contemplation of an object similar [to another] experiences utility for the direct perception of that other similar object, just as the study of one scripture is useful for the knowledge of another scripture similar to it.
However, proximity is the cause of direct perception with respect to one's own self, but not with respect to another's self; thus, everything is clear. 1.29.
Disease, languor, doubt, heedlessness, laziness, lack of renunciation, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage, and instability—these distractions of the mind are the obstacles. 1.30.

He asks: "Now, what are they? The answer in general terms is: "Those which... He asks for the specific number: "Which ones? The answer is the sūtra beginning with "disease" (vyādhi). There are nine obstacles. These fluctuations of the mind are obstacles to yoga, antagonistic to yoga, and distractions of the mind; indeed, these—disease and the rest—disturb and remove the mind from yoga, and thus they are called "distractions" (vikṣepa). He states the reason for their being opposed to yoga: "These, together with... (sahaita iti).

Regarding doubt and error, they are states of mental activity (*vṛtti*); therefore, [the means of restraint] are their opposites because they suppress such activity. Even those which are not themselves mental activities—such as disease and so forth—are also opposites of them by virtue of being associated with such activity; this is the meaning. He explains the terms: "Disease" (*vyādhi*) refers to the humors (*dhātu*), namely wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*), so called because they sustain the body. "Humor" (*rasa*) is a specific transformation of the food that has been eaten and drunk. "Organs" (*karaṇa*) are the sense-faculties (*indriya*); their "improper state" (*vaiṣamya*) is a condition of deficiency or excess. "Incapacity" (*akarmaṇyatā*) is the unfitness for action.

Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a cognition that touches upon two alternatives. Although doubt and error (*viparyāsa*) are not distinct insofar as they both lack establishment in the true nature of the object, they are presented here as distinct with the intention of highlighting the internal difference between touching and not touching both alternatives. Non-cultivation (*abhāvanā*) means non-performance; that is to say, a lack of effort toward it. Heaviness of the body is caused by phlegm (*kapha*) and so forth; heaviness of the mind is caused by darkness (*tamas*). Greed (*gardha*) is thirst (*tṛṣṇā*). The "Honeyed" (*madhumatī*) and other stages refer to the levels of meditative absorption (*samādhi-bhūmi*).

If, upon having attained a stage, one who considers himself well-established should suffer a lapse in concentration, then there would be a fall even from that stage. Therefore, since it remains stable only when concentration is attained, one must strive for that. (1.30)
Suffering, mental distress, restlessness of the body, and inhalation and exhalation are concomitants of distraction. (1.31)

Not only are there nine obstacles, but sufferings and so forth also arise for him simultaneously with them; thus he says "suffering," etc. Suffering (*duḥkha*) is that which is experienced as disagreeable: internal (*ādhyātmika*), being bodily due to disease or mental due to desire and the like; external (*ādhibhautika*), produced by tigers and such; and celestial (*ādhidaivika*), produced by planetary afflictions and the like. And since this suffering is to be abandoned because it is experienced as disagreeable by all living beings, he says: "by which they are struck."

When the breath, even against one's will, inhales—that is, drinks in, takes in, or causes the entry of—external air, that is inhalation (*śvāsa*), which is opposed to *recaka*, a limb of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). When the breath, even against one's will, exhales—that is, emits or expels—the abdominal air, that is exhalation (*praśvāsa*), which is opposed to *pūraka*, a limb of meditative concentration. (1.31)
To prevent that, one should practice concentration on a single principle (ekatattva). 1.32.

He introduces the sutra that summarizes the meaning already stated: "Now, these... The connection is as follows: immediately after what has been said, he states this sutra while summarizing. The reason for their being subject to cessation has been stated: "because they are obstacles to samādhi. Although only practice (*abhyāsa*) was mentioned in the phrase "from devotion to the Lord," nevertheless, detachment (*vairāgya*) must be understood here as its auxiliary; thus he says: "they are to be ceased by those two—by practice and detachment, precisely as defined above."

In that context, between those two—practice and dispassion—it refers to practice mentioned immediately prior. The phrase "for the purpose of its cessation," and so forth, [is explained as follows]: "The one reality is Īśvara, because He is the subject under discussion. For the Nihilists (Vaināśikas), there is no such thing as a mind that is entirely one-pointed; rather, they hold that everything is distracted. Thus, he states "But for one who... to show the futility of their teachings and the activities directed toward those ends.

In whose view [it is held that] a cognition, being presented with respect to an object—whether one or many—is necessarily produced as the manifestation of the object in its entirety, and having reached its conclusion therein, does not go elsewhere. To the question, "Why does it not first grasp another object and then later grasp yet another? he says: "And it is momentary"; the sense is that because a moment is indivisible, there is no such thing as a prior or posterior state within it.

In our view, however, the non-momentary mind is not fixed upon a single or multiple objects; rather, because it abandons and takes up various objects at every moment, it is indeterminate with respect to its objects and thus distracted. Therefore, by removing this transformation of distraction, one-pointedness can be established; hence, the instruction and the practice thereof are not purposeless. Thus he says: "If, on the other hand, this... He concludes: "Therefore, not... He raises the objection of the Nihilist (Vaināśika): "As for him who also..."

Let there be no effort to establish one-pointedness in a single momentary mind; rather, the meaning is that within the beginningless mental continuum (*cittasaṃtāna*), which is non-momentary, distraction will be removed and one-pointedness will be established. Having thus formulated this position, he refutes it with the words "of that" (*tasya*). If, in the view of that [opponent], one-pointedness is a property of the "stream-mind" (*pravāhacitta*) or of the mental continuum, then among those conditions that arise successively, there exists no single "stream-mind" that persists throughout them.

Why? Because everything that exists is momentary (*kṣaṇika*), and nothing non-momentary exists according to your own view; such is the sense. He takes up the second alternative—*atha* (now)—[as follows]: "A condition (*pratyaya*) is a part of the conventional stream (*saṃvṛta-pravāha*); its one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*) is a quality (*dharma*) to be accomplished through effort. He refutes this: "All of that [one-pointedness], in relation to the conventional stream, must be either a stream of similar conditions or a stream of dissimilar conditions."

Furthermore, because [the mind] is restricted to each respective object by way of its ultimate reality (*paramārthasattā*), and because it is complete within that which appears as an object when it has arisen, it is indeed one-pointed; thus, a distracted mind is untenable—that is, there is no such thing as a mind from whose removal one-pointedness is established. He concludes with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). For this reason also, he states that the mind is single, manifold in its objects, and stable: "If, moreover," and so forth. For just as Caitra does not remember a treatise studied by Maitra.

Just as Caitra, who is unrelated to it, does not experience the fruit of merit or demerit accumulated by Maitra, so too one cognitive moment (*pratyaya*) would not remember what was seen by another cognitive moment; nor would one cognitive moment experience the fruit of the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) accumulated by another cognitive moment—this is the meaning.

[Objection: "Surely these two [fallacies] do not over-extend [to all cases], because of the qualification 'when there is a causal relation' (*kāryakāraṇabhāve sati*). For we observe that in rites such as the *Śrāddha* or the *Vaiśvānarī-īṣṭi*, the fruit accrues to the performer's mother, father, or son; and in the case of mango seeds and the like, which have been infused with a sweet taste, there is a rule that the sweetness of the fruit follows through a continuous succession. To this, he says: "Even this being resolved... (*samādhīyamānam apy etat*).

This is the intended meaning: what indeed is the distinction between conditions occurring within a single continuum (*saṃtāna*) and those occurring within other continua, such that only a condition belonging to that same continuum—and not one belonging to another continuum—should be the rememberer and the experiencer of the latent impression (*karmāśaya*) that was experienced and accumulated by a condition within that single continuum? For there is no such thing as a "continuum" existing as a real entity (*vastusan*) that could distinguish this continuum from those occurring in other continua.

Furthermore, a conceptual distinction is not tenable in the case of an action; for indeed, a boy whose nature as fire is merely imagined does not cook. Nor is the relationship of cause and effect real; for such a relationship is impossible between two things that exist simultaneously, like the left and right horns of a cow, and it is likewise impossible for non-simultaneous things, since they cannot have a present locus. Indeed, the past and the future cannot coalesce to function in the present.

Therefore, conditions (*pratyaya*) that are not conditioned by either a causal sequence (*saṃtāna*) or an intrinsic causal relationship (*svābhāvika-kāryakāraṇabhāva*), but are ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), do not differ from other conditions—whether they belong to their own continuum (*svasaṃtāna*) or to another continuum (*parasaṃtāna*)—because they lack mutual contact. This is the same logical argument (the *nyāya*) applied to cow-dung and milk-rice: "Cow-dung is milk-rice because it is 'cow-derived' (*gavyatva*), like milk-rice established for both parties. He rejects this on the grounds that it is a fallacy of reasoning (*nyāyābhāsa*), as it is even more excessive than that.

Nor is there here the objection regarding the loss of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*) or the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*), because the mind alone is the agent of actions, and that very mind is joined with the pleasure and pain produced by them. Furthermore, it is the mind—having assumed the reflection of consciousness—that experiences pleasure and pain; thus, the attribution of experience to the *puruṣa* arises from the failure to perceive the difference between consciousness and the mind. It is simply the nature of those things, arisen in dependence upon their own respective conditions, that they alone remember and enjoy the fruit, and not others.

Furthermore, intrinsic natures do not admit of being enjoined or questioned such that one might say, "Let it be thus," "Let it not be thus," or "Why is it not thus? To one who is not satisfied with what was stated previously, he says: "Moreover, its own self... Even though there is a multiplicity of experiences characterized by arising and passing away, as well as the memories of those experiences, how could the cognition "I"—which links them together—take as its object a mind that is non-different from them, when those cognitions themselves are absolutely distinct?

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is no single cognition called "recognition" (pratyabhijñāna), because of the difference in its causes—namely perception (*grahaṇa*) and memory (*smaraṇa*)—or because of the association with contradictory properties such as mediacy (*pārokṣya*) and immediacy (*apārokṣya*), from which the unity of the cognizing mind (*citta*) would follow? To this, he says: "[It is established] by one's own experience... [Objection: But have not the difference in causes and the association with contradictory properties been stated here as the very subverters [of recognition]? To this, he says: "And not of perception..."

In the *Nyāyakaṇikā*, it has been demonstrated that the non-difference of causal complexes and the lack of contradiction between the properties of being remote and non-remote follow precisely from the nature of perception; furthermore, the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of the non-momentary has been established in both the *Nyāyakaṇikā* and the *Brahmatattvasamīkṣā*. Thus, everything is clear. (1.32)

The clarification of the mind arises from the cultivation of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, directed toward objects that are pleasant, painful, virtuous, or non-virtuous. 1.33.

He begins to set forth the means for clarifying the mind—means that oppose envy and other such defects—in order to produce the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and its prerequisites for one whose mind is unrefined and possessed of envy and so forth: "Of that mind which is established... and so on, ending with "clarification" (*prasādana*). For one who cultivates friendliness (*maitrī*), that is, benevolence, toward those who are happy, the turbidity of envy (*īrṣyā*) ceases from the mind.

For one who cultivates compassion toward those in suffering—the desire to eliminate their pain as if it were one’s own—the turbidity of the mind that wishes to inflict harm upon others ceases. For one who cultivates sympathetic joy (muditā)—the feeling of gladness—toward beings of virtuous character, the turbidity of the mind consisting of envy ceases. And for one who cultivates equanimity (upekṣā) or neutrality toward those of non-virtuous character, the turbidity of the mind consisting of resentment ceases. Consequently, upon the cessation of qualities characterized by passion (rājasatāmasa), a pure, sattvic quality arises within him.

One endowed with an excellence of being (sattva) arises on the side of the cessation of mental fluctuations; because of its inherent clarity, his mind becomes serene. And once serene, it attains a state of stability through one-pointedness by means of the methods to be described hereafter. However, in the absence of the cultivation of friendliness and the other [immeasurables], those methods are not capable of leading to stability. (1.33)
Or [the mind becomes steady] by means of the expulsion and retention of the vital breath. 1.34.

He now states those means for stability: "Or, by means of exhalation and retention of the breath. The word "or" (*vā*) implies an alternative with respect to other means that will be mentioned hereafter, not with respect to the cultivation of friendliness and so forth, because it is to be combined with them. He explains "exhalation" (*pracchardana*): "of the abdominal air," meaning that by means of a specific effort prescribed in the Yoga Śāstra, the abdominal air is slowly expelled through the two nostrils. He explains "retention" (*vidhāraṇa*): "retention is breath control" (*prāṇāyāma*).

The recaka is the expansion—meaning the external placement—of the breath, that is, the internal air, rather than its sudden re-entry. Through these two, namely expulsion (pracchardana) and retention (vidhāraṇa), the mind of one whose body has been lightened by the breath attains a state of stability. Here, the term "sthitim" (stability) should be understood as being drawn from the phrase "sthitinibandhanī" (the cause of stability) found in the subsequent sūtra; thus, it is to be connected with the sense already established. 1.34.
Or, when an activity of the mind directed toward an object has arisen, it becomes a means for stabilizing the mind. (1.35)

He states another means for stability: "Or, an activity directed toward an object that has arisen is a basis for the stability of the mind. He explains: "One should fix [the mind] on the tip of the nose. For one who performs *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*, through mastery of these, there arises the perception and direct realization of divine fragrance. This should be applied to other activities as well. And this is to be understood from scripture (*āgama*), not through logical reasoning (*upapatti*).

It might be asked: "What is the use of such fluctuations (*vṛtti*) which are of no utility toward *kaivalya*? To this he says: "These fluctuations, having arisen in a very short time, bind the mind to a state of stability (*sthiti*) directed toward the Lord or toward discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). Now, one might ask: "How can a fluctuation directed toward one object produce stability in something else? To this he says: "They dispel—that is, they remove—doubt; for this very reason, [they lead] to the wisdom of *samādhi*."

He extends [the principle of] having objects to other modes of knowledge (*vṛtti*) established by scripture as well, with the words "by this" (*etena*). Now, one might ask: "But how can there be doubt regarding objects already understood through scripture and the like? To this he says: "For even though... (*yady api hi...*). For yoga is rooted in faith; and when one perceives directly even a single portion of the object taught, an excellence of faith arises. And meditation (*dhyāna*) and the rest, which are rooted in that [faith], proceed for him without obstruction—this is the meaning. (1.35)
Or it is free from sorrow and luminous. 1.36.

Or it is "free from sorrow" (*viśokā*) and "luminous" (*jyotiṣmatī*). Free from sorrow means devoid of suffering; luminous means possessing light, thus having the nature of radiance. Regarding "the lotus of the heart": in the center of the belly and the chest, there is an eight-petaled lotus that stands with its face downward; by means of exhalation (*recaka*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should turn it upward and fix the mind there. In its center is the solar orb, the letter *a*, the locus of the waking state; above that is the lunar orb, the letter *u*, the locus of dreaming.

Above that is the fire-maṇḍala, the letter *ma*, the locus of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Above that, the exponents of Brahman declare the half-measure (*ardhamātra*)—the resonance of Brahman (*brahmanāda*) consisting of the supreme ether—to be the locus of the fourth state (*turīya*). There, within the pericarp, is the channel of Brahman (*brahmanāḍī*), facing upward and situated in the midst of the solar and other maṇḍalas. Extending further upward from there is the channel named Suṣumnā; by it, indeed, even the external solar and other maṇḍalas are strung together. For that is the locus of the mind (*citta*).

For the yogin who maintains concentration upon that [light], the consciousness of the mind (*cittasaṃvit*) arises. He demonstrates the form of the consciousness of the intellect (*buddhisaṃvit*) by means of a logical argument, beginning with the words "for the sattva of the intellect... By the phrase "resembling space," he expresses its all-pervasiveness. The radiance of the sun and other luminaries—its form—is conceptualized through that [intellectual] form and becomes manifold in appearance. And here, "mind" (*manas*) is intended as the intellect (*buddhi*), and not the Great Principle (*mahattattva*).

And for that [mind] which resides in the *suṣumnā* and is born from the *vaikārika-ahaṃkāra*, its nature as light is intended because of its abundance of *sattva*. Furthermore, its pervasiveness is established by its range extending toward various objects. Having shown the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in the mind, which is the effect of the sense of "I" (*asmitā*), he states the essential nature of the absorption in "I-ness" with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). It is "calm," meaning free from the waves of *rajas* and *tamas*; it is "infinite," meaning all-pervasive; it is "mere I-ness," and not, moreover, a form consisting of manifold radiance.

He harmonizes his own view with another scripture: "In this regard, it has been said by Pañcaśikha that having known and contemplated that subtle self (*aṇu*)—which is the locus of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*)—because it is difficult to grasp, one perceives it simply as 'I am'. This might be so; however, [one might ask]: let the luminous state (*jyotiṣmatī*) consist of various forms of light; how can it consist of the mere form of "I-am-ness" (*asmitāmātra*)? To this he says: "This is twofold. The sense is that when the stains of *rajas* and *tamas* have been shaken off, *asmitā* itself, consisting of *sattva*, is the light. He states the fruit of both types of the luminous state: "By which... (1.36).
Or the mind has as its object one who is free from passion. 1.37.

Or, the mind has as its object those who are free from passion. Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana and others are such persons; their minds are the very object [of the yogi's meditation], and thus the [yogi’s] mind is colored by that. (1.37)
Or it has as its objective support the cognition of dreams and sleep. (1.38)

Or [it is] the objective support of dream-consciousness during sleep. For instance, when one has awakened with a serene mind from a dream in which one was worshipping an image of the Blessed Maheśvara—situated in a secluded forest grove, as if carved out of the lunar orb, endowed with delicate limbs and minor members resembling bits of tender lotus stalk, made of noble moonstone, and captivating with garlands of highly fragrant jasmine and *mallikā* flowers—one then takes that very image, which served as the objective support of the dream-consciousness, as the object of one's thought.

As he reflects thus, with a mind focused on that single form, his consciousness attains a state of stability right there. And here, "sleep" should be understood as that which is characterized by goodness (*sāttvikī*); for one who has awakened from it, there arises the reflective awareness, "I slept happily. Indeed, in that state, the mind becomes one-pointed. It is said merely on that account: "This very state of deep sleep they declare to be the form of Brahman for the knower of Brahman.
Furthermore, since knowledge devoid of an object of knowledge cannot be made an object of experience, the object of knowledge is also brought within the range of perception. (1.38)
Or from meditation on whatever is desired. (1.39)
Or from meditation on whichever [form] is preferred; what need for more? Whatever is preferred, that is the form of that very deity. (1.39)
Its mastery extends from the smallest atom to the greatest magnitude. 1.40.

How, then, is the internalization of the state of stability (sthitipada-sātmyabhāva) to be understood? To this he says: "His mastery extends from the smallest atom to the greatest magnitude. He explains [the term] "subtle" [in this context]. Summarizing the meaning already stated, he states the meaning of the term "mastery": "Thus, that twofold [objectivity]. He states the intermediate fruit of that mastery: "From that mastery... (1.40).

For one whose fluctuations have ceased, there is, as it were, a jewel of noble birth, a meditative attainment consisting in abiding in and being colored by those [objects] with respect to the grasper, the grasping, and the graspable. 1.41.

Thus, the means for the stabilization of the mind have been shown, and the mastery over the mind that has attained stability has also been shown. Now he asks—beginning with "Now" (*atha*)—what is the object and what is the nature of the *saṃprajñāta* [samādhi] of the mind that has attained stability? He introduces the aphorism as the answer to this, saying: "That is being stated" (*tad ucyate*). He recites the aphorism: "Of one whose fluctuations have ceased," and so on, ending with "attainment" (*samāpatti*). He explains it, beginning with "Of one whose [fluctuations] have ceased" (*kṣīṇa*).

[This refers to] the mind whose rājasa and tāmasa fluctuations, such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), have been attenuated through practice (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*). Its explanation is given by the phrase "of that [mind] whose cognitive functions (*pratyaya*) have subsided. By this, it is stated that the sattva of the mind, which is naturally transparent, is no longer overwhelmed by rajas and tamas. He clarifies the illustration with the word "just as" (*yathā*): "upāśraya" means an adjunct (*upādhi*), such as a hibiscus flower, by which [the crystal] is colored—that is, it has acquired its reflection.

Whatever is the specific form belonging to the support (*upāśraya*), such as red, blue, and so forth—that very form (*ākāra*) appears as characterized by it. He applies this to the case under discussion: "likewise, as the object" (*tathā grāhya*). It is both the object (*grāhya*) and the objective support (*ālambana*); it is colored by that, permeated by that. By this, he distinguishes it from the subject (*grahītṛ*) and the act of grasping (*grahaṇa*). Having concealed its own internal organ-form, it has become identified with the object; that is to say, it has attained, as it were, the state of being an object. Therefore, it appears in the form of the essential nature of the object.

He distinguishes the very coloring of the object (*grāhyoparāga*) by means of its subtle and gross states—namely, "the subtle elements" (*bhūtasūkṣma*), and so forth. The manifoldness of the universe (*viśvabheda*), consisting of the nature of sentient and insentient things such as cows and the like, as well as jars and the like, is to be understood. By this, the two types of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) accompanied by reasoning (*vitarka*) and reflection (*vicāra*) are shown. Likewise, [he applies this] "to the instruments of perception (*grahaṇa*), that is, the sense organs (*indriya*) as well. They are called "instruments of perception" because objects are perceived (*gṛhyante*) by means of them; he clarifies this very point with the words "having the instruments of perception as their objective support" (*grahaṇālambana*).

The phrase "grahaṇālambana" means that which consists of both the act of grasping (*grahaṇa*) and its object (*ālambana*). Being colored and permeated by that, it conceals its own nature as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and becomes, as it were, the act of grasping itself or the external organ itself. Having thus described [the mind] as accompanied by pleasure (*ānanda*), he speaks of it as accompanied by egoism (*asmitā*): "likewise, the grasping subject, the person (*grahītṛpuruṣa*)," etc. The point is that the person is the locus of egoism (*asmitā*).

Because there is no distinction in being a *puruṣa*, even one who is liberated—such as Śuka, Prahlāda, and others—is to be included as an object of meditative absorption (*samādhi*); thus he says, "likewise, the liberated one. Concluding [the section], he explains the phrase "abiding in that and colored by that" (*tatsthatadañjanatā*) with the words, "in this way, therefore."

When the mind-substance (citta-sattva)—which is established in and supported by those [objects] consisting of the grasper, the grasping, and the graspable, and which has had its impurities of *rajas* and *tamas* removed through the maturation of meditation—attains a state of being fixed in them and colored by them (*tad-ākāratā*), that is called "attainment" (*samāpatti*) and is defined as yoga characterized by clear awareness (*saṃprajñāta*). Furthermore, in this context, the sequential order of the words in the Sūtra—"the grasper, the grasping, and the graspable"—should not be observed, as it contradicts the logical order of meaning.
Likewise, even the initial presentation of the subtle elements (*bhūta-sūkṣma*) in the Bhāṣya is not to be taken literally; thus, everything is consistent and beautiful. 1.41.
Therein, the attainment mixed with conceptual constructions of word, meaning, and knowledge is "with vitarka. (1.42)

Attainment (*samāpatti*) has been described in general terms; it becomes fourfold according to its internal subdivisions, namely: with applied thought (*savitarka*), without applied thought (*nirvitarka*), with sustained thought (*savicāra*), and without sustained thought (*nirvicāra*). Regarding this, he states the definition of attainment with applied thought, beginning with "In that regard" (*tatra*) and so forth. Among those attainments, attainment with applied thought is to be understood. Of what nature? It consists of the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of words, objects, and cognitions.

In reality, even though sound and the other factors are distinct, through their mutual superimposition (*adhyāsa*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) displays difference within the one and non-difference among the many. Therefore, the meaning is that [the cognition] is "intermingled" (*saṃkīrṇā*), that is, mixed with the conceptual constructions of word, object, and knowledge. For example: "The word 'cow'. Here, regarding the word "cow," the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the word is shown in relation to the object and the knowledge which have been presented as "cow. "The object 'cow'. Here, regarding the word "cow," the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the object is shown in relation to the word and the knowledge which have been presented as "cow. "The knowledge 'cow'. Here, regarding the word "cow," the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the knowledge is shown in relation to the word and the object which have been presented as "cow. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of all three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. It is not that there is actually no distinction between them; rather, it is because they are mutually superimposed that they appear as if non-distinct. This is what is meant by the term "intermingled. Just as when one says, "Bring the white cow," the word "white" is not used to exclude blackness and so forth from the cow, nor does the word "cow" exclude whiteness and so forth from the white object; rather, the word "white" is employed to produce a conceptual construction of the non-difference of the white color within the cow, and the word "cow" is employed to produce a conceptual construction of the non-difference of the cow within the white object. In this way, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is established. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is also seen in cases such as: "The word 'cow' is eternal," "The object 'cow' is eternal," and "The knowledge 'cow' is eternal. In these instances, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is likewise established. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. Moreover, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is also seen in cases such as: "The word 'cow' is impermanent," "The object 'cow' is impermanent," and "The knowledge 'cow' is impermanent. In these instances, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is likewise established. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is also seen in cases such as: "The word 'cow' is a substance," "The object 'cow' is a substance," and "The knowledge 'cow' is a substance. In these instances, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is likewise established. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. Moreover, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is also seen in cases such as: "The word 'cow' is a quality," "The object 'cow' is a quality," and "The knowledge 'cow' is a quality. In these instances, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is likewise established. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is also seen in cases such as: "The word 'cow' is an action," "The object 'cow' is an action," and "The knowledge 'cow' is an action. In these instances, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is likewise established. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. Moreover, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is also seen in cases such as: "The word 'cow' is a universal," "The object 'cow' is a universal," and "The knowledge 'cow' is a universal. In these instances, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is likewise established. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is also seen in cases such as: "The word 'cow' is a particularity," "The object 'cow' is a particularity," and "The knowledge 'cow' is a particularity. In these instances, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is likewise established. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. Moreover, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is also seen in cases such as: "The word 'cow' is inherence," "The object 'cow' is inherence," and "The knowledge 'cow' is inherence. In these instances, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is likewise established. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is also seen in cases such as: "The word 'cow' is non-existence," "The object 'cow' is non-existence," and "The knowledge 'cow' is non-existence. In these instances, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is likewise established. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. Moreover, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is also seen in cases such as: "The word 'cow' is a negation," "The object 'cow' is a negation," and "The knowledge 'cow' is a negation. In these instances, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is likewise established. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is also seen in cases such as: "The word 'cow' is a compound," "The object 'cow' is a compound," and "The knowledge 'cow' is a compound. In these instances, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is likewise established. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. Moreover, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is also seen in cases such as: "The word 'cow' is a sentence," "The object 'cow' is a sentence," and "The knowledge 'cow' is a sentence. In these instances, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is likewise established. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is also seen in cases such as: "The word 'cow' is a phoneme," "The object 'cow' is a phoneme," and "The knowledge 'cow' is a phoneme. In these instances, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is likewise established. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. Moreover, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is also seen in cases such as: "The word 'cow' is a letter," "The object 'cow' is a letter," and "The knowledge 'cow' is a letter. In these instances, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is likewise established. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is also seen in cases such as: "The word 'cow' is a name," "The object 'cow' is a name," and "The knowledge 'cow' is a name. In these instances, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is likewise established. Thus, the conceptual construction of the non-difference of the three is demonstrated. This is the meaning. The conceptual construction of non-difference in cognition regarding the word and the object grasped as "cow" is as follows: thus, in the world, the apprehension of word, object, and cognition—even though they are distinct—should be understood as being observed to occur without separation (*avinirbhāgena*).

If they are apprehended without distinction, how then is there a distinction? To this he says: "And when analyzed by investigators through the methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*), other properties of sound—such as the high-pitched (*udātta*) and so on, which belong to sound as a mere transformation of the *dhvani*—are distinct; others, such as insentience and corporeality, are properties of the object; and others, such as the absence of luminosity and form, are properties of cognition. Therefore, their paths are divided; that is, the way to infer the difference in their essential natures (*svarūpa-bheda*) is distinct."

In that context, it is conceptualized as belonging to one who has attained meditative absorption (*samāpanna*) regarding objects such as a cow. By this, another form of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) for the yogi is stated. The remainder is easy to understand. (1.42)
When memory is purified, [the samādhi] is called *nirvitarka* (free from conceptualization), wherein the form [of the mind] itself becomes void and only the object appears. 1.43.

To apply the Sūtra, he first explains the state free from discursive thought (*nirvitarka*): "But when... Removal (*pariśuddhi*) means elimination. Indeed, scripture (*āgama*) and inference (*anumāna*) proceed preceded by the recollection of linguistic conventions (*saṃketa*). And this convention consists of the mutual superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of word, object, and cognition, such as "this is a cow. Consequently, there arise the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of scriptural and inferential cognitions. Therefore, the wisdom of meditative concentration (*samādhiprajñā*) preceded by that is "with discursive thought" (*savitarka*).

When, however, through the repeated practice of a mind inclined toward the object alone and independent of the mere object, the memory of linguistic conventions—which is invariably concomitant with it—is abandoned; and when that [memory] is abandoned, the conceptual constructions of knowledge derived from scripture and inference, which are rooted in it, are also abandoned; then, in the wisdom of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) which is empty of those [constructions], the object, abiding in its own essential nature alone, is discerned as being merely that essential nature and not by way of a conceptualized form. That is the "attainment without deliberation" (*nirvitarkā samāpatti*).

That [knowledge] of the yogins is supreme perception (*pratyakṣa*), because there is not even a trace of the superimposition of the non-existent. It might be argued: "The yogins, having grasped the reality of the object through another's perception, teach and establish it. But how can that object be taught and established by scripture (*āgama*) and inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), which do not have that [reality] as their domain? Therefore, since scripture and inference have that as their domain and are conceptual (*vikalpa*), the other [yogic] perception must also be merely conceptual. To this he says: "And that [is known] from scripture... [and so on].
