Because of hearing the prohibition "not otherwise," he asks: "And how many are these? The answer is: "Only nine."

He shows these by means of a verse: "Namely—arising," and so forth. Here he states the examples: "In that regard, the cause of arising" and so on. For the mind (*manas*), having removed consciousness (*vijñāna*) from its indeterminate state and brought it into the present state, is the cause of the arising of consciousness. The purpose of the person (*puruṣārthatā*) is the cause of the stability of the mind; for the mind, once produced from the sense of self (*asmitā*), remains only so long as it does not accomplish the two-fold purpose of the person.

Then, once the two purposes of the person have been accomplished, [the mind] departs from its state of persistence. Therefore, for the mind produced from its own cause, the future purpose of the person is the cause of its persistence. He provides an illustration: "as in the case of the body. Just as light is the cause of the manifestation of form through the refinement of the object—whether by means of the senses or directly, serving as the basis for perceptual knowledge—so too another object is the cause of transformation for the mind.

For instance, as soon as Mṛkaṇḍu, whose mind was in a state of meditative concentration, heard the fifth note being played on a lute, his eyes opened; and as he beheld the Apsaras Pramlocā, endowed with beauty, grace, and youth, his mind abandoned its concentration and became attached to her. Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration: just as fire is the cause of a transformation in rice and other grains to be cooked—characterized by the loosening of the conjunction of their hard constituent parts.

The cognition of smoke is the cause of the cognition of fire only when the object [fire] actually exists. "Cognition" (*jñāna*) means that which is known; thus, "fire-cognition" (*agnijñāna*) refers to that which is both fire and a cognition. What is meant is this: it is the cause by virtue of being the cause of the cognition of the fire that is currently present as the object of knowledge. The "attainment" (*prāpti*) is the operation of effects by causes that are generally independent; its "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*) is the failure of that operation due to some exception.

Just as there is an obstruction by a dam to water whose nature is to flow downward, so too here, the attainment (*prāpti*) is the natural capacity of the *buddhi-sattva*—which has the character of pleasure and luminosity—to produce the discernment of pleasure from pain. That [capacity] does not manifest due to some obstruction caused by demerit (*adharma*) or by *tamas*. When that obstruction is removed through merit (*dharma*) or the practice of the limbs of yoga, it attains that [discernment] precisely because its inherent nature is to function unobstructed and thus produce it.

As he will say: "The cause is not the motivator of the *prakṛtis*; rather, from it comes the breaking of the obstruction, as in the case of the farmer. Thus, with reference to the effect characterized by discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), that very [cause] has been described as the cause of attainment. However, with reference to the intermediate effect, that same [cause] is the cause of disjunction; thus he says: "the cause of disjunction."

He states the cause of otherness: "The cause of otherness is, for example, a goldsmith [in relation] to gold, which is both different and non-different from bracelets, earrings, armlets, and so forth. When there is a desire to express its difference, gold is different from the bracelet and such; when there is a desire to express its non-difference, gold is non-different from the bracelet and such. Thus, the goldsmith, who makes the bracelet, is the cause of otherness by producing something other than the gold that is non-different from the earring."

Although fire is also a cause for the alteration of what is to be cooked (*pākyasyānyatvakāraṇam*), nevertheless—since one does not intend to express a difference between the two properties of the substrate (*dharmi*), namely the state of being parched rice (*pulākatva*) and the state of being rice-grains (*taṇḍulatva*)—the substrate persists even when those two properties arise and perish. Thus, it cannot be said that the substrate itself undergoes alteration; rather, it is stated to be merely the cause of a modification (*vikāra*). Therefore, there is no confusion [between the two types of causes]. Furthermore, it should not be explained that "a difference in configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is the cause of the substrate's alteration," because that would render the mention of the "goldsmith" (*suvarṇakāra*) incoherent.

Having presented an external cause for difference, he illustrates an internal one with the words, "In this way, for a single [person]": ignorance is the cognition that "this girl is desirable" and so forth. Due to the connection with that delusion, that very same perception of a woman becomes deluded and dejected for Caitra or Maitra, thinking, "Alas, this jewel of a wife belongs to the meritorious one, but not to me, who am devoid of fortune. In this way, there is hatred toward her on the part of the co-wives; such is the suffering inherent in the perception of a woman.

Thus, for that husband who is full of affection, passion arises toward his wife as an object of pleasure; however, for those who possess discernment, the knowledge of reality—that the female body is a mere aggregate of skin, flesh, fat, bone, and marrow, and is impure by virtue of its location, seed, and so forth—is the cause of equanimity and dispassion. The body is the cause of support for the senses, acting as their sustainer, and the senses are likewise the cause of support for the body; for the common function of the instruments (the senses) consists of the five vital airs, such as prāṇa and the rest, since in their absence the body falls away.

In this same way, there is also a mutual relationship of being supported and supporting among the bodily parts such as flesh and so forth. Likewise, the great elements—earth and the rest—are the supports for the bodies of those dwelling in the worlds of humans, Varuṇa, Sūrya, Gandhavaha, and the Moon, and they themselves are mutually related. For in earth, which possesses the qualities of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound, the five great elements exist in a state of mutual support and supportedness; in water, four; in fire, three; and in air, two.

The animal, human, divine, and other [bodies] exist in a relationship of the supported and the supporter. Now, one might ask: "How can there be such a reality for things that lack the relationship of container and contained? To this he says: "Because they serve each other's purposes. For the human body is sustained by the utility of the bodies of animals, birds, wild beasts, reptiles, and immobile beings. Likewise, the body of a tiger and the like is sustained by the utility of the bodies of humans, domestic animals, wild beasts, and so forth. Similarly, the bodies of domestic animals, wild beasts, and the like are sustained by the utility of immobile beings and so on.

In this way, even the body of a deity, when worshipped with offerings such as the flesh of goats, deer, and *kapiñjala* birds presented by humans, clarified butter, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), mango branches, and bundles of grass, is sustained by that utilization. Likewise, the deity also sustains humans and others through the granting of boons, rain, and so forth. Thus, there is a state of mutual service; this is the meaning. The rest is easy to understand. (2.28)

The eight limbs are restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi). 2.29.

Now, in order to exclude both fewer and more [than the correct] number, he determines the limbs of yoga: "In that regard, the limbs of yoga are determined. The eight limbs are restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi). Practice (abhyāsa), dispassion (vairāgya), faith (śraddhā), vigor (vīrya), and so forth, should also be included within these very same [limbs], according to their respective nature, either by way of their essential form or as being inseparable from them. 2.29.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the restraints (yamāḥ). ||2.30||

Having indicated the limbs beginning with *yama* and *niyama*, he introduces the Sūtra defining *yama* with the word "therein" (*tatra*). He states that non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), truthfulness (*satya*), non-stealing (*asteya*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*) are the *yamas*. He speaks of non-violence as a limb of yoga with the word "in every way" (*sarvathā*). He praises such non-violence with the words "and the subsequent [limbs] also" (*uttare ca*). The phrase "having that as their root" means that even if they are performed, they are as if unperformed because they are fruitless if non-violence is not maintained; thus, their practice is solely for the sake of its perfection.

If non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the root of the subsequent [virtues], how is it that they are for the sake of the perfection of non-violence? To this he says: "for the purpose of establishing that. The meaning is that "perfection" (*siddhi*) refers to knowledge, not to origination. This might be the case: if the subsequent [virtues] are for the sake of the knowledge of non-violence, then what is the use of them, since that [knowledge] is understood from other sources? To this he says: "purified by that. The meaning is that if the subsequent [virtues] were not practiced, non-violence would be defiled by untruthfulness (*asatya*) and so forth. On this very point, he states the consensus of those who follow the scriptures (*āgamika*): "And thus..."

This is easy to understand. He states the definition of truth: "Speech and mind are in accordance with reality. He completes the elliptical expression "in accordance with" [reality] by saying, "as it was perceived. He supplies the correlative term "so" by stating, "and so too are speech and mind when there is a desire to speak."

Otherwise, however, this would not be true; he states it with a supporting argument: speech is uttered and spoken for the sake of transferring one's own cognition to another person, or for generating a cognition similar to one's own cognition. Therefore, if that [speech] is not deceptive—that is, not a deceiver—then consider the case of the teacher Droṇa, who, when asked by Yudhiṣṭhira, "O long-lived one, is Aśvatthāman, whose wealth is truth, dead?", replied "Aśvatthāman is dead" while intending the elephant. This is an example of a response to what was said.

It does not transmit Yudhiṣṭhira’s own cognition—since his own cognition regarding the killing of the elephant was produced by the senses—nor has that [cognition] been transmitted; rather, a different cognition altogether has arisen for him regarding the killing of his son. Furthermore, it is either erroneous or born of error; and this error occurs either at the time of the intention to speak or at the time of determining the object to be known.

"Barren of practice" (*pratipatti-vandhyā*) means useless with respect to the goal, like a Mleccha language; or it may mean purposeless, as when speech expresses what is not required. For in such a case, even the transmission of one's own understanding to another is effectively no transmission at all, because it serves no purpose. Thus, he says "this" (*eṣā*) to show that even truth characterized in this way is a mere semblance of truth (*satyābhāsa*), having the result of harming others, and is not true truth.

For example, when Satyatapas was asked by thieves whether he was traveling with a caravan, he replied that he was traveling with a caravan. "Abhidhīyamānā" means being uttered or spoken. The rest is easy to understand. Since non-existence (*abhāva*) is defined in dependence upon existence (*bhāva*), he states the definition of theft: "Theft is that which is not preceded by the scriptures. The meaning is that the general is indicated by the particular. Because verbal and physical activities are preceded by mental activity, the mental operation is stated as primary; thus, it is described as having the form of "non-covetousness" (*aspṛhā*).

He states the essential nature of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) with the word "guarded" (*gupta*). For even one whose organ of generation is restrained is not truly celibate if he is attached to looking at women, conversing with them, visiting temples of the god of love (*Kandarpa*), or touching their limbs; therefore, it is said "of one whose senses are guarded" (*guptendriyasya*) to exclude such behavior. This implies that the other senses as well must be protected from longing for those objects. He states the essential nature of non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*) with the words "of objects" (*viṣayāṇām*).

In this regard, the fault of attachment has been stated: "Passions and the skillfulness of the senses increase in accordance with the practice of enjoyments. Furthermore, there is the fault characterized by violence, for enjoyment is not possible without harming living beings. Since one observes the fault in the acquisition of objects—even those that come unbidden and are not prescribed by scripture—such as through censurable acceptance and the like, and since one observes the faults of protecting and so forth even those objects acquired in accordance with scripture, non-acceptance is *aparigraha*. (2.30)
Unrestricted by birth, place, time, or circumstance, these universal vows constitute the Great Vow (mahāvrata). 2.31.

Having stated [the restraints] in general, he introduces the sūtra—"But those..."—to explain what kind of restraints are to be adopted by yogins: "Unrestricted by class, place, time, or circumstance, they are universal; this is the great vow. Universal means known across all stages (*bhūmi*) characterized by class and so forth. That non-violence and the others are also restricted in other ways should be inferred. The commentary is easy to understand. (2.31)
Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (niyamas). 2.32.

He explains the observances (*niyama*) such as purity and so forth: "Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances. He explains [the first]: "Purity. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), cow-dung and other such items are included. This refers to the consumption of pure substances such as cow-urine and barley-gruel (*yāvaka*). From the word "and so forth," the rules regarding the size and number of morsels, etc., are to be understood. Although it should have been stated as "produced by the consumption of pure substances and so forth," it is stated as "the consumption of pure substances and so forth" because the cause is figuratively applied to the effect.

The impurities of the mind are intoxication, pride, envy, and so forth; their removal is mental purity (*manaḥśauca*). Contentment (*saṃtoṣa*) is the lack of desire for anything in excess of what is necessary merely to sustain life, let alone for what has already been acquired or rejected—this is the remainder [of the definition]. Wooden silence (*kāṣṭhamauna*) is the non-manifestation of one’s own intention even by gesture. Verbal silence (*ākāramauna*) is the mere absence of speech. "With the web of discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) completely destroyed"—discursive thought will be explained below, or it refers to doubt and error. By this much, pure intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) has been described. And these restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) are stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:

"The seeker of yoga, free from desire, should practice celibacy, non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and non-possessiveness, thereby leading his own mind toward fitness. With self-restraint, he should perform study, purity, contentment, and austerity, so that his mind may be inclined toward the Supreme Brahman. These five restraints (yamas) and five observances (niyamas) have been proclaimed; when performed with desire, they yield specific fruits, but for those free from desire, they grant liberation. (2.32)
The cultivation of the antidote for the obstruction of discursive thought. 2.33.

Regarding the saying, “Prosperous undertakings have many obstacles,” he introduces the following sūtra, which is intended to teach the remedies for those obstacles when they arise: “Of these restraints and observances... The sūtra states: “When there is affliction by discursive thoughts (vitarka), one should cultivate their opposites. Regarding these discursive thoughts, there is nothing in the commentary that remains obscure. (2.33)

For thoughts such as violence and the like—whether performed, caused to be performed, or approved; whether preceded by greed, anger, or delusion; and whether mild, moderate, or intense—result in endless fruits of suffering and ignorance; this is the cultivation of the counter-measures. (2.34)

In this regard, with the intention of explaining the nature of the cultivation of the counter-measures (pratipakṣabhāvanā), [the author] states in a sutra the distinctions of the essential nature, types, causes, qualities, and results of discursive thoughts (vitarka), as well as their objects and the cultivation of their counter-measures: "Discursive thoughts, such as violence and so forth—whether performed, caused to be performed, or approved; whether preceded by greed, anger, or delusion; whether mild, moderate, or intense—have as their endless results suffering and ignorance; this is the cultivation of the counter-measure. He explains this with the words: "In that context, violence... and so on.

Since the varieties of living beings are innumerable, rules, options, and combinations are possible regarding acts such as violence (*hiṃsā*). Among these, when demerit (*adharma*) arises due to a predominance of *tamas*, ignorance (*ajñāna*), characterized by the fourfold error, also emerges; thus, these [acts] have ignorance as their fruit. Indeed, the cultivation of the opposites [of these acts] has as its result the endless cessation of suffering and ignorance, because one desists from them through the power of that cultivation.

This very point clarifies the cultivation of the counteragent: first, by means of tethering to the sacrificial post, one strikes away the vigor—the effort that is the cause of bodily activity—of the animal to be slaughtered. For by that means, the animal becomes devoid of boldness. The rest is very clear. (2.34)
When non-violence is firmly established, hostility ceases in his presence. (2.35)

The restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) have been stated, as well as their abandonment through the cultivation of counter-measures against the discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) that oppose them. Now, he introduces the signs indicating the thorough knowledge of their perfection resulting from the unimpeded practice of the restraints and observances—by knowing which, the yogi, having accomplished his purpose in each case, proceeds toward what remains to be done. He says: "When... (referring to the counter-measures). "Upon the firm establishment of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), there is the cessation of enmity in its presence."

Even those who are eternally hostile, such as horses and buffaloes, mice and cats, snakes and mongooses, abandon their enmity upon coming into the presence of the Blessed One, who has established non-violence, because they come to mirror his state of mind. (2.35)
When truth is established, there is the state of being the locus for the fruits of action. 2.36.

In the establishment of truth lies the state of being the locus for the fruits of action. Dharma and adharma are accomplished through action; likewise, heaven, hell, and so forth are their fruits. That which serves as the locus for these is the "locus" (āśraya); the state of being such a locus is its "nature" (tattva). This is the quality of the speech of this Blessed One. He states that it is the locus of action with the word "the righteous one" (dhārmikaḥ); he states that it is the locus of the fruit with the word "heaven" (svargam). It is unfailing and unimpeded. (2.36)
When non-stealing is firmly established, all jewels present themselves. 2.37.
When non-stealing is firmly established, all jewels present themselves; this is easily understood. 2.37.
When established in the holy life, there is the attainment of vigor. ||2.38||

Upon the establishment of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), there is the attainment of vigor (*vīrya*). Vigor is capability; by the attainment of which one enhances and accumulates unimpeded qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest. And having attained [these], being endowed with the eight perfections (*siddhi*)—such as *tārā* and so forth, also known by other names such as *ūha* and so on—one becomes capable of instilling in those to be trained, namely the disciples, knowledge concerning yoga and its ancillaries. || 2.38 ||
For those established in non-possessiveness, there is the awakening to the nature of birth and its origins. ||2.39||

For one established in non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*), there is the thorough understanding of the "how" of birth (*janmakathaṃtā-saṃbodha*). Birth is the connection with a specific class of body, sense organs, and so forth; its "how" is its particular mode. Its thorough understanding is its direct realization—that is to say, the complete knowledge of birth in all its modes, whether it be past, present, or future, and whether it be beyond the senses, quiescent, arisen, or yet to be designated. One desires to know the past: "Who was I? One desires to know the specific modalities of that very [past self] regarding its arising and duration: "How was I?"

He desires to know the nature of the present birth: "What indeed?"—is the body merely an aggregate of the elements, or is it something other than them? Here too, the phrase "how indeed" (*kathaṃ svid*) is to be supplied. In some recensions, however, it is actually read. He desires to know the future: "And who shall we become? Here too, the phrase "how indeed" is to be supplied. Thus [the question] "of this [birth]."

The "prior limit" is past time, the "subsequent limit" is the future, and the "middle" is the present; the "state of the self" (bhāva) in relation to these is its connection with the body and so forth. There is an inquiry into that, and from that, knowledge arises—according to the maxim: "He who desires something does that [to attain it]. (2.39)
From purification comes disgust for one's own body and non-association with others. 2.40.
From purity comes self-disgust for one's own body and non-association with others; by this, the accomplishment of external purity is indicated. (2.40)
And [the results are] purity of being, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery over the senses, and fitness for the vision of the Self. 2.41.

He states what indicates the attainment of internal purity: "And furthermore... [namely]: purity of *sattva*, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery over the senses, and fitness for the vision of the Self. When the impurities of the mind are washed away, the pure *sattva* of the mind manifests; from that purity comes cheerfulness (*saumanasya*), which is clarity. Being clear, it becomes one-pointed. From that, because the senses are dependent on the mind, there is mastery over them through such mastery. Thereafter, the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi*) attains fitness for the vision of the Self. (2.41)
From contentment comes the attainment of unsurpassed happiness. (2.42)

From contentment comes the attainment of unsurpassed happiness. It is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttama*) because there exists nothing superior to it. As was said by Yayāti when he offered his youth to Pūru: "The wise man, by completely abandoning that craving which is so difficult for the foolish to relinquish and which does not age even as one ages, is filled with happiness."
He demonstrates this very point with the words: "And whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world," and so forth (2.42).
The perfection of the sense of touch results from the destruction of impurities through austerity. 2.43.

He states that which indicates the perfection of austerity: "The perfection of the body and the senses results from the destruction of impurity through austerity. Impurity is characterized by obscuration, consisting of tamasic qualities such as unrighteousness (*adharma*) and the like. [The perfections are] *aṇimā* and the others, namely *mahimā*, *laghimā*, and *prāpti*. This is easy to understand. (2.43)
From the private recitation of sacred texts comes communion with one's chosen deity. 2.44.
He states that which indicates the perfection of self-study: "From self-study comes communion with the chosen deity. This is easy to understand. (2.44)
Success in samādhi comes from devotion to the Lord. 2.45.

The perfection of samādhi results from devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna). Nor should it be argued that if the perfection of the cognitive (saṃprajñāta) samādhi—the primary factor—arises from devotion to the Lord alone, then the seven ancillaries (aṅgas) are redundant; for they are useful through their intermediate operation, whether visible or invisible, in bringing about the perfection of devotion to the Lord. And regarding the perfection of the cognitive samādhi, [the ancillaries serve] both as means to the ritual act and as means to the human goal, by virtue of the principle of "separateness of connection" (saṃyogapṛthaktva), just as curd serves both purposes.

Nor is it the case that concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*) are not "inner limbs" (*antaraṅga*) for the attainment of cognitive (*saṃprajñāta*) samādhi; for, because they share the same object as cognitive samādhi, this [triad] is understood to be inner relative to the other limbs which do not share that object. Furthermore, devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) has the Lord as its object and not the object of cognition; thus it is an outer limb (*bahiraṅga*). Everything is thus clarified. The etymological derivation of the word *prajñā* as "that by which one discerns" (*prajānāti*) has been shown. (2.45)
Posture is that which is steady and comfortable. 2.46.

He introduces the subsequent aphorism: "The restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), along with their [attendant] perfections, have been explained. We shall now speak of the postures (āsana) and so forth. Among these—'A posture is firm and pleasant. The meaning of the aphorism is that a posture is that which is firm (*sthira*), meaning motionless, and pleasant (*sukha*), meaning conducive to ease. It is called 'posture' (*āsana*) because one sits (*āsyate*) upon it or by means of it. He states its divisions: 'For example,' etc. The lotus-posture (*padmāsana*) is well known."

Standing with one foot placed on the ground and the other placed above the bent knee—this is *vīrāsana*. Having placed the soles of the feet together near the scrotum, one should place the hands in the shape of a tortoise (*kacchapikā*) upon them; that is *bhadrāsana*. One should place the left bent foot between the right calf and thigh, and the right bent foot between the left calf and thigh; this is *svastika*.

Sitting down with the fingers joined and the ankles joined, one should practice the staff posture (*daṇḍāsana*) by extending the shins, thighs, and feet so that they touch the ground. By means of employing a yoga-band, it becomes the supported posture (*sopāśraya*). The bed posture (*paryaṅka*) consists of lying down with the arms extended over the knees. The crane-sitting (*krauñcaniṣadana*) and other such postures are to be understood from observing the physical positions of cranes and other birds as they sit.

The mutual pressing together of the two [feet] when both are bent, with the heels and the tips of the toes, is the "even posture. That posture in which stability and ease are achieved for one who remains established is the "firm and easy" seat (*sthirasukham āsanam*). This is the view of the Blessed Sūtra-author; its explanation is given by the words "at ease" (*yathāsukham*). (2.46)
By relaxation of effort and by meditative absorption in the infinite. 2.47.

Having described the essential nature of posture (*āsana*), he states its means of accomplishment: "Through relaxation of effort and meditative absorption in the Infinite. For natural effort merely sustains the body; it is not the cause of the posture to be taught as a limb of yoga. If that [natural effort] were its cause, instruction would be useless, as the posture would be established by its own inherent nature alone. Therefore, this innate effort is neither a means for the posture to be taught nor is it compatible with it; because it serves as the cause for casual postures, it obstructs the prescribed regulation of posture.

Therefore, by one practicing the instructed posture, an effort must be made for the sake of relaxing natural exertion; otherwise, the instructed posture is not accomplished. Thus, the relaxation of natural exertion is the cause of success in posture. Alternatively, when the mind is absorbed in Ananta, the lord of serpents, upon whose thousand most steady hoods the circle of the earth is supported, the posture is perfected. 2.47.
From that follows non-affliction by the pairs of opposites. 2.48.
He states that which indicates mastery over posture: "Then there is no affliction from the pairs of opposites. The commentary is self-explanatory. Posture is also described in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Having thus assumed the Bhadrāsana and other postures, endowed with their qualities. (2.48)
When that [posture] is present, the cessation of the flow of inhalation and exhalation is breath control (prāṇāyāma). 2.49.

Immediately after [the description of] posture (*āsana*), showing that breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is preceded by it, he states its definition: "When that [posture] exists, the cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation is breath control. This is the general definition of breath control, because there is a cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation in exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*). To illustrate: in inhalation, where external air is drawn in and held within, there is a cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation.

Even in exhalation (recaka), where the abdominal air is expelled and held outside, there is a cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation; the same applies to retention (kumbhaka). This is stated in the commentary: "When the posture [is mastered]," etc. (2.49).
The flow of the breath, characterized by external and internal suspension, is observed in terms of place, time, and number; it becomes long and subtle. (2.50)

He introduces the sūtra defining the three specific types of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the words "But that... [YS 2.50]: "Having external, internal, or suppressed movement, regulated by place, time, and number, it is long and subtle. The word *vṛtti* (movement) is connected to each [term]. He describes exhalation (*recaka*) with the words "where there is exhalation" [YS 2.51]. He describes inhalation (*pūraka*) with the words "where there is inhalation" [YS 2.51]. He describes the third, retention (*kumbhaka*), with the words "the third" [YS 2.51].

He clarifies that very point: where there occurs the simultaneous cessation of both inhalation and exhalation through a single effort of restraint, and not—as before—the effort of restraining the flood of the filling-in breath, nor the effort of restraining the flood of the exhaling breath.

However, just as water placed upon a heated stone dries up entirely and undergoes contraction, so too this air, though mobile by nature, has its movement obstructed by a powerful restraining effort; it remains within the body itself in a subtle state, neither filling it—which would constitute *pūraka*—nor emptying it—which would constitute *recaka*.

Its location and field of operation (*viṣaya*) are as follows: externally, it consists of a windless space measured by a span, a cubit, a forearm, and so forth, inferred from the movement of blades of grass, cotton, and the like; internally, it extends from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, inferred by a tactile sensation similar to the touch of an ant. Its temporal limit is a *kṣaṇa*, which is one-fourth of the time taken for the act of closing the eyes, defined by the determination of its duration.

Having touched one's own knee-circle three times with the hand, the time delimited by a finger-snap (*cchoṭikā*) is a *mātrā*. The first *udghāta* (upward breath-exertion), measured by thirty-six such *mātrās*, is gentle (*mṛdu*). That same [exertion] doubled is the second, moderate (*madhyama*). That same [exertion] tripled is the third, intense (*tīvra*). He describes this breath-restraint (*prāṇāyāma*), which is observed through counting, as "by numbers" (*saṃkhyābhiḥ*).

For a person in a state of health, the time of a finger-snap as previously described is equal to the time delimited by the activity of inhalation and exhalation. When the *udghāta* has been brought to the state of being performed, it is "conquered," meaning it is mastered, controlled, and restrained. A specific measure of moments is intended here as the duration; there is some distinction in that the number refers to the measure of inhalations and exhalations. This very practice, when cultivated daily, becomes "long" by pervading an accumulation of space and time through the sequence of days, fortnights, months, and so forth.
And because it is to be attained through supreme skill, it is "subtle," but not because of sluggishness. (2.50)
The fourth [type of breath restraint] is that which projects the objects both externally and internally. 2.51.

Thus, three specific types [of breath control] have been characterized. He characterizes the fourth: "The fourth involves the projection of external and internal objects. He explains: "By means of place, time, and number. "Projected" means displaced from the form mastered through practice; that too is long and subtle. Preceded by that, the breath control (prāṇāyāma) involving external and internal objects is preceded by the observation of place, time, and number.

And this fourth [state] does not arise immediately through a single effort like the third; rather, being practiced, it comes about through the successive mastery of each respective stage. Thus he says: "from the mastery of the stages" (*bhūmijayāt*). Now, one might ask: since the absence of movement exists even in the state of the pillar (*stambhavṛtti*), what is the distinction of this [fourth state] from that? To this he says: "the third. The third is that which is preceded by non-observation and accomplished through a single effort.

The fourth [type of breath], however, is preceded by mental visualization (*ālocana*) and must be accomplished with great effort; this is the distinction. The meaning is that while the scope of the former two—the *pūraka* and *recaka*—is not visualized, this one is visualized in terms of place, time, and number. (2.51)
Thereupon, the veil over the light is destroyed. (2.52)

He states the intermediate purpose of *prāṇāyāma*: "From that, the covering of light is destroyed. That by which the light of the *sattva* of the intellect is covered is a "covering" (*āvaraṇa*), namely, the afflictions (*kleśa*) and sin (*pāpman*). He explains [the compound] as "of the *prāṇāyāmas*. That by which something is known is "knowledge" (*jñāna*), which is the light of the *sattva* of the intellect; the knowledge of discrimination is "discriminative knowledge" (*vivekajñāna*). That which covers discriminative knowledge is "that which covers discriminative knowledge" (*vivekajñānāvaraṇīya*).

Since the formation of words such as *bhavya*, *geya*, and *pravacanīya* is intended to illustrate their derivation in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), here too the *kṛtya* suffix denotes the agent, just as in the case of *kopanīya* and *rañjanīya*. By the word "action" (*karman*), it indicates both the demerit (*apuṇya*) produced by that action and its cause, which is the affliction (*kleśa*). Regarding this very point, he states the consensus of the followers of the Āgamas with the phrase "which they call that. "Great delusion" (*mahāmoha*) is passion (*rāga*); ignorance (*avidyā*), which exists inseparably from it, is also included by the mention of that [delusion]. "What should not be done" (*akārya*) is non-dharma (*adharma*).

Now, one might object: "If *prāṇāyāma* alone destroys evil, then what is the use of austerity (*tapas*)? To this he says: "It becomes weak. This means that it is not destroyed entirely; therefore, austerity is required for its complete destruction. Regarding this point as well, he states the consensus of those who follow the scriptures: "And so it has been said. Manu also says: "One should burn away defects by means of *prāṇāyāmas*.
The status of *prāṇāyāma* as a limb of yoga is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:

"He who, through practice, brings the vital air called *prāṇa* under control—that is to be known as *prāṇāyāma*, both with seed (*sabīja*) and without seed (*abīja*). When the two vital airs, *prāṇa* and *apāna*, mutually overcome each other according to that method, that is the third [type] resulting from their restraint. (2.52)
And there is fitness of the mind for the meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās). ||2.53||
Furthermore: "And there is fitness of the mind for the concentrations (dhāraṇās). For breath control (prāṇāyāma), by steadying the mind, renders it fit for the concentrations. (2.53)
Pratyāhāra (withdrawal) is the imitation, as it were, by the senses of the nature of the mind when they are not in contact with their own objects. 2.54.

Thus, having been refined by the restraints (yama) and other practices, he begins withdrawal (pratyāhāra) for the sake of concentration. To introduce the aphorism defining it, he asks: "Now" (atha). Withdrawal is the state of the senses as if conforming to the nature of the mind when they are not in contact with their own objects.

The mind also does not come into contact with objects such as sounds that are deluding, pleasing, or provoking; because of that non-contact, the eyes and other senses likewise do not come into contact. This is the imitation of the nature of the mind by the senses. Furthermore, since the reality to which the mind becomes attached is not something external for the senses, there is also a non-imitation. Therefore it is said: "as if an imitation."

By means of the locative case, he shows that the common property of non-association with its own objects is the cause for the mind’s imitation [of the senses], using the word "sva" (its own). He explains this imitation with the words "cittanirodhe" (in the cessation of the mind). The similarity consists in the fact that the effort which is the cause of the cessation of both is identical. Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration: "yathā madhukararājam" (just as the king of bees). He applies this to the subject of the example with the word "tathā" (so too). On this point also, there is a statement from the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "The knower of yoga, devoted to withdrawal (pratyāhāra), having restrained the senses attached to sound and other objects, should make them imitate the mind."
Its purpose is shown in that very same place:
"By means of that, supreme mastery over the senses arises for those of steady mind; one who has no mastery over them is not a practitioner of yoga. (2.54)
Thereafter follows the supreme mastery over the senses. 2.55.

(Thus ends the second chapter, the Sādhanapāda, in the *Yogasūtras* composed by the venerable Patañjali. The sūtra that restates this is: "From that [practice], there arises supreme mastery over the senses. Now, one might ask: are there not other, non-supreme forms of mastery over the senses, in relation to which this is called "supreme"? Indeed, he shows them: "In regard to sound and the other [objects]. He explains this very point: "Attachment, passion, and addiction. By what derivation (*vyutpatti*)? It is so called because it casts away, hurries away, or rejects one from the highest good (*śreyas*). The absence of that is non-addiction (*avyasana*), which is mastery.

He describes another form of mastery (*vaśyatā*): "Non-contradiction" (*aviruddhā*) means the practice of sound and other objects that are not opposed to scripture and so forth, and the non-engagement with those things that are opposed to them; for that alone is "righteous" (*nyāyyā*), since it does not deviate from reason (*nyāya*). He describes yet another form of mastery: "The contact of the senses with sound and so forth" (*śabdādisaṃprayoga*). The meaning is that this contact of the senses with sound and other objects—which are to be enjoyed according to one's own will—is indeed independent (*svatantra*), and not dependent on the objects themselves (*bhogyatantra*).

He describes another form of mastery: "Some say that in the absence of passion and aversion, there is a cognition of sound and so forth through equanimity, devoid of pleasure and pain. He states the mastery intended by the author of the Sūtras and approved by the Supreme Sage: "Jaigīṣavya says it is simply the non-functioning of the mind along with the senses toward sound and so forth due to one-pointedness of mind. He declares this to be the supreme form: "But the supreme... The word "but" distinguishes this from the other forms of mastery.

For other forms of subjugation (*vaśyatā*) do not eliminate the fear of contact with the poison of the afflictions (*kleśa*), since they involve association with the venomous serpents that are the sense-objects. Indeed, even one who is highly skilled in the science of poisons and has brought a serpent under his control does not sleep confidently while placing the serpent on his lap. This particular subjugation, however, is called "supreme" because it is free from all entanglement with sense-objects and is thus devoid of fear; it is not like the other types of mastery over the senses.

The meaning is that, just as in the stage of "conception through effort" (yatamāna-saṃjñā), even when one sense-organ has been conquered, one requires a further effort to conquer the other sense-organs, it is not so in the cessation of the mind (citta-nirodha); for the cessation of the external organs does not require a separate effort. ||2.55||

In this [first] quarter [of the Yoga-sūtras], he has taught the yoga of action (kriyāyoga), the afflictions (kleśas), the ripening of karmas, their nature as suffering, and likewise the fivefold divisions [of the limbs] of yoga. Thus [ends the first quarter]. ||1||
Thus ends the second chapter, the Sādhanapāda, in this commentary on the Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra Bhāṣya composed by the venerable Vācaspati Miśra.
Therein begins the third chapter, the Vibhūtipāda.
Binding the mind to a place is dhāraṇā (concentration). 3.1.

By means of the first and second quarters [of the Yoga Sūtra], meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and its means were explained. In the third quarter, the supernormal powers (*vibhūtayaḥ*), which are the causes for generating faith conducive to the practice of that [absorption], must be discussed. These [powers] are to be accomplished through *saṃyama*. Since *saṃyama* is the aggregate of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*), these three limbs are presented here in order to distinguish them as "inner" (*antaraṅga*) limbs—by virtue of being the means for attaining the supernormal powers—as opposed to the five other limbs of yoga, which are "outer" (*bahiraṅga*).

Furthermore, since *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* possess a fixed sequence of priority based on their relationship as cause and effect, they are presented in that order. Thus, he says "they have been stated" (*uktāni*), indicating that *dhāraṇā* must first be defined. *Dhāraṇā* is the binding of the mind to a location (*deśabandhaś cittasya*). He specifies an internal location: "the navel-center" (*nābhicakra*) and so forth; by the word "etc.," the palate and other such sites are to be understood. *Bandha* means connection. He specifies an external location: "external" (*bāhya*).

Furthermore, it has been stated that no connection with the mind is possible for external objects in their own form; rather, [the connection occurs] through a mental mode (*vṛtti*) alone, that is, through mere cognition. Regarding this, there is also a Purāṇic passage:

"Having brought the breath under control by means of *prāṇāyāma* and the senses by means of *pratyāhāra*, one should thereafter establish the mind upon an auspicious support. The "auspicious supports" (*śubhāśraya*) are external, such as Hiraṇyagarbha, Vāsava, Prajāpati, and so forth. And this is stated therein:

"The embodied form of the Blessed One, which is free from desire for any support—this indeed should be known as *dhāraṇā*, wherein the mind is fixed. And that embodied form of Hari which is to be meditated upon, O lord of men, let that be heard; for a supportless *dhāraṇā* is not possible. [It is] with a serene face, eyes resembling the petals of a beautiful lotus, fine cheeks, and radiant with a broad forehead-slab; adorned with beautiful earrings placed as far as the ears."

One should meditate upon Him who has a neck like a conch shell, a chest marked with the broad Śrīvatsa, and a belly with a sunken navel and three folds; who is Viṣṇu with eight long arms—or even four arms—with thighs and shanks standing straight, and feet like excellent lotuses in the svastika posture; who is the embodiment of Brahman, clothed in pure yellow garments, adorned with a crown, beautiful armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments, and equipped with the Śārṅga bow, discus, mace, sword, conch, and a rosary of beads.

"The yogi, having concentrated his own mind, should contemplate [the object] with total absorption until, O King, concentration (*dhāraṇā*) becomes firmly established in that very place. Whether he remains in this state or performs other actions according to his will, when the mind does not depart, then he should consider that concentration perfected. (3.1)
In that regard, meditation (dhyāna) is the one-pointed continuity of the cognition. 3.2.

He defines meditation (*dhyāna*), which is to be accomplished through concentration (*dhāraṇā*): "Meditation is the one-pointedness of the mental state (*pratyaya*) upon that [object]. One-pointedness means single-mindedness. The commentary is easy to understand. Regarding this as well, there is a Purāṇa passage:
"O King, that meditation—which is a continuous flow of one-pointed mental states having that [object] as its form and free from longing for anything else—is accomplished by the first six limbs. (3.2)
That very [state] in which only the object appears, as if devoid of its own nature, is samādhi. (3.3)

He characterizes the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that is to be accomplished through meditation (*dhyāna*): "That very [meditation], when only the object appears and it is as if devoid of its own nature, is meditative absorption. He explains: "Meditation itself... [and so on]. "Appearing in the form of the object of meditation" means that only the form of the object of meditation appears, not the form of the meditation itself. For this very reason, he says: "empty. Now, if it is empty, how can the object of meditation be manifested? To this he says: "as if" (*iva*). He states the reason for this very point: "due to the penetration of the intrinsic nature of the object of meditation. On this point also, there is a Purāṇa:
"That very grasping of its own nature, free from conceptual construction, which is to be accomplished by the mind through meditation—that is designated as samādhi."

The meaning is that conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is the distinction between the object of meditation and the act of meditating; [the state] free from that is what is intended. Having explained the eightfold yoga to Khāṇḍikya, Keśidhvaja concluded:

"The knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is the agent, and knowledge is the instrument; once that insentient instrument has accomplished the task of liberation, it ceases to function, having fulfilled its purpose. (3.3)
The three together in one place constitute *saṃyama*. (3.4)

Since there would be the burden of pronouncing individual technical names for each of these three—*dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*—when they are applied here and there, he introduces a definitional aphorism (*paribhāṣā-sūtra*) for the sake of brevity: "The three together in one place is *saṃyama*. He explains: "having a single object" (*ekaviṣayāṇi*), referring to the phrase "that very thing" (*tad etad*). He removes the suspicion that this term might be a mere synonym by saying: "it belongs to that" (*tad asya*). That treatise (*tantra*) by which yoga is strung together (*tantryate*) and explained is the *tantra*; that which arises from such a treatise is *tāntrikī*.
The locations of the application of *saṃyama* are such as "from *saṃyama* on the three transformations," and so forth. (3.4)
From the conquest of that, there is the light of wisdom. 3.5.

He states the fruit of the practice and means for the conquest of that [mind]: "From its conquest, there is the light of wisdom. The "light" of wisdom is its abiding in a stainless flow, unoverpowered by other mental modifications. The commentary is easy to understand. (3.5)
Its application is to the stages. 3.6.

But where is the fruit of this *saṃyama* when it has been applied? To this he says: "Its application is upon the stages (*bhūmi*s). The author of the Commentary specifies the stage with the word "its": application is upon that stage which is immediately subsequent to the stage already mastered—that is, upon the state not yet mastered by *saṃyama*. When the *samādhi* accompanied by deliberation (*savitarka*) regarding gross objects has been brought under control through *saṃyama*, there is application of *saṃyama* to the *samādhi* free from deliberation (*nirvitarka*), which is not yet mastered. When that too has been brought under control, there is application to the *samādhi* accompanied by reflection (*savicāra*).

Thus, the meaning is that there is application to the state of *nirvicāra* (reflection-free). For this very reason, once the attainment of the gross object has been accomplished, the *Purāṇa* introduces the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) upon a subtle object by means of the removal of their respective weapons and ornaments.

"Then the wise one should contemplate the form of the Blessed One as peaceful, devoid of the conch, mace, discus, Śārṅga bow, and other [attributes], yet holding a rosary. When concentration becomes firmly established upon that, he should then remember Him as devoid of ornaments such as the crown and armlets. Then the wise one should again regard the Lord as a single limb, thinking 'I am He'; thereafter, he should become intent on the meditative resolve 'I am [He]'" (iti).

Why, then, does one conquer the higher stage after conquering the lower stage, and why does the reverse not occur? To this he says: "For one has not conquered the lower stage. Indeed, one who sets out for the Gaṅgā from a rocky ravine does not reach the Gaṅgā without first reaching Meghavana. And as for the phrase "of one who has conquered the higher stage through the grace of the Lord," it is because that purpose—the conquest of the higher stage—is understood to be imminent precisely through the practice of devotion to the Lord (*īśvara-praṇidhāna*) alone.

"For an instrument that does not produce any further distinction once its function has been accomplished would overstep the very logic of being an instrument. This might be asked: "Even if the various intermediate stages are understood in general through scripture, how is their sequence of priority and posteriority known? To this he says: "Of this stage... The preceding yoga has been mastered; it is the cause for the arising and attainment of knowledge regarding the subsequent yoga. This should be understood with the intention that the state itself is the possessor of the state. (3.6)
The triad is more internal than the preceding ones. 3.7.

But why, even though there is no difference in their being limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*), is *saṃyama* applied here and there while the other five are not? To this he says: "The triad is internal compared to the preceding ones. This means that these three means of accomplishment are internal because their object is identical to that of the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), whereas the restraints (*yama*) and so forth are not thus; therefore, they are external. (3.7)
Even that is external for one who is seedless. ||3.8||

The three means of accomplishment are internal factors only with respect to *samprajñāta* [samādhi], but not with respect to *asamprajñāta*; for the latter is seedless and thus lacks the same object of focus as those means, and because it arises only after those means have long since ceased and after the supreme detachment—which is another name for the ultimate limit of *samprajñāta* and consists in the clarity of knowledge—has occurred. Thus he says: "That too is external to the seedless."

In this context, having established that having a common object (*samānaviṣayatva*) is the determinant of being "internal" (*antaraṅga*), and not its immediate succession—because the latter is subject to deviation since it occurs even in the case of the external practice of devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*)—it follows that although the definition of being internal may be subject to deviation, immediate succession does not apply here. Therefore, it is stated "because [the result] exists in its absence" (YS 3.8) in order to show that the state of being internal is far removed from *saṃyama* with respect to *asaṃprajñāta* samādhi.

The transformation of cessation (nirodha-pariṇāma) is the sequence of moments of consciousness during cessation, characterized by the suppression of the saṃskāras of emergence and the manifestation of the saṃskāras of cessation. (3.9)

In the context of the sūtra "From saṃyama upon the three transformations" (YS 3.16), wishing to explain the three transformations that are about to be employed, he asks "Now" (atha) by way of introducing the seedless [samādhi]. Since the differences in the increasingly clearer transformations of the mind during the states of active fluctuation (vyutthāna) and cognitive samādhi (saṃprajñāta) are experienced, no question would arise there; however, in the state of cessation (nirodha), transformation is not perceived. Yet, the meaning is that what is not being perceived does not necessarily not exist, because since the mind consists of the three guṇas and is mobile, it is impossible for the guṇas to remain untransformed even for a single moment.

The Sūtra on Question and Answer: The transformation of cessation (*nirodha-pariṇāma*) consists in the succession of moments of the mind during cessation, characterized by the suppression of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence and the manifestation of the latent impressions of cessation. With respect to the *asaṃprajñāta* samādhi, the *saṃprajñāta* state is "emergence" (*vyutthāna*). That by which [the mind] is ceased is "cessation" (*nirodha*), which is the clarity of knowledge (*jñānaprasāda*), namely supreme detachment (*para-vairāgya*). Of these two—the latent impressions of emergence and the latent impressions of cessation—there is the suppression of the former and the manifestation of the latter.

In this regard, there is the suppression of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of emergence and the manifestation of the latent impression of cessation; this is the persistence (*anvaya*) of the two states within the substratum (*dharmin*) of the mind during the moment of cessation and the occasion of cessation. For the mind as the substratum does not differ in its essential nature between the state of cognitive absorption (*saṃprajñāta*) and the state of non-cognitive absorption (*asaṃprajñāta*), despite the suppression and appearance of the latent impressions.

Now, one might object: "Just as the subsequent afflictions (kleśas) have ignorance (avidyā) as their root and cease when ignorance ceases—so that no further separate effort is required for their cessation—in the same way, the latent impressions (saṃskāras) rooted in the emergent state (vyutthāna) would cease simply upon the cessation of the emergent state; therefore, the impression of restraint (nirodha-saṃskāra) need not be sought for their cessation. To this, he says: "The latent impressions of the emergent state... [and so forth].

The mere cessation of a cause is not the reason for the cessation of its effect; otherwise, the cessation of the weaver would entail the cessation of the cloth. Rather, when an effect whose nature is identical to its cause ceases upon the cessation of that cause, then the cessation of that effect follows. Furthermore, it has been stated that the subsequent afflictions (*kleśa*) have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their essence; therefore, their cessation upon the cessation of that [ignorance] is logically established. However, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) do not have cognition (*pratyaya*) as their essence, because we observe the recollection of things even now, long after the original cognition has ceased.

Therefore, even when cognition has ceased, the meaning is that one should continue to cultivate the accumulation of the impressions of cessation (*nirodha-saṃskāra*) until that [cognition] itself ceases. The rest is easy to understand. 3.9.
Its state of tranquil flow arises from mental conditioning. (3.10)

But when the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence have been completely overcome by the powerful latent impressions of cessation, what kind of transformation does the mind undergo? To this he says: "Its flow becomes tranquil due to the latent impressions. Flowing solely through a succession of latent impressions of cessation, which are free from the stain of the latent impressions of emergence, is "tranquil flow. Why, then, is intensity of the latent impressions required, rather than the mere presence of latent impressions? To this he says: "Due to the weakness of those latent impressions. The word "those" refers back to cessation.
But those who read "ye tu nābhibhūyate" (but those who are not overcome) then refer to emergence from meditative absorption. ||3.10||
The transformation of the mind in concentration consists in the disappearance of all-objectedness and the arising of one-pointedness. (3.11)

He shows the state of transformation of the mind during conscious concentration (*saṃprajñāta-samādhi*): "The transformation of the mind into concentration is the waning of its capacity for all objects and the arising of one-pointedness. 'Waning' (*kṣaya*) means disappearance, in the sense that what exists does not perish; 'arising' (*udaya*) means manifestation, in the sense that what is non-existent does not come into being."

Regarding the two qualities that have become one's own nature—omnipresence (*sarvārthatā*) and one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*)—there occur their respective disappearance and appearance; namely, the disappearance of omnipresence and the appearance of one-pointedness. The mind that follows these two is concentrated (*samādhīyate*), becoming characterized by a specific concentration (*samādhi*) that is being cultivated as a process occurring in temporal succession. || 3.11 ||
Then again, when the subsided and the arisen [states] have identical objects of cognition, that is the transformation of the mind into one-pointedness. 3.12.

Then again, the transformation of the one-pointedness of the mind consists of two similar mental modifications (pratyaya), one subsided and the other arisen. When the perfection of concentration (samādhi) has occurred from a state of concentration that exists as a continuous sequence of prior and subsequent moments, there are two similar modifications—one subsided (past) and one arisen (present)—which are called "similar modifications. The similarity between the two lies in their being directed toward a single object. By the phrase "of the concentrated mind," the perfection of concentration is indicated. It remains one-pointed in that very same way until the limit is reached—until the lapse or fall from concentration. (3.12)
By this, the transformations of property, characteristic, and state in the elements and the sense organs are explained. (3.13)

He analyzes the transformation of the elements and the senses, which is both incidental and useful for what is to be explained later: "By this, the transformations of dharma, characteristic, and state in the elements and the senses have been explained. He explains [the meaning of] "by this": [one might object,] "But only the transformation of the mind was mentioned, not its specific modes—the transformations of dharma, characteristic, and state; so how can there be an extension of those [rules]? To this he says: "In that regard, of emergence and suppression..."

The concise meaning is this: the words "dharma," "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), and "state" (*avasthā*) have merely been uttered [in other contexts], but the transformations of dharma, characteristic, and state have not yet been explicitly stated. For instance, the transformation of dharma (*dharmapariṇāma*) was already mentioned in that very sūtra concerning the "formations of emergence and suppression" (*vyutthāna-nirodha-saṃskāra*). By demonstrating this transformation of dharma, the transformation of characteristic (*lakṣaṇapariṇāma*), which has dharma as its locus, is also indicated; thus he says: "the transformation of characteristic. That by which something is characterized is a "characteristic," namely, the differentiation of time.

Therefore, an object characterized by that [mark] is distinguished from other objects belonging to different times. Cessation has three characteristics. Its explanation is that it is "endowed with the three time-periods" (*adhvan*). The word *adhvan* signifies time. Indeed, having first abandoned the future characteristic period, does it then transcend its nature as a dharma? No; he says: "not transcending its nature as a dharma, it has entered the present characteristic."

The very cessation that was future is now present; the meaning is not that the cessation becomes a non-cessation. An explanation of the nature of its present state: where there is its manifestation—that is, its active functioning—in its own form, which performs its appropriate causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). This is its second path (*adhvan*), in relation to its first path, the future.

It might be argued: "If, having abandoned the future time-period (*adhvan*), it attains the state of the present, and having abandoned that, it attains the state of the past—then alas! there would be arising and destruction of the time-periods themselves. But these are not accepted, for there is no arising of what is non-existent, nor destruction of what is existent. To this, he says: "And it is not separated from the past and the future, which persist in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*)."

Having shown that the future cessation possesses the characteristic of being present, he speaks of the third time-period—the pastness of the present emergence—stating: "In the same way, the emergence [is past]. One might ask: is it only the cessation that is future and not the emergence? He says: "In this way, moreover, there is emergence. This recurrence is with respect to the genus (*jāti*) of emergence, not with respect to the individual instance (*vyakti*); for what has already passed does not come into being again. Manifestation of its own nature (*svarūpa*) is the appearance of that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

And since this transformation characterized in such a way occurs repeatedly among things of that same kind, he says: "In this way again. He describes the transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*), which is indicated by the transformation of attributes (*dharma-pariṇāma*): "Likewise. The state (*avasthā*) consists in the strength or weakness of attributes (*dharmas*) belonging to the present time-path; the transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the gradation of that state at every moment. He concludes: "This..."

He determines the distinction between the various transformations based on the distinction between their correlates: "In that regard, [it is] of the substrate (dharmī) according to experience. One might ask: is this transformation of the *guṇas* occasional? He says: "Thus" (*evam*). Why, then, is this transformation eternal? To this he says: "And mobile" (*calaṃ ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of a reason. "Vṛtta" means activity or movement. Why is it exactly so? To this he says: "The nature of the *guṇas*" (*guṇasvābhāvya*). This was stated previously in this very same work.

This threefold transformation of the mind has been indicated by the author of the Sūtras with respect to the elements and the sense organs; thus he says, "By this. This variety of the transformation of attributes (dharma-pariṇāma) is based on the distinction between the attribute and the substratum (dharmin). In that regard, for the elements such as earth and so forth, which are the substrata, the cow, the jar, and so forth, constitute the transformation of attributes. And for those attributes, their states of past, future, and present constitute the transformation of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma).

The transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*) consists of childhood, youth, adulthood, and old age for cows and the like that have entered the characteristic of the present; for jars and the like, it is the transformation of state consisting of newness and antiquity. Similarly, for the sense organs as substrata (*dharmin*), the perception of various objects such as blue is the transformation of attribute (*dharma-pariṇāma*); the transformation of the attribute into the characteristics of the present and so forth is [the transformation of state]; and for the perception of blue and other objects characterized by the present, its clarity or lack of clarity is the transformation of state.

This aforementioned transformation of the elements and the senses is to be understood by relying on the distinction between the substrate (dharmī) and its qualities (dharma), characteristics (lakṣaṇa), and states (avasthā). With reference to their non-distinction, he says: "But from the perspective of ultimate reality" (*paramārthatas tu*). The word "but" (*tu*) distinguishes this from the position of difference. It makes known its status as ultimate reality, but it does not deny the transformative nature of anything else. Why? Because [the author says]: "For [it is] merely the essential nature of the substrate."

Now, one might ask: "If the modification of the substrate (*dharmin*) itself is the property (*dharma*), how is there a cognition of non-confusion regarding modifications in the world? To this he says: "By means of the properties" (*dharmadvāra*). By the word "property," the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and states (*avasthā*) are included. Through these as the medium, the modification belongs to the substrate alone; thus it is both unitary and non-confused, because even though the media themselves are not distinct, they do not mutually confuse the substrate.

Now, if it is argued that since the attributes (*dharma*) are non-different while the substratum (*dharmin*) and the temporal phases (*adhvan*) are different, then because the substratum is not distinct [from its states], the attribute here must also become like the substratum itself—therefore, he says: "In that case, of the attribute... The term *bhāva* refers to a difference in configuration (*saṃsthāna-bheda*). Just as in the case of gold and the like, there occurs a difference in the designations of the vessel, such as a *rucaka* (necklace) or a *svastika* (cross), and only that [configuration] changes; however, the substance, the gold, does not turn into something that is not gold, because there is no absolute difference [between them].

With the following intention, he raises the Buddhist who maintains an extremist view, saying: "Another says... For it is only the *dharmas*—such as bracelets and the like—which, having arisen in such a manner, are ultimately real; there is no single substance called "gold" that persists through many [individuals]. If, however, a substance were to persist even while the *dharmas* undergo change, then it would not transform like the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), but would instead revolve with absolute immutability (*kauṭasthya*).

*Parivṛtti* (transformation) is the transition into another form by abandoning a form consisting of modification, while remaining immutable (*kauṭasthyena*). For example, just as the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) remains eternally immutable, never deviating from its own nature even while the *guṇas* undergo various states of change, so too would gold and other substances [behave]—yet this is not accepted [of them]. Therefore, substance (*dravya*) is not something distinct from its attributes (*dharma*). He refutes this: "This is not a fault. Why? Because we do not admit absolute [identity].

If we were to accept the absolute permanence of substance, as one might of the power of consciousness (*citिशक्ति*), then we would indeed be subject to such a reproach. However, we do not maintain absolute permanence; rather, this triple world—which is not merely substance—departs from its manifest form (*vyakti*) which performs purposeful action (*arthakriyākārin*). Why? Because permanence is negated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For if a jar did not depart from its manifestation, then even in states such as shards, gravel, and powder, it would still perform the functions of perception and causal efficiency as a manifest jar, just as before; therefore, the three worlds are impermanent. [Objection: Let it be that they are indeed impermanent, since they are utterly insignificant like a sky-lotus due to being devoid of perception and causal efficiency. To this, he says: "Even when departed, it exists"; the meaning is that there is no absolute insignificance by which it would be exclusively impermanent.

Why? Because destruction is negated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, that which is non-existent (*tuccha*) never performs either apprehension or purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), such as a sky-lotus. Yet this triple world (*trailokya*) does perform apprehension and purposeful action at some time. Likewise, other reasons for existence (*sattva-hetu*)—such as having an origin, being a substance, possessing properties, having characteristics, and being connected with states (*avasthā*)—should also be cited, as they exclude things like the utterly non-existent sky-lotus or a man's horn.

And thus, the substratum (dharmin) is not absolutely eternal, such that it would be unchangingly eternal like the power of consciousness (citiśakti); rather, it is eternal in a qualified sense. Consequently, it is established that it is subject to transformation (pariṇāmin). By this, one should understand the existence of future effects, such as jars, in states such as that of a lump of clay. This might be argued:

If it is asked, "Even if [the effect] has departed, why is it not perceived as before?", he says: "Due to conjunction and dissolution into its own cause, there is subtlety, which is the state of being unfit for perception; therefore, there is non-perception. Thus, having established the transformation of qualities (*dharmapariṇāma*), he establishes the transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapariṇāma*) through the mutual interpenetration of the characteristics: "The transformation of characteristics" means that each individual characteristic is permeated by the other two characteristics.

Now, one might object: "If there is a connection with a single characteristic, the other two characteristics are not experienced; how then can there be a connection with them? To this he says: "Just as in the case of a person. For the absence of experience does not negate what is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The very production [of an effect] is the proof for the existence of that [cause] therein, because the production of what is non-existent is impossible, like a human horn. He raises an objection stated by others: "In this regard, there is the transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapariṇāma*)."

The point is this: if a dharma were present and yet simultaneously past and future, then all three time-periods would become conflated; furthermore, if the time-periods were to exist sequentially, it would follow that what is non-existent could arise. He provides the rebuttal: "This is the refutation. For the very state of being present is established by experience for dharmas, and from that [experience], one understands their connection with prior and subsequent times. Indeed, what is non-existent does not arise, nor does what is existent perish.

This is what he says: "For thus, the mind does not [exist]. For after the time of anger, the mind is experienced as having the nature of passion (*rāga*). And since passion did not exist at the time of anger because it was future, how could it arise? And if it has not arisen, how could it be experienced? He asks—"But what?"—meaning, "What is the reason that there is no confusion of the time-periods (*adhvan*) even if this were so? The word "but" (*ca*) has the sense of "furthermore."

He states the answer: "The simultaneous occurrence of the three characteristics is not possible in a single mental modification (*cittavṛtti*). However, by way of succession, there may be the existence—that is, the occurrence—of one of the characteristics through its own manifesting agent (*vyañjaka*), because the characteristics are defined in dependence upon the characterized (*lakṣya*); thus, they possess that [characterized] form. In this very context, he cites the agreement of the teacher Pañcaśikha: "And it has been said," etc., which has already been explained above. He concludes: "Therefore," etc.

"Because of the association with contradictory properties consisting of manifestation and disappearance, there is no confusion among the time-periods (adhvan). He states an illustration: 'Just as in the case of passion' (rāga). Previously, the comprehension of the connection of anger with passion was shown; now, however, it is the comprehension of the connection of a passion residing in one object with another passion residing in a different object. He states the application to the subject of the illustration: "In the same way, of the characteristic (lakṣaṇa)."

[Objection: Even if non-absolutism (anekānta) is accepted, since there is non-difference [between the substratum and its attributes], it would follow that when there is a difference in the characteristics (lakṣaṇa), the temporal states (avasthā), or the attributes (dharma), the substratum (dharmī) which is non-different from them must also be different. Yet this is not desired, because it contradicts the experience of its persistence. To this, he says: "The substratum does not belong to the three times, because the attributes non-different from it do belong to the three times. He clarifies precisely how the attributes are connected with the three times: "They are characterized, manifested, or—so to speak—present."

"Unperceived," "unmanifested," "future," and "past"—this refers to [the states] up to the past. Among these, those that are "perceived" are designated as distinct when they attain various states such as strength or weakness; this distinction is due to a change of state (*avasthāntara*), not a change of substance (*dravyāntara*). By the term "state," the states of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and qualities (*dharma*) are meant. This is what is being said: it is experience alone that establishes the difference and non-difference between the substratum (*dharmin*) and its qualities (*dharma*) and so forth.

For if there were absolute non-difference, the properties and so forth would not possess the status of being "properties" and so on, just as the substratum does not possess its own form as a property; nor, if there were absolute difference, would they possess the status of being "properties" and so on, just as a cow and a horse do not stand in such a relation.

And that experience, while establishing its own non-erroneous nature, is personally experienced as following after a single substratum (*dharmin*) even when it persists through qualities (*dharmas*) subject to arising and passing away, while simultaneously distinguishing those qualities from one another. Therefore, we who follow that experience are not able to set aside that experience and establish our own arbitrary definitions of the qualities. On this very point, he states a worldly example: "Just as a single line... and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: just as that very same form of a line is designated as "one hundred" and so forth depending on its various positions, so too that very same substratum (dharmī) is pointed out as being distinct due to the differences in its various attributes (dharma), characteristics (lakṣaṇa), and states (avasthā). To illustrate this point of the subject at hand (dārṣṭāntika), he provides another example, saying: "And just as even in the case of unity... In this context, he raises an objection stated by an opponent, beginning with: "The state (avasthā)..."

Regarding the transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*), it has been stated that in the case of the transformation of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and states (*avasthā*) of the attributes (*dharma*), there would follow the defect of immutability (*kauṭasthya*) for the substratum (*dharmin*), the attributes, and the characteristics and states. He asks: "How so? The answer is: "By means of the operation of the time-period (*adhvan*). It is said that the future time-period of curd is its operation; because [the attribute] is separated from that by the present state of the milk, when the attribute characterized as curd—though existing in the milk—does not perform its own operation, namely the production of yogurt and the like, then it is "future."

When it acts, it is present; when, having acted, it has ceased from its own operation and begins another operation such as curd-making, then it is past. Thus, because of their existence throughout the three times, both the attributes (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), as well as the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the states (*avasthā*), would result in being immutable (*kūṭastha*). For eternity consists in existing at all times; and if all four [the attribute, the substratum, the characteristic, and the state] exist at all times—or do not exist at all—there can be no origination. And that alone is the definition of immutable eternity.
