The sense is that there is no other distinction whatsoever even for the power of consciousness (*citi-śakti*), which is immutable and eternal. He offers a rebuttal: "This is not a fault; why? Because, despite the eternity of the *guṇas*, there is their mutual suppression and being suppressed (*vimarda*), due to the diversity of their modifications."

This is what is meant: although all four—the substratum and its qualities—are always existent, they nevertheless lack immutability because they possess transformation (*pariṇāma*), through which there is the manifestation and concealment of modifications that constitute their very nature, brought about by the diversity of the suppression of the qualities. However, for the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), there is no manifestation or concealment of modifications that constitute its own nature; thus, it possesses immutability. As they have said: "The wise call that eternal whose own nature does not perish."

He demonstrates that the very variety of dissolution (*vimarda*) is the cause for the variety of modifications (*vikāra*), both in the case of the primal nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikṛti*). Just as form (*saṃsthāna*), characterized as a transformation of earth and the other elements, is a mere attribute (*dharma-mātra*) that has a beginning, is perishable, and subject to disappearance—[this being] with respect to its own effects, [namely] sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, which are the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) that are imperishable and non-disappearing; so too he shows it in the case of the primal nature: "In this way, the mark (*liṅga*)."

The meaning is that there is no notion of modification in that [consciousness], for the power of consciousness is not itself subject to modification. Thus, having illustrated both the modified (vikṛti) and the primal nature (prakṛti) as established by the investigator, he provides an example—stating "In this regard, here is an illustration"—of the variety of the suppression of the qualities (*guṇa*) within the modified state itself, which is well-known in the world, as the cause of the variety of modifications in terms of property (*dharma*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and condition (*avasthā*). Furthermore, it is not a rule that the modification of conditions applies only to characteristics.

Since all distinctions of the characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) and states (*avasthā*) of things are denoted by the term "state" (*avasthā*), there is only one transformation of state common to all; thus he says: "of the substratum (*dharmi*) as well. He states the pervading definition of transformation: "of a persisting substance. The word *dharma* denotes the characteristics, marks, and states by virtue of being dependent [upon the substratum]. (3.13)
The substrate (dharmin) conforms to attributes (dharmas) that are quiescent, emergent, or indeterminable. 3.14.

He defines that substratum (*dharmī*) which possesses this threefold transformation by means of the aphorism: "In this regard, the substratum is that which conforms to attributes (*dharma*)—past, present, and imperceptible. Since it is not possible to know the substratum as long as its attribute is unknown, he shows the nature of the attribute: "capacity" (*yogyatā*). The very power of the substance that is the substratum, such as clay and so forth—the power to produce powder, a lump, a jar, and so on—is the attribute; the meaning is that these exist there in an unmanifest state.

[Objection: "In that case, let those things exist in an unmanifest state and then manifest from that [state]. But as for the capacity for fetching water and so forth—which were not obtained by them from their own causes—whence did they come? To this it is said: "delimited by fitness" (*yogyatāvacchinna*). That very power of production belonging to jars and the like is delimited by the fitness for fetching water and so forth; therefore, even the fetching of water and such are obtained by the jars and the like from their own causes alone, and thus they are not accidental. This is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, the answer to the question "What are the substrata (dharmin)? is: "The substrata are those delimited by capacity (yogyatā). The answer to the question "What is the property (dharma)? is: "Power (śakti) alone is their property; the meaning is that their very capacity is the property. Thus, it is established that the substratum is that which possesses such [a property]. He states the proof for its existence: "And that [property], inferred from the difference in the production of results, is one for a single substratum, yet it appears as various other forms, such as powder, a lump, or a jar. This is the meaning.

And because a difference in function is observed, it follows that [the cause] is distinct. "Observed" means perceived. In this regard, he states the distinction of the present lump of clay—which has ascended into experience—from the clay-dust and the clay-pot, which are respectively past and yet-to-be-designated, by saying: "there, the present. The sense is that if it were not distinct, then just as with the lump, the dust and the pot would also necessarily be pervaded by their own respective functions in exactly the same way.

Since no means for differentiating the unmanifested aggregate (*piṇḍa*) has been stated, he says: "But when..."—meaning, by what means of differentiation would it be differentiated? Having thus explained the means of differentiating the attributes (*dharma*), he analyzes that differentiation: "In that regard, those which indeed... The word "arisen" (*uditāḥ*) means "present. He establishes the sequence of the time-periods (*adhvan*): "And those... He raises an objection: "For what purpose?"

For what reason do present [moments] not constitute the immediate antecedent of the past? The proponent states the reason: because of the absence of priority and posteriority. By means of the object (*viṣaya*), he indicates the non-perception of the subject (*viṣayin*). He demonstrates this very non-perception by contrasting it with the nature of perception: "as in the case of the future and the present. He concludes: therefore, only the future is the immediate antecedent of the present by virtue of its priority, not the past.

The present [moment] cannot be designated as "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*) with respect to the past because it stands prior to it; therefore, it is established that among the time-periods (*adhvan*), the past is the youngest. One might argue: "The past and the arisen [present] can be inferred from their being experienced or having been experienced; however, the indeterminate (*avyapadeśya*) factors cannot be inferred in this way precisely because they are indeterminate. With this intention, he asks: "Then what are the indeterminate ones, and in which [factors] do we observe them? To this, he gives the reply: "Everything has everything as its nature" (*sarvaṃ sarvātmakam*). As for where this was stated: [in the following verse].

He establishes this very point with the words, "Of water and earth. For, in plants, creepers, shrubs, and the like, a manifold variety of tastes and other qualities is observed in the roots, fruits, flowers, and sprouts; this transformational diversity belongs to water—which possesses taste, form, touch, and sound—and to earth—which possesses smell, taste, form, touch, and sound. This [transformation] cannot be the modification of an earth that does not possess such a nature, nor of a water that is not of such a kind. Indeed, it has been established that what is non-existent does not arise.

Likewise, the transformative (pāriṇāmika) [quality] of stationary things is seen among mobile beings, such as humans, cattle, and wild animals, in the form of the diversity of their juices and so forth; for those who consume fruits and other such things obtain a perfection of various forms, colors, and qualities. Similarly, the transformative quality of mobile beings is seen in stationary things: it is said that by the sprinkling of blood, pomegranate fruits become as large as palm fruits. He concludes: "In this way, everything—water, earth, and so forth—is composed of all tastes and other qualities."

Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because of the non-interruption of genus," meaning that since the genera such as "water-ness" and "earth-ness" are recognized everywhere, they are not interrupted. Now, one might object: "If everything is of the nature of everything, then alas! because everything is present at all times, in all places, and in every way, it would follow that the manifestation of entities occurs simultaneously; for indeed, an effect whose complete causes are present ought not to be delayed. To this, he replies: "Space, time... [and so forth].

Although every cause contains everything within its nature, nevertheless, that which is the specific locus for a particular effect—such as Kashmir being the locus for saffron—is not present in places like Pañcāla even though those things exist there; thus, saffron is not manifested in Pañcāla and similar regions. Likewise, because the rainy season is not manifest during the summer, rice does not appear then. Similarly, a doe does not give birth to a human, because the form of a human is not manifest within her.

Thus, one who lacks merit does not experience that which has the nature of happiness, nor does the manifestation of the cause of merit occur therein. Therefore, due to the obstruction and departure of place, time, form, and cause, there is no simultaneous manifestation of selves and entities. Having thus distinguished the attributes (dharmas), he shows the persistence of the substratum (dharmin) within them with the words "those which among these... The meaning is that the universal is the form of the substratum, while the particular is the attribute; thus, it consists of both.

Having thus demonstrated the persisting substratum (*dharmin*), the author recalls the undesirable consequence that follows for the nihilist (*vaināśika*) who does not accept it, but instead maintains that the mind consists of nothing but momentary consciousness (*vijñāna-mātra*): "But for one who... and "Because of the recognition of the object. For Yajñadatta does not recognize what was seen by Devadatta. Therefore, he who is the experiencer is the very same person who recognizes. (3.14)
The difference in sequence is the cause for the difference in transformation. ||3.15||

The difference in sequence is the cause for the difference in transformation. Is there only one transformation—characterized by quality (*dharma*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and state (*avasthā*)—of a single substratum (*dharmin*), or are there many transformations characterized by quality, characteristic, and state? In this regard, what is the prima facie position? Because the substratum is one, there can be only one transformation; for a diversity of effects cannot arise from a cause of a single nature, as that would entail the fallacy of their being accidental. To this, it is replied: "Because of the difference in sequence, there is a difference in transformation."

The successive sequence of transformations of a single lump of clay—into powder, a ball, a jar, shards, and fragments—is perceived directly by worldly investigators. Furthermore, the immediate succession between the powder and the ball is one thing; that between the ball and the jar is another; that between the jar and the shards is another; and that between the shards and the fragments is yet another, because in one case [the former] follows the latter, while in another it precedes it. This very distinction of sequence, being impossible within a single transformation, necessitates a plurality of transformations.

The meaning is this: even a single substratum (*dharmī*), by means of the sequential conjunction of various successive auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), undergoes a succession of transformations (*pariṇāma*) and does not bring about these [transformations] spontaneously. Since the sequence is the same in the case of the distinctness of the transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*) as it is in the case of the distinctness of the transformation of states (*avasthā-pariṇāma*), it serves as the cause for the distinctness of sequence. This is clarified by the commentary with the words: "of a single substratum. By maintaining the non-difference between the sequence and that which possesses the sequence, it is said: "that [sequence] is its [the substratum's] sequence."

Likewise, there is the sequence of transformation of states (*avasthā-pariṇāma-krama*). For instance, even grains of rice that have been carefully preserved by a granary-owner in a storehouse are seen, after many years, to undergo the state of atoms (*paramāṇu-bhāva*), their parts and structures crumbling at the mere touch of a hand. And this [transformation] cannot arise suddenly in things that are new.

Therefore, as [the process] is reached through a sequence of momentary successions—in the order of subtle, subtler, subtlest, gross, grosser, grossest, and so forth—this [evolute] is perceived as distinct. This difference in sequence exists only on the view that there is a distinction between the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin); thus he says: "These [are those... From the modifications (vikāra) down to the unmanifest (aliṅga), the relationship of property and substratum is relative, because even earth and the like are properties in relation to their own constituent elements (tanmātra); thus he says: "The property also..."

When there is the application of figurative non-difference (*abhedopacāra*) toward the ultimate subject (*paramārthadharmī*), which is itself devoid of marks (*aliṅga*), by means of that [figurative usage]—that is, by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—it amounts to saying that the property (*dharma*) is indeed the subject (*dharmī*). In that case, there is only a single transformation; the meaning is that it is simply the transformation of the subject. This is because the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), temporal states (*avasthā*), and properties (*dharma*) are superimposed upon the very nature of the subject. By this, it has essentially been stated that the immutability (*kūṭasthanityatva*) of the subject is utterly cast aside.

While establishing the transformation of phenomena (*dharmapariṇāma*), he incidentally states the different types of mental factors (*cittadharma*) with the words "of the mind" (*cittasya*). Among these, "perceived" (*paridṛṣṭa*) means direct (*pratyakṣa*), and "unperceived" (*aparidṛṣṭa*) means indirect (*parokṣa*). Therein, those consisting of conditions (*pratyaya*) are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, as well as passion (*rāga*) and so forth. By the term "mere entities" (*vastumātra*), he indicates that they do not have a luminous nature (*aprakāśarūpatā*). One might object: "If they are unperceived, they do not exist at all. To this he replies: "Those whose existence is established by inference as mere entities are so described."

Because it possesses the same nature as mental cognition, scripture (*āgama*) is also inference (*anumāna*). He summarizes the seven [objects] not previously perceived in a verse, beginning with "cessation" (*nirodha*): Cessation is the state of the mind during *asaṃprajñāta* [samādhi], where only residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) remain; this is understood through scripture and inferred through reasoning. By the mention of "dharma," he indicates both merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*apuṇya*). In some versions, the reading is "karma"; even there, only the merit and demerit produced by that [action] are intended.

These [the past and future] are understood through scripture or through inference from the observation of the experience of pleasure and pain; whereas the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is inferred from memory. Thus, because the mind consists of the three *guṇas* and the functioning of the *guṇas* is mobile, its transformation at every moment is inferred. Likewise, life—the maintenance of the vital breaths—is a particular kind of effort, an imperceptible property of the mind, which is inferred from inhalation and exhalation.

In this way, the activity of the mind—its movement—is inferred precisely from its conjunction with various sense organs or parts of the body. Likewise, the power of the mind, which is the subtle state of manifested effects, is also inferred solely from the experience of gross effects that are its attributes (dharma). ||3.15||
Through saṃyama upon the three transformations, there arises knowledge of the past and the future. (3.16)

From here until the conclusion of the chapter on the feet (*pāda*), the objects of *saṃyama* and the supernormal powers (*vibhūti*) that indicate mastery over them must be explained. Among these, first he introduces the threefold transformation previously described as the object of *saṃyama* for the yogi who has already acquired all the limbs of yoga: "From *saṃyama* upon the threefold transformation comes knowledge of the past and the future."

Now, one might object: "Where there is *saṃyama*, there is direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of that very object; how then can *saṃyama* upon the three transformations bring about the direct perception of the past and the future? To this he replies: By means of that [saṃyama], the three transformations are being directly perceived, and this brings about knowledge whose objects are the past and future which are inherent within those transformations.

The meaning is that the direct perception of the three transformations itself consists in the direct perception of the past and future contained therein; thus, there is no difference in the object between the *saṃyama* and its resulting direct perception. (3.16)
Due to the mutual superimposition of word, object, and idea, there is a confusion; by performing *saṃyama* on their distinction, knowledge of the cries of all beings arises. 3.17.

Another field of *saṃyama* is now introduced: through *saṃyama* on their mutual superimposition (*adhyāsa*), which causes the confusion of word, object, and idea, there arises knowledge of the cries of all beings from the discernment of their distinction. Here, wishing to explain the expressive word, [the author] first states the subject matter of the activity of speech: therein, speech is the organ of speech (*vāg-indriya*), which manifests phonemes (*varṇa*) and has eight locations. As it is said: "There are eight locations for the phonemes: the chest, the throat, and likewise the head; the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate."

The meaning is that speech is meaningful only with respect to the phonemes (*varṇa*) as established by common worldly cognition, and not with respect to the denoter (*vācaka*). He defines the object of the operation of the auditory organ: "Furthermore, the ear has as its object only the subtle element (*tanmātra*), meaning it is transformed into the form of the phoneme—which is a specific modification of the *udāna* sound impinging upon the vocal organ—and not the denoter."

He distinguishes the expressive unit from the phonemes established by worldly convention: the word (*pada*), moreover, is the expressive unit; furthermore, it is apprehended by a cognition that synthesizes the sounds (*nāda*). Having first grasped each of the phonemes as they are established by convention, that cognition which subsequently synthesizes them—bringing them to a state of unity such that one thinks "this single word is 'gauh' (cow)"—by means of that cognition, the word is apprehended.

Although the preceding cognitions each take as their object only the word consisting of the form of the letters, nevertheless it does not appear clearly. But in the final cognition, that [word] appears extremely clearly; thus it is said to be apprehended by the cognition that synthesizes the sounds (*nādānusaṃhārabuddhi*). To one who, failing to understand the experience of a single word due to its distinctness from other classes, maintains that the letters themselves are the expressive agents, he says: "The letters... [and so forth].

Now, do these phonemes (varṇas) produce a cognition whose object is the meaning individually—like pegs supporting a sling—or collectively—like stones supporting a cooking pot? The first alternative is not tenable; for if the cognition of the meaning were not produced from a single phoneme, it would follow that the second and subsequent phonemes need not be uttered. Alternatively, if it were produced [from the first], then the utterance of further phonemes would be redundant, because a means of accomplishment (sādhana) that contributes no further distinction to an action already completed would violate the very logic of being a "means. Therefore, the second alternative remains.

For it is possible for stones joined together to support a cooking pot because they exist at the same time; however, since simultaneity is impossible for phonemes, they cannot stand in a relationship of mutual assistance or being assisted. Therefore, even when combined, they do not produce the cognition of meaning. Not touching the single form of the word (*pada*), and for that very reason not presenting it through identity, these phonemes—appearing and disappearing like iron rods—are said to be individually devoid of the nature of a word.

If, however, the phonemes were to touch a single word through identity (*tādātmya*), then the aforementioned fault would not follow; thus he says: "Furthermore, each individual phoneme is the essence of a word, accumulated with all expressive powers (*sarvābhidhānaśakti*), filled with all expressive powers. For instance, the letter *g* is seen in words such as *go*, *gaṇa*, *gaura*, and *naga*, which express meanings such as 'cowness' (*gotva*) and so forth; therefore, it possesses those respective expressive powers. Likewise, the letter *o* is seen in words such as *soma* and *śociḥ*, which express meanings such as 'Lord' (*īśvara*) and so forth; therefore, that too possesses those respective expressive powers. This should be inferred in all cases."

And each individual phoneme, such as the letter *ga*, has as its "counter-correlate" (*pratiyogin*)—that is, its relational counterpart—the other phoneme, such as the letter *o*; the state of being that is its "nature" (*tattva*). Because of that nature, it appears as if it has attained "multiformity" (*vaiśvarūpya*), or diversity, yet it has not actually attained diversity because of that very same nature. Thus, the preceding phoneme *ga* is distinguished from words such as *gaṇa* by the subsequent phoneme *o*, and the subsequent phoneme *o* is distinguished from words such as *śociḥ* by the preceding phoneme *ga*, [resulting in the specific word] denoting "cowness" (*gotva*).

"Established in the cognition of synthesis upon the bursting of the cow's footprint"—this is the intended meaning: for it is impossible for a cognition of meaning to be produced by letters that are mutually incapable of coexistence due to their fixed order. Nor is it tenable to argue that, as in the case of the Āgneya and other sacrifices producing the ultimate apūrva or heaven through the medium of latent impressions (saṃskāra), there is a "conjunction" (sāhitya) of letters—even if their order is not fixed—for the production of the cognition of meaning, because such an argument cannot withstand logical scrutiny.

Indeed, this mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of the phonemes—which is the cause for the generation of memory—is either distinct [from the phonemes] or, like that produced by the Agnihotra sacrifice and so forth, designated as *apūrva*. It cannot, however, be something immediately following [the phonemes], because that would entail the fault of excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*). First of all, such an unseen entity (*adṛṣṭa-pūrva*) must be postulated; furthermore, it is impossible for a single [impression] to be produced by sequential experiences of the phonemes. Thus, one must postulate multiple intermediate impressions of that same class, which results in conceptual complexity.

Nor is this [latent impression] a member of the inferential mark (jñāpaka-hetu); for it does not attain the status of being a member [of an inference] while remaining unknown. Indeed, a relation does not become a member of the process of conveying meaning while it remains unknown. Furthermore, the latent impression (saṃskāra), which is inferred from the production of the result that is memory, is restricted to the object of its own cause—the original experience—and is not capable of producing a cognition regarding a different object. Otherwise, having experienced just anything at all, everyone would know everything.

Nor is it tenable that the letters, having attained simultaneity by ascending onto the mirror of memory—which arises from the aggregate of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each individual letter—are the expressive agents. For there would follow the absurd consequence that they produce the cognition of the meaning without distinction in cases where they are experienced out of order, in reverse order, or without any sequence at all. Furthermore, this recollective cognition cannot take as its object the priority and posteriority existing in the prior experiences.

Therefore, since the cognition of meaning cannot arise from the individual phonemes (*varṇa*), it postulates the experience of a single word (*pada*) as its own cause. Nor does this same consequence apply to the word itself; for when the various sounds (*dhvani*), produced by distinct articulatory efforts, manifest each individual word, they—being similar because they are produced by the same places and organs of articulation as the mutually dissimilar sounds that manifest other words—render one word similar to another through their mutual dissimilarity with those [other] words, according to the difference of their counterparts.

Due to the differences among those various similarities and because of their proximity, they cause even that which is one and partless to appear as if it possessed parts and as if it were manifold—just as a single face, though fixed in its color, size, and shape, is displayed by jewels, swords, mirrors, and the like as many faces with different colors, sizes, and shapes, yet not in reality.

The phonemes (*varṇa*) are merely parts of the partless word, imagined through the distinction of their proximity to similarity; therefore, the cognition of that [word] in its form as phonemes takes as its object the non-differentiated *sphoṭa*—which is indeed without parts—as if it were differentiated, as if it possessed parts, when there is a difference in words.

Therefore, the *ga*-portion of a single *sphoṭa* of the word "cow" (*gopada*) does not determine its own possessor [the whole word] because of its similarity to the *sphoṭa* of words such as "white" (*gaura*); thus, it is determined only when qualified by the *o*-portion. Likewise, the *o*-portion, being similar to words such as "light" (*śociḥ*), is not capable of determining its own possessor, the *sphoṭa* of the word "cow"; thus, it is determined only when qualified by the *ga*-portion. Furthermore, even for those [phonemes] that do not coexist simultaneously, there is coexistence by way of their residual impressions (*saṃskāra*); hence, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is logically established.

Nor is there a difference in the objects of the two impressions, because both the experiences—which have the two parts as their objects—and the impressions produced from them have the single word as their object. The distinction is this: by the experience of the individual parts alone, the word is experienced indistinctly; however, by the synthesizing cognition (*anusaṃhāradhī*), which is born from the impressions produced by those experiences of the parts, it is experienced distinctly.

Furthermore, it is observed that prior unmanifest experiences, by means of depositing latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), produce a manifest experience; for example, the unmanifest cognitions of "existence" regarding a tree from a distance serve as the cause for a manifest cognition of the tree. However, this mode of operation is not possible for phonemes (*varṇa*) in the communication of meaning. Indeed, it cannot be maintained that phonemes individually produce an unmanifest cognition of the meaning which becomes manifest at the end; for the distinction between manifest and unmanifest is restricted solely to perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣajñāna*).

The cognition of meaning derived from the phonemes is not perceptual; therefore, if it were produced from the phonemes, it would necessarily be clearly manifest—or else it would not be produced at all, rather than being indistinct. However, in the case of the *sphoṭa*, which is perceptible and manifested by sounds (*dhvani*), its clarity or lack thereof is merely postulated; thus, the two cases are not comparable.

Thus, when the synthetic cognition (*anusaṃhārabuddhi*) arises through the auditory organ aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each individual phoneme, the phonemes, being combined therein, attain the state of a single word-sphoṭa. Because they are manifested by a specific effort (*prayatnaviśeṣa*), and because that specific effort depends upon a fixed sequence, if the sequence were otherwise, there would be no manifestation of the sphoṭa due to the absence of the specific effort that manifests it. Therefore, these [phonemes], which conform to the sequence and are delimited by the worldly convention (*saṃketa*) regarding meaning, constitute that very delimitation by convention.

They show that the domain consists of similar words: "these *ga*, *au*, and *visarjanīya* sounds—whether two or three, three or four, or five or six—are surrounded by the power of all denotation and illuminate the object possessing a dewlap and so forth. Now, if this is so, does it mean that the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves possess the capacity to denote according to convention, and thus there is no such thing as a single word? To this he says: "Therefore, of these... The sequence caused by the sounds is the "sequence of sounds" (*dhvanikrama*).

Those [phonemes] in which the sequence of sounds (*dhvanikrama*) has been withdrawn are so described. They are called "manifestations in the intellect" (*buddhinirbhāsa*) because they are manifested—that is, revealed—by the intellect. It was stated that the *ga*, *au*, and *visarjanīya* are delimited by convention (*saṃketa*) in accordance with the inclinations of people who perceive only gross forms. Since even the *ga*-sounds and the others possess denotative power either as parts of that [word] or through identity with it, the meaning is that, according to actual cognition, the word is indeed a single denotative entity.

This very point is clarified as follows: the connection is that "that single word is perceived by worldly cognition. Why is it one? To this he says: "It is the object of a single cognition"; since it is the object of a cognition having a single form—namely, "the word *go* is one"—therefore it is one. He states its manifestor: "projected by a single effort. The effort that manifests the word *rasa* is distinct from the effort that manifests the word *sara*.

And that [word], delimited by the fruit characterized by the manifestation of the word-sound *sara* through its commencement (*upakrama*), is a single entity existing as a sequence of prior and posterior parts; yet, because those parts—which are differentiated by the imposition of similarity—are ultimately non-existent, being merely conceptual constructs, it is partless (*abhāga*). Precisely for this reason, due to its nature as a sequence of prior and posterior, it is without succession (*akrama*). Now, one might object: "The phonemes (*varṇa*) are sequential, and they are its parts; so how can it be without succession and partless? To this he says: "It is without phonemes" (*avarṇam*).

For its letters are not constituent parts; rather, it is the word itself that manifests through various forms which, though not ultimately real, are conditioned by similarity. Indeed, the faces reflected in a gem, a sword, or a mirror are not the ultimate constituent parts of the face that exists in reality. That which is known in the synthetic cognition (*anusamhārabuddhi*) is the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), which is the function of the final perception of the letter; this [word] is presented and made an object of cognition by that [synthetic cognition] together with the impressions produced by the experience of the preceding letters.

It has been established above that the phonemes (*varṇa*), their perceptions, and their respective mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) constitute the object of the word (*pada*). It might be argued: "If the reality of the word is indeed partless, without sequence, and devoid of phonemes, why is such a thing never manifested? For a crystal gem, which has acquired a red hue through the application of lac-dye, is not perceived as clear and white once that [dye] is removed; therefore, the phonemes must be ultimately real. To this, he says: "Elsewhere... (*paratra*).

Through the desire to communicate, by means of the very phonemes being denoted, uttered, and heard by listeners—this beginningless linguistic usage which is based upon distinct phonemes and words—the latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced thereby is likewise beginningless. By means of the worldly cognition permeated by and infused with that [impression], which grasps words as colored by distinct phonemes, and through the consensus and agreement of elders who regard them as established and as ultimate reality, the word is cognized.

This is what is meant: there exists some limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) which is conjoined with and disjoined from that which is to be qualified (*upadheya*). For example, lac and the like; when they are removed from it, the crystal shines with its own natural, transparent, white form—this is logical.

But in the case of the cognition of a word (*pada*), since it does not arise from anything other than the specific sounds brought about by various efforts, and since those [sounds] are always tainted by the defect of similarity, the cognition is produced by the word in the very nature of the phonemes (*varṇa*). Thus, how could there be the manifestation of a word free from limiting adjuncts? As they say:

"Sounds that possess a similar nature are the causes of error; the means of perceiving these [sounds] is the cause of error. Furthermore, because it is a means [to an end], for those who see what has already been shown by words, this sublation of cognition is certainly a constant affliction in the world."

Since the word-soul manifests as colored by distinct phonemes, the world of coarse vision, regarding the phonemes themselves as the word, establishes conventions for those very phonemes—which possess various modes—to denote different meanings. Thus he says: "Of that... Of that word, although it is a single undivided entity, there is a division into the nature of phonemes for the sake of the world of coarse vision, based on the cognition of convention.

He states the distinction: "Of this many," meaning neither fewer nor more; such a specific sequence of uninterrupted succession is the synthesis (*anusaṃhāra*), which constitutes the apprehension by a single cognition as the denoter of a single object, such as "cowness" (*gotva*). Now, if this convention (*saṃketa*) holds that "this word is the denoter of this single object," then, alas! there would be no mutual superimposition (*itaretarādhyāsa*) between the word and the object. To this he says: "But the convention... [The compound] *smṛtyātmā* means that whose nature (*ātman*) is memory (*smṛti*). Thus it is described.

For a convention does not determine its object merely by being established; rather, it does so when it is being recollected. What is meant is this: although the convention possesses a single, undifferentiated form, the genitive case is employed by conceptualizing some kind of distinction. One who knows this distinction becomes all-knowing and a knower of the cries of all beings through mastery over that [distinction].

Having thus established that a single word is partless, consisting of the various phonetic segments as they are conceptually constructed, he says the following in order to establish that a single sentence is likewise partless, consisting of the conceptual division of words: "In all words, there is the power of the sentence. This is the intended meaning: a word is employed for the purpose of communicating to another; and in that context, it is precisely that which is desired to be communicated to the other person which must be conveyed by those [words]. And that which is desired to be communicated by them is precisely that which falls within the scope of [the speaker's] purposeful action (*upādāna*) and so forth.

Nor is that [cognition] directed toward the mere word-meaning; rather, it is directed toward the sentence-meaning. Therefore, all words have the sentence-meaning as their primary object, and thus that alone is their meaning. Consequently, even where a single word is employed in isolation, its meaning is understood only by being unified with another word, and not from the isolated word alone. Why? Because the isolated word lacks such capacity. Thus, in those various instances, it is the sentence itself that is expressive, not the individual words.

However, by virtue of being a part of that [sentence], even those [words] possess the power to express the sentence-meaning, just as phonemes possess the power to express word-meanings by virtue of being parts of words. Therefore, just as each individual phoneme possesses the power to denote all word-meanings only when accumulated, so too each individual word possesses the power to denote all sentence-meanings only when accumulated. This has been stated: "In all words there is the power of the sentence; when 'tree' is uttered, 'is' is understood."

The word "tree" (*vṛkṣa*), accompanied by the supplied word "is" (*asti*), functions as the meaning of the sentence; because it is a constituent part of that [sentence-meaning], the word "tree" occurs there. But why is it understood that "it is"? To this he says: "A word-meaning does not deviate from existence. For in the world alone lies the means for determining the meanings of words.

And he, by merely synthesizing the word-meaning with the sense of "existence" (*asti*), constructs the sentence-meaning in every case; this is the non-deviation [of the meaning] from existence. For this very reason, there is the conventional usage among those who know the operation of words that "wherever another verb is absent, the verb 'to be' (*asti*) in its present form (*bhavantī*) should be employed. Having stated that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is inseparable from the distinction of action (*kriyābheda*), he now demonstrates that the distinction of action is inseparable from the factors of action (*kāraka*): "And likewise, when it is said 'he cooks' (*pacati*)," and so forth.

For when "he cooks" is said, since there is an understanding of any agent whatsoever capable of being connected with that action, the mention of its specific varieties is merely a restatement intended to exclude others. Thus, since the meaning of the sentence is indeed the particular (bheda), a word is seen to function toward the meaning of the sentence even without depending [on other words]; therefore, the capacity of words for the sentence-meaning certainly exists. This is what he says: "And it is observed."

Nor does the word *śrotriya* and the like convey such a meaning by its own power alone, so long as it is not compounded with words such as *asti* (is). Thus, the point is that this [compound] also possesses only a constructed nature (*kalpitatva*), because it is a constituent part of a sentence. It might be argued: "If the power of the sentence resides in the words themselves, then what is the use of the sentence, since that meaning is already determined from those [words] alone? To this he says: "In that regard, in the sentence..."

This has been stated: the meaning of a word is not understood from the word alone when one intends to comprehend it, as long as it is not combined with another word. And thus, having extracted words from a sentence and having extracted from the sentence-meaning its constituent parts—whether a *kāraka* (participant) or an action—that word must be analyzed and explained by means of the conceptual division into base (*prakṛti*), suffix (*pratyaya*), and so forth. But for what purpose is it explained with such great effort? To this he says: "Otherwise... (anyathā).

Because of the similarity between nouns and verbs in such cases as "the pot exists" (*ghaṭo bhavati*) and "give alms, it exists" (*bhikṣāṃ dehi bhavati*), or "it stands" (*tiṣṭhati*); likewise in "you are a horse" (*aśvas tvam aśvaḥ*) and "the horse goes" (*aśvo yāti*); and similarly in "drink goat's milk" (*ajāpayaḥ piba*) and "slay the enemies of the goat-herder" (*ajāpayaḥ śatrūn*)—due to this formal identity between noun and verb, how could that which is not yet determined as either a noun or a verb be analyzed, since there would be no basis for its specific designation? Therefore, words must be extracted from the sentence and then explained.

However, it is not from grammatical derivation alone that the ultimate division of words is established. Having thus explained the nature of the word, he now begins to describe the non-confusion of word, object, and cognition—which appear to be conflated due to convention—by means of their distinction: "The distinction between those [three], namely word, object, and cognition, is as follows: in the expression 'the palace whitens,' the word has action as its meaning."

For here, in the case of "it whitens" (*śvetate*), there is a distinct word whose meaning is an action in a state of accomplishment, which is different from the action in a state of being accomplished consisting of prior and posterior stages. Even where both the word and its meaning possess a state of accomplishment, he says that there is nonetheless a distinction of the word by virtue of the meaning: "the white palace" (*śvetaḥ prāsādaḥ*) is a word whose meaning is a *kāraka* (participant in an action). And because [the *kāraka*] has already been expressed, there is an absence of the *kāraka*-case ending.

He analyzes the meaning: "the meaning of those two words consists of action and the factors of action" (*kriyākārakātmā tadarthaḥ*). The meaning of those two words consists of that which is the nature of action and that which is the nature of the factors of action. He analyzes the suffix: "and the suffix" (*pratyayaś ca*). By the word "and" (*ca*), the term "that meaning" (*tadartha*) is drawn over here. That [term] is connected here as having another word as its predominant referent (*anyapadārthapradhāna*). That very thing whose meaning consists of action and the factors of action is what is thus described.

Objection: Since there is a cognition [of these] without distinction, and because of the confusion (*saṃkara*) of word, object, and cognition, how can there be any differentiation? With this intention, he asks: "Why? He provides the answer: "Because of the connection [expressed as] 'this is that'. The meaning is that the single-formed cognition is conditioned by convention (*saṃketa*), but it is not real. The fact that convention is the cause is shown by the locative case in the word "saṃkete" (in convention). He states the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*): "But the white object... etc. "States" (*avasthā*) refers to newness, oldness, and so forth.

[Speech] accompanied [by other elements] is mixed. Thus, through *saṃyama* on this distinction, for the yogin there is the unmanifest word, its meaning, and the cognition thereof even in the cries of all beings—beasts, deer, reptiles, birds, and so forth. Therefore, *saṃyama* performed here upon the words, their denotations, and the cognitions of human speech is effectively performed upon those as well, due to their common nature. It is established that the yogin knows their cries, the distinctions of their meanings, and the cognitions thereof. ||3.17||
Through the direct realization of formative forces, there arises knowledge of previous births. (3.18)

From the direct realization of formative forces (*saṃskāra*), there arises the knowledge of previous births. For formative forces are born of cognition and are the causes of memory; the formative forces of ignorance and so forth are the causes of the afflictions such as ignorance. Maturation (*vipāka*) consists of birth, lifespan, and experience, and its causes are merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). It is understood that these were "constructed" (*abhisaṃskṛta*)—that is, produced—by their own causes in previous existences, according to how they were formed, just as a manifestation is produced.

Transformation, activity, inhibition, capacity, and vitality are indeed the properties of the mind; likewise, there are other imperceptible mental properties. When these, along with their accessories, have been heard of or inferred, *saṃyama* upon them is capable of bringing about the direct perception of both types of latent impressions (*saṃskāras*). Granted that direct perception of those [properties] occurs through *saṃyama* upon them, but from where does the direct perception of previous births come? To this he says: "And not by place... The "cause" (*nimitta*) consists of the previous body, the sense organs, and so forth.

The meaning is that the direct perception of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) together with their consequences necessarily implies the direct perception of [the results of those impressions], such as birth and so forth. He extends the practice of *saṃyama* on one's own latent impressions to those belonging to others by saying, "it is the same with respect to others. In this regard, he introduces the dialogue between Āvaṭya, who was experiencing the cause for the arising of faith, and Jaigīṣavya, stating: "In this connection, the following narrative is heard. A "great eon" (*mahākalpa*) is a great creation. By the term "wearing a body" (*tanudhara*), the perfection of the emanated body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is expressed.

"Bhavya" means auspicious, in the sense that the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas* have been washed away. Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) consists in mastery over *pradhāna*; for by means of this, having agitated *pradhāna*, one bestows upon whoever one desires whatever perfection of body and senses one wishes to give. Having manifested thousands of one's own bodies and senses, one wanders at will through the atmosphere, heaven, and earth. Contentment (*saṃtoṣa*), indeed, is the destruction of craving; it is the tranquility of the *sattva* of the intellect, which is its essential nature (*dharma*). (3.18)
The supernormal knowledge of another's mind is the result of [the perfection of] wisdom. 3.19.
The knowledge of another's mind is [the result] of the condition; it is because of the direct realization of the mind-only that constitutes the condition for another. ||3.19||
And that [emptiness] does not have an object, because it has not become an object for it. 3.20.

Just as the direct perception of *saṃskāras* necessarily implies the direct perception of their concomitants and previous births, so too the direct perception of another's mind would imply the direct perception of its objects; to this [objection], he says: "And that [perception] does not have an object, because that [object] has not become its field. The intention is this: the aforementioned *saṃyama* has as its object the *saṃskāras* together with their concomitants, whereas this [present *saṃyama*] has as its object only the other person's mind. (3.20)
Through *saṃyama* on the form of the body, when the power of its perceptibility is suppressed and there is no contact with the light of the eye, invisibility occurs. (3.21)

Through *saṃyama* on the form of the body, when the power of its being perceived is suppressed and there is contact with the light of the eye, invisibility occurs. The body consists of the five elements; it becomes visible to the eye because it possesses form. For it is through form that both the body and its form experience the capacity for the act of visual perception. In that regard, when a specific *saṃyama* is performed by the yogi upon form, then the power of form to be perceived—the cause of the visibility of the body which possesses form—is suppressed.

Therefore, when the power of the object of perception is suppressed, the yogin’s disappearance occurs; that is to say, his body becomes an object no longer accessible to visual cognition produced by the eyes of others due to the lack of contact with their light-like knowledge. The meaning is that in order to achieve that [state], disappearance is the means. By this [same principle], the sūtra should be inferred as follows: "From *saṃyama* on the body, when the power of its objects—sound, touch, taste, and smell—is suppressed, there is disappearance upon the lack of contact with the illuminations of the ear, skin, tongue, and nose. (3.21)
Action is either with effort or without effort; through saṃyama upon that, there is knowledge of the end of life, or else from portents. 3.22.

Action is both with-impediment (*sopakrama*) and without-impediment (*nirupakrama*); through *saṃyama* upon that, or from portents (*ariṣṭas*), there is knowledge of the end of life. Action that ripens as lifespan (*āyurvipāka*) is of two kinds: with-impediment and without-impediment. That action which pertains to a single birth and is the cause of birth, lifespan, and experience is what ripens as lifespan.

And that [karma], having set out to grant its enjoyment regardless of any lapse of time, having bestowed much enjoyment and leaving only a small remainder of fruit while its activity is already underway, merely delays because it is impossible to experience its fruit all at once with a single body; this is "with effort" (*sopakrama*). "Effort" (*upakrama*) means activity; thus, the meaning is "accompanied by that. But that very same [karma], having given only a small amount of fruit, being occupied in granting fruit while awaiting that specific time, and possessing only occasional or slow activity, is "without effort" (*nirupakrama*).

He clarifies this very point by means of two illustrations, beginning with "In that regard, as... Here, for the sake of even greater clarity, he shows another illustration: "Or, as fire... In this context, the "later limit" (*aparānta*) refers to death, in relation to the "great dissolution" (*mahāpralaya*). Through *saṃyama* on action (*karman*) regarding both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), knowledge of the later limit arises. Consequently, having understood his own action to be "with haste" (*sopakrama*), the yogi creates many bodies, experiences the fruit immediately, and dies at his own will.

He states an incidental point: "Or from omens (*ariṣṭa*). Like enemies (*ari*), they terrify; thus, *ariṣṭas* are the three kinds of signs of death. Or else, everything is perceived in reverse: apart from [mere] illusions such as those of Mahendra, one considers villages, cities, and so forth to be heaven, and the world of men alone to be the world of the gods. (3.22)
The powers [are cultivated] in relation to loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables]. ||3.23||

The powers regarding loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables]. From the practice of self-restraint (*saṃyama*) regarding loving-kindness and the others, his powers of loving-kindness and so forth arise. In that regard, from the cultivation of loving-kindness comes a power by which he makes the world of living beings happy; consequently, he becomes a benefactor to all. Likewise, through the power of compassion, he delivers sentient beings from suffering or from the causes of suffering. Similarly, through the power of sympathetic joy, he establishes equanimity toward the world of living beings.

He states that concentration (samādhi) is the cause of cultivation (bhāvanā), which is necessary for what is to be explained hereafter: "That concentration which arises from cultivation is *saṃyama*. Although *saṃyama* consists of the triad of fixation (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and concentration (samādhi), and not concentration alone, nevertheless, because the effect is produced immediately after concentration, concentration is predominant; thus, the term *saṃyama* is applied metaphorically to it. In some places, the reading is "cultivation is concentration" (*bhāvanā samādhiḥ*). In that case, cultivation and concentration are the two constituent parts of the aggregate that is *saṃyama*, serving as its causes.

Vīrya is effort; by means of it, the effort of a person who possesses the power of loving-kindness (maitrī) and the other [immeasurables] toward others who are happy and so forth becomes unfailing. Equanimity (upekṣā) is indifference; there is no cultivation (bhāvanā) therein, nor is there anything to be cultivated like happiness and so forth. ||3.23||
Among the forces, the elephant-force and so forth [are foremost]. 3.24.
Among types of strength, the strength of an elephant and so forth are [the lowest]; for one who has self-restraint within their own strength, that person attains true strength. (3.24)
Through the application of the light of activity, there arises knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, and the distant. 3.25.

Through the application of the light of the process [of perception], there arises knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, and the remote. By fixing the *saṃyama* upon an object—whether it be subtle, concealed, or remote—one attains that object. (3.25)
Knowledge of the worlds [is attained] through *saṃyama* upon the sun. 3.26.

"Knowledge of the worlds [is attained] through *saṃyama* on the sun. From the Pole Star (*dhruva*) down to the summit of Mount Meru. Thus, having briefly introduced the seven worlds by means of this concluding summary verse, he explains them in detail, beginning with "There, [starting from] Avīci. By the word "mass" (*ghana*), the earth is meant; the meaning is that it is the ground or location. It should be understood that these great hells are surrounded by numerous secondary hells (*upanaraka*). He concludes these very same [hells] under another name—namely, "the Great... (mahā-).

For him, night and day proceed as if attached to the movement of the sun: wherever the sun leaves a portion of it, there is night; wherever it adorns a portion, there is day. He states the total measurement of Jambūdvīpa: "This [is] one hundred thousand *yojanas*. To the question, "Of what kind is this hundred thousand *yojanas*? he says: "It is arranged—that is, compressed—on each side of Sumeru by half of that, namely fifty thousand *yojanas*."

Since Mount Sumeru stands in their center and the oceans are like heaps of mustard seeds, the connection is that they are double, then double again. The meaning is that just as a heap of mustard seeds is neither as high as a heap of rice nor level with the ground, so too are the oceans. The continents (dvīpas) are "possessing various mountains as their ornaments" because they exist together with diverse mountains that serve as their crowning ornaments.

Thus, this entire circle of the earth—encircled by the garland of oceans, mountains, forests, islands, and cities, and surrounded by the Lokāloka mountain—is situated within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*); it is that whose configuration and arrangement are thus described as being compacted, well-established, and firmly fixed. He shows those who dwell therein: "There, in Pātāla. He describes the configuration of Sumeru: "Sumeru."

Having thus described the *bhūrloka* with its various divisions, he describes the *antarīkṣaloka* with its divisions as well, beginning with "the planets" (*graha*). "Activity" (*vikṣepa*) means functional operation. He shows the *svarloka* with the words "those who dwell in the realm of Mahendra. "Divine hosts" (*devanikāya*) refers to the classes of gods. He describes the excellence of form for all six divine hosts with the words "all have their desires fulfilled by mere volition" (*sarve saṃkalpasiddhāḥ*); objects of enjoyment approach them simply through the act of will. "Vṛndārakas" means those worthy of worship. "Enjoyers of desire" (*kāmabhoginaḥ*) means those who delight in sexual union.

Their bodies are of spontaneous birth (*aupapāduka*); without the union of parents, a divine body arises for them spontaneously from atoms and elements highly refined by the excellence of their merit (*dharma*). Regarding the *Maharloka*, he says: "Great" (*mahatī*). They are masters over the great elements (*mahābhūta*). Whatever these beings desire, that very thing the great elements provide. And by their will, the great elements abide in various forms. Sustained by meditation (*dhyāna*), satisfied by meditation alone, they become free from thirst.

He speaks of Janaloka as "the first," according to the sequence already stated. "Masters of the elements and the senses" means that the elements, such as earth and the rest, and the senses, such as hearing and the rest, are employed exactly as they wish to employ them. With reference to the aforementioned sequence, he speaks of the second Brahmā-world, Tapoloka, as "the second. "Masters of the elements, the senses, and primordial nature (prakṛti)" [is the description].

The primordial nature (*prakṛti*) consists of the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*). For, by the power of that [nature] and according to its will, the subtle elements themselves transform into the form of a body; such is the view of the followers of the Āgamas. "Twice as much" means that the Mahābhāsvaras have twice the lifespan of those in the Ābhāsvara [heaven], and the Satyamahābhāsvaras have twice the lifespan of those [Mahābhāsvaras]; this is the meaning. "Above" means that in the Satyaloka above, their knowledge is unimpeded; from the Avīci hell upwards, up to the Tapoloka, they perceive everything, including the subtle, the obstructed, and so forth; this is the meaning.

He speaks of the third [abode], Brahmā’s Satyaloka, with the words "the third. Those for whom the construction (nyāsa) of a dwelling or house has not been made are so described. Because of the very absence of a support, they are self-established (svapratiṣṭhāḥ). Those whose establishment is within their own bodies are so described. They are masters of primordial matter (pradhāna); by its will, the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas proceed as long as the duration of creation lasts. And thus it is heard in scripture: "When the time of universal dissolution arrives, all those perfected souls, at the end of the Supreme [Brahmā], enter the supreme state along with Brahmā."

Thus, having described the common characteristics of the four classes of gods, he speaks of their specific qualities by mentioning their specific names—beginning with "Therein": the gods named Acyutas find delight in the meditative bliss of coarse objects; the gods named Śuddhanivāsas find delight in the meditative bliss of subtle objects; the gods named Satyābhās find delight in the meditative bliss of the objects of the senses.

The gods known as Saṃjñāsaṃjñins find delight in the meditative happiness of mere "I-am-ness" (asmitā); therefore, they are satisfied by that. All these [preceding categories] practice *samprajñāta-samādhi*. Now, one might ask: why are those who have reached the culmination of *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*—namely, the *videha*s and *prakṛtilaya*s—not included among the worlds? To this he says: "But the *videha*s and *prakṛtilaya*s... For it is those possessing fluctuations of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), who display objects and sustain the course of worldly life, that exist within the worlds.

And the meaning is that those who have dissolved into the nature of Videha do not [attain liberation] in this way, even though they possess a remaining task (*sādhikāratva*). This very state must be directly realized by the yogi from Satyaloka down to Avīci, within the *suṣumnā* channel at the "gate of the sun. Yet, even by this much, direct realization does not occur; therefore he says: "In this manner, first elsewhere as well—in other places taught by the teacher of yoga—until this entire world has been seen."

For the sattva of the intellect is by its very nature capable of illuminating the universe, yet it is veiled by the impurities of tamas; wherever it is opened up by rajas, that alone it illuminates. When, however, the gateway of the sun is opened by saṃyama, it illuminates the entire world. Nor does this lead to an over-extension of the principle elsewhere, because the power of that particular saṃyama is limited to opening only that much. Thus, everything is clear. 3.26.
In the moon, there is the knowledge of the array of stars. 3.27.
From the pole star, the knowledge of its motion [is obtained]. 3.28.
At the navel wheel, there is the knowledge of the array of the body. 3.29.
In the pit of the throat, there is the cessation of hunger and thirst. ||3.30||
Stability in the tortoise-channel (kūrmanāḍī). ||3.31||

Knowledge of the arrangement of the stars is gained through the moon; knowledge of their motion through the pole star (dhruva); knowledge of the arrangement of the body through the navel-center (nābhicakra); the cessation of hunger and thirst through the throat-pit (kaṇṭhakūpa); and steadiness through the tortoise-channel (kūrmanāḍī). In each case where there is a desire for knowledge, the yogin applies *saṃyama*. Thus, the *saṃyama* that causes the cessation of hunger and thirst and the cause of steadiness has been taught by the words of the Sūtra and explained by the commentary (*bhāṣya*)—which requires no further verbal explanation—and therefore it is not further commented upon here. 3.27–3.31.
In the light at the crown of the head, there is the vision of the perfected ones (siddhas). ||3.32||
"There is the vision of the perfected ones in the light at the crown. By the word "crown" (mūrdhan), the *suṣumnā* channel is indicated; [the practice] consists of *saṃyama* upon that. ||3.32||
Or everything [is known] through intuition (prātibha). 3.33.

Or, everything [is known] through intuition (*pratibhā*). Intuition is that which arises from *pratibhā*; it is called *prātibha*. For one who possesses restraint (*saṃyama*) with respect to the cause of discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), when that [restraint] reaches its culmination, there arises an inferential knowledge born of reasoning (*ūha*) which is preceded by the dawning of discernment; by means of this, the yogi knows everything. And because it saves one from *saṃsāra* by bringing about the proximity of discernment, it is called "the deliverer" (*tāraka*). (3.33)
In the heart is the consciousness of the mind. 3.34.

The consciousness of the mind is in the heart. He explains the word "heart" (*hṛdaya*): "That which is in this city of Brahman. Because it is vast (*bṛhat*), the Self (*ātman*) is Brahman; its city is its abode, for there one knows oneself. That very small cavity is the lotus, the downward-facing dwelling of the mind. He states the reason for the consciousness of the mind: "Therein is cognition; through *saṃyama* on that, one knows the mind as distinguished by its own modifications" (3.34).

Experience is the non-differentiation of the cognition of the sattva and the puruṣa, which are absolutely distinct; from saṃyama upon one's own nature, as distinguished from that which exists for another, comes knowledge of the puruṣa. 3.35.

Experience is the non-distinction of the cognitions of the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, which are absolutely unmixed. Through *saṃyama* upon one's own nature as distinct from that which exists for another, there arises knowledge of the *puruṣa*. The intention of the author of the Sūtra in stating "of the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*" is this: when there is an absolute lack of confusion between the *sattva* of the intellect—which is luminous by nature, extremely clear, and transformed into the form of discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) because its *rajas* and *tamas* have been utterly suppressed—and consciousness (*caitanya*), then what need is there to mention the case of *rajas* and *tamas*, whose natures are insentient? It was with this in mind that the Sūtrakāra spoke thus.

Adopting this very intention, the author of the Bhāṣya also says: "The *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi*) has the nature of luminosity. It is not merely luminous by nature, but rather it has transformed into the form of discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*); therefore, due to its state of extreme purity and clarity, there is a complete similarity with consciousness (*caitanya*), which leads to a confusion between them. To address this, he says: "Common" (*samāna*). The connection (*upanibandhana*) with *sattva* is an inseparable relation; those two, *rajas* and *tamas*, which have a common connection with *sattva*, are described as such.

Subjugation (*vaśīkāra*) means overcoming. He states the non-confusion [of the self] with the words "and therefore" (*tasmāc ca*). The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "also. The meaning is that it is not only [distinguished] from *rajas* and *tamas*. By the term "transforming" (*pariṇāmin*), the difference from the unchanging Puruṣa is stated. The non-distinction of the cognition (*pratyaya-aviśeṣa*) refers to the superimposition of forms such as "calm," "fierce," or "deluded" upon consciousness by the intellect (*buddhi*)—which takes on those forms—through its grasping the reflection of consciousness; this is like the superimposition of trembling upon the moon reflected in clear water due to the shaking of that water.

He states the cause of experience: "because its object has been shown. This has been explained more than once. Now, one might ask: let the intellect (*buddhi-sattva*) be distinct from the Spirit (*puruṣa*), but how is experience itself distinct from the Spirit? To this he says: "That cognition of experience"—meaning the cognition whose form is experience—"is an object of sight and is to be experienced because it exists for the sake of another. For the intellect (*sattva*) exists for the sake of another because it is a composite; and since experience is a property of that [intellect], it too exists for the sake of another. And for whichever other it exists, it is the object of experience for that experiencer.

Alternatively, experience (*bhoga*) is the perception of pleasure and pain as agreeable or disagreeable. This [experience] does not itself make the Self agreeable or disagreeable, because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself; therefore, experience consists of objects that are to be made agreeable or disagreeable. That experiencer is the Self, and experience is its object of perception. As for the phrase "that which is distinct from that which exists for another," the ablative *parārthāt* is explained by supplying the word *anya* (other) after it.

It might be argued as follows: "If cognition has the person (*puruṣa*) as its object, then—alas!—the person must be cognized by another cognition, and that [second] cognition by yet another, leading to an infinite regress. To this he says: "And not by means of a cognition of the person. The underlying intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) is this: the insentient (*jaḍa*) is made manifest by the sentient (*cit*), but the sentient is not made manifest by the insentient. How, then, could a cognition of the person—which is itself insentient in nature—make the sentient self manifest? It is logical, however, that the sentient self, whose manifestation is independent of anything else, makes the insentient manifest.

By the phrase "of the nature of the *buddhi*-sattva," he states its insentience (*jaḍatva*) through its identity with that which is non-conscious. Its "taking the Puruṣa as its object" occurs because it takes the reflection of the Puruṣa residing within the *buddhi*-sattva as its object; it does not take the Puruṣa as its object by means of illuminating the Puruṣa. Rather, it is the *buddhi*-sattva itself—which has received the reflection of the Puruṣa through that cognition and has assumed the shadow of the Puruṣa—that takes consciousness (*caitanyam*) as its object; such is the purpose of the Puruṣa. On this very point, he cites scripture: "For thus it has been said by the Lord: 'There is no knower...'"—the meaning being that [the Puruṣa] is not known by anything. (3.35)
From that, intuitive perception, hearing, touch, sight, taste, and awareness arise. (3.36)

And as long as that restraint upon one's own objects does not accomplish its primary purpose—the knowledge of the Puruṣa—it displays all those powers it brings forth before him: from that arise prescience, supernatural hearing, feeling, seeing, tasting, and smelling. By this, it is stated that the mind, ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—when assisted by dharma born of yoga—become respectively the causes for prescient knowledge and the direct perception of divine sounds and so forth.
The technical (tāntrikī) designations for the five [faculties], beginning with hearing, which perceive divine sounds and so forth, are "śrāvaṇa" and so on. The commentary is easy to understand. 3.36.
These are obstacles to concentration, but they are accomplishments when one has emerged from it. (3.37)

Sometimes, one who has engaged in self-restraint (*saṃyama*) regarding the self might, through its power, attain these various supernatural accomplishments (*siddhis*) and, considering his purpose fulfilled, desist from further restraint. Therefore, he says: "These are obstacles (*upasargas*) during meditative absorption (*samādhi*), but accomplishments (*siddhis*) during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*). For one whose mind has emerged [from concentration] regards those accomplishments as such—just as a person born into poverty regards even a single grain of wealth as a vast fortune. However, the yogi with a concentrated mind must desist even from those [accomplishments] when they arise.

The meaning of the Sūtra and its Commentary [is this]: how indeed could one who has as his supreme human goal (paramapuruṣārtha) the absolute cessation of the threefold suffering he has aimed to eliminate take delight in those supernatural powers (siddhis) which are contrary to that goal? || 3.37 ||
Through the loosening of the cause of bondage and by the awareness of the movement of the mind, there is entry into another's body. 3.38.

Thus, having described the sovereignty consisting of knowledge as the fruit of *saṃyama* culminating in the vision of the *puruṣa*, he now states the sovereignty consisting of action as the fruit of *saṃyama*: "By the loosening of the cause of bondage and by the awareness of the movement of the mind, there is entry into another's body. [The phrase] "by the power of *samādhi*" refers primarily to the mention of *samādhi* because it is the power of *saṃyama* directed toward the objects that are the causes of bondage. "Movement" (*pracāra*) means that by which or in which the mind moves.

The channels are the paths of the mind's coming and going; by practicing *saṃyama* upon that movement, there is knowledge of them. And because of the loosening of the causes of bondage resulting from that, one is no longer obstructed by it. Even though unobstructed, if the mind travels by a wrong path, it does not emerge from its own body without impediment, nor does it enter another body. Therefore, its movement must also be known. Furthermore, the senses follow the mind and settle in their respective locations within another body. (3.38)
From mastery over the udāna breath, there is non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and the like, as well as the power of upward departure. (3.39)

From mastery over *udāna*, there is non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and the like, as well as the power of upward departure (*utkrānti*). Life (*jīvana*) is that which has the functions of the vital breaths (*prāṇa* and so forth) as its characteristic; it is so described because its defining marks are the vital breaths and their kindred forces. The activity of the senses is twofold: external and internal. The external is characterized by the perception of forms and other objects. The internal, however, is life itself; for it is a specific kind of effort, the common cause of all the organs, and the motive force behind the various actions of the wind (*māruta*) sustained within the body. As they say: "The general function of the organs consists of the five vital winds, beginning with *prāṇa*."

Because these [functions] are to be characterized by it, the activity (*kriyā*)—which is the effect (*kārya*)—of that effort is fivefold: 1. *Prāṇa* is situated from the tip of the nose down to the heart; it carries the essence (*rasa*)—the differentiated transformation of what is eaten and drunk—to its respective locations in a balanced and appropriate manner. 2. *Samāna* has its location from the heart down to the navel. 3. *Apāna* is the cause for the removal of urine, feces, the fetus, and so forth; its function extends from the navel down to the soles of the feet.

The *udāna* is so called because it leads (*unnayana*) the *rasa* (nutrient fluid) and other elements upward; its function extends from the tip of the nose up to the head. The *vyāna* is all-pervasive (*vyāpī*). Among those mentioned, the *prāṇa* is the primary one, because scripture declares that when it departs, everything else departs: "When the *prāṇa* departs, all the vital breaths depart after it. Having thus established the distinction between the *prāṇa* and the others based on their respective functions and locations, he introduces the meaning of the aphorism: "By the conquest of the *udāna*..."

By practicing restraint upon the *udāna* breath, one is no longer obstructed by water and other such elements due to its mastery; furthermore, at the time of death, the soul's departure (*utkrānti*) occurs via the path beginning with light (*arcis*). Therefore, through mastery, one attains control over that departure. Through restraint upon the *prāṇa* and other vital airs, their conquest is achieved, and from this comes the conquest of the elements; these effects are to be understood according to the distinctions of the "conquest of locations" (*sthānavijaya*) and so forth. (3.39)
From the conquest of the *samāna* [vāyu], there is the blazing [of the inner fire]. 3.40.
From the friction of rubbing together comes the kindling of fire; it is the fanning and stimulation of the bodily heat. 3.40.
Through *saṃyama* on the connection between the ear and space, divine hearing arises. (3.41)

Through *saṃyama* on one's own nature, the powers such as clairaudience were previously mentioned as being taught as secondary consequences (*anvācaya-śiṣṭa*). Now, he states that clairaudience and the others arise from *saṃyama* upon the very objects of those powers—clairaudience and so forth: "Through *saṃyama* on the connection between the ear and space, divine hearing [is attained]."

He states the relationship between the auditory organ and space—which is the object of restraint—as one of container and contained: "Space is the support and the locus of all auditory organs, even those derived from the *ahaṃkāra*, because it is observed that the auditory organ benefits or is impaired by what benefits or impairs space. Furthermore, when the auditory organ situated within the cavity of the ear-lobule must apprehend sounds such as those originating from earth, it requires a non-common sound residing in the space that constitutes its own substratum, which acts as a cooperative factor for the auditory organ."

It is observed that the olfactory and other senses, acting as auxiliary causes through qualities such as odor, perform the function of perceiving external odors and so forth residing in earth and the other elements. Furthermore, it has been stated that although the nose, tongue, skin, eyes, and ears are derived from the *ahaṃkāra*, they have the elements as their substrata, because the benefit or harm of the olfactory and other senses is seen to follow directly from the benefit or harm of the elements.

And this auditory organ, which is composed of *ahaṃkāra* and is like iron, perceives the sound—produced by the mouth of the speaker, residing within that mouth, and drawn toward it by the magnet-like jewel of the word—as it arrives at the speaker's mouth through a succession of its own functions. Thus, the perception of sound as existing in a particular direction and location for every living being will not be rendered invalid, provided there is no subverting evidence.

And thus is the statement of Pañcaśikha: "For those whose auditory organs occupy the same location, there is the property of hearing from a single location for all. Those Caitra and others whose auditory organs (*śravaṇa*, i.e., *śrotra*) occupy the same location are so described. The meaning is that the auditory organs of all [beings] reside in space (*ākāśa*). And that space, which is the substratum of the auditory organ, is produced from the subtle element (*tanmātra*) whose quality is sound; it possesses the quality of sound, and by means of that sound as a concomitant cause, it perceives sounds belonging to the earth and other elements.

Therefore, the meaning is that for all [sounds], audition (*śruti*) is of a single kind; this is what is meant by "sound" (*śabda*). By this, it is shown that space (*ākāśa*) has the ear as its locus and that sound is its quality. Furthermore, this fact of having audition in a single location is the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of space. For that audition, which is of a single kind and manifests sound, must have a substratum; that very substratum is what is designated by the term "space. Indeed, without such audition, there would be no manifestation of sound.

Nor is such an audition a quality of earth and the other elements, because it is impossible for something to be both the manifested and the manifestor within its own self. Furthermore, non-obstruction is a mark (liṅga) of space. If space did not exist, material objects joined together would not have been pierced even by needles; consequently, everything would be obstructed by everything else. Nor does non-obstruction arise merely from the absence of material substances, because absence depends upon a positive entity (bhāva), and thus [non-obstruction] would be absent in the absence of that [space].

Nor can the power of consciousness (citiśakti) be its substratum, because, being unchanging (apariṇāminī), it lacks the capacity to act as a delimiting factor (avacchedakatva). Furthermore, space, time, and so forth do not exist as substances distinct from earth and the other elements. Therefore, such a specific modification belongs to space alone; thus everything is clear. Since the mark of space (ākāśaliṅga) has been established as non-obstruction, and since wherever there is non-obstruction, there is space everywhere, the all-pervasiveness (sarvagatatva) of space is also established. Thus he says: "In this way, of that which is formless... (tathāmūrtasya).
