He concludes the topic under discussion: "Thus, there is no coming into being after having not existed. (4.12)
These manifest and subtle [objects] have the qualities (guṇa) as their essence. ||4.13||

It might be argued as follows: "This manifold proliferation of distinctions in the universe, consisting of the various states and transformations of the properties of the substrate (*dharmi*), cannot possibly arise from a single *pradhāna*. For a diversity of effects cannot arise from a cause that lacks differentiation. To this, he says: "Those manifest and subtle [entities] have the *guṇas* as their essence. These properties (*dharma*) belonging to the three times—both manifest and subtle—have the *guṇas* as their essence; there is no cause for them apart from the three *guṇas*.
Their diversity, however, arises from the diversity of the beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*) deposited therein. As it is said in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:
"This transformation of the Pradhāna is wonderful because of its manifold nature (vaiśvarūpya).

This means that for the manifest elements such as earth and the eleven sense organs—which exist in the present—the states of pastness and futureness occur according to their respective conditions, as do the six non-specific (aviśeṣa) qualities. Now, dividing the universe into its eternal and non-eternal forms, he describes the eternal form with the words "all this. The meaning is that what is perceived is a transformation characterized by a specific arrangement and distinct configuration. In this very context lies the instruction of the *Ṣaṣṭitantra* scripture: it is like illusion (*māyā*), but not illusion itself; it is utterly fragile and perishable.

For just as an illusion changes into something else even while being called by that same name, so too do modifications, which possess the nature of appearance and disappearance, change into something else at every moment; whereas primordial matter (prakṛti), by virtue of its permanence, does not share the characteristics of an illusion and is thus the ultimate reality. ||4.13||
The reality of things [is established] because of the unity of transformation. 4.14.

"Let it be that there is such a variety of transformations of the three *guṇas*; however, from where does this single transformation—such as 'earth' or 'water'—arise? For it would contradict the unity of the Self. Anticipating this objection, he introduces the *sūtra*: "But when all the *guṇas*... [The reality of things arises] from the unity of the transformation. Even for many [causes], a single transformation is observed.

For example, when cows, horses, buffaloes, and elephants are cast into the *rumā* salt mine, there occurs a single transformation characterized by the nature of salt; and likewise, from wicks, oil, and fire, there arises a single entity known as a lamp. In this way, although the *guṇas* are manifold, their transformation is a unity; consequently, each of the *tanmātras*, the elements (*bhūtas*), and the elemental derivatives (*bhautikas*) possesses its own essential oneness (*tattva-ekatva*). Among those whose nature is apprehension and which consist primarily of *sattva*—being of the nature of light—the intermediate products of ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*) undergo a single transformation in the form of instruments, namely, the sense organ of hearing.

Of those very *guṇas*, through their predominance of *tamas* and their insentient nature as objects of perception, there is one transformation in the form of the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*), which is the object, namely sound. By the word "sound," the subtle element of sound is meant; by the word "object," its insentience is indicated, for it is not possible for the *tanmātra* itself to be an object of the sense of hearing. The rest is easy to understand. Now, he raises the objection of the nihilistic Vijñānavādin: "There is no object that does not accompany consciousness."

For if the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) were distinct from consciousness alone, then such a *pradhāna* (primordial matter) would have to be postulated as their cause of origination; however, they do not exist as something over and above consciousness in the ultimate sense. Therefore, how can there be a postulation of *pradhāna*, and how can there be a postulation of the "graspers"—the sense organs—which are transformations of the *ahaṃkāra*? For instance: because an insentient object lacks self-luminosity, no object exists apart from consciousness. "Sahacarya" (coexistence) means a relationship.

The non-existence of that [object] is its non-concomitance with cognition. The prefix *vi-* has the sense of negation. The meaning is that there is no connection with cognition such that it would be fit for conventional usage. However, cognition does exist as non-concomitant with the object; because it is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*), it lacks dependence on the insentient object when performing the conventional usage regarding the existence of its own domain. Thus, by this, the proponent of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*) has indicated both the necessity of being cognized (*vedyatva*) and the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*).

And these two [arguments] proceed as follows: "That which is perceived by a particular cognition is not different from that cognition, just as the self of a cognition is. And the elements and their derivatives are perceived. This is an "observation of what is pervaded by the contradictory" (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). Since perceptibility is pervaded by non-difference—which is the opposite of the difference to be negated—the observed perceptibility establishes its own pervader, non-difference, and thereby rejects its opposite, difference. Likewise: "Whatever is invariably perceived simultaneously with something else is not different from it."

Just as there is no second moon from a single moon, so too an object is necessarily perceived simultaneously with its cognition; this is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). Since necessity (*niyama*) is incompatible with the lack of necessity (*aniyama*), which is the pervader of the difference that is to be negated, necessity—by excluding the lack of necessity—rejects the difference pervaded by it. One might object: "If the object is not distinct from cognition, how does it appear as if distinct? To this he says: "It is imagined" (*kalpitam*). As the Nihilists (*vaināśika*) say:

"Because they are necessarily perceived together, there is no difference between the blue object and the cognition thereof; and their difference is seen by erroneous cognitions, like [the appearance of] duality in the moon."

He clarifies the state of being imagined (*kalpitatva*) with the words "the conceptual construction of cognition" (*jñānaparikalpanā*). He refutes this with the words "those [people]" (*ta iti*). The connection is: "How could those people be ones whose words are to be trusted? The term *pratyupasthitam* means "presented at every moment of cognition. How so? "In that very way" (*tathā*). Just as this [object] appears as the locus of the notion of "this-ness," in that very way it is presented by itself; it is not something fashioned by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) and brought within the range of consciousness (*vijñāna*). By the phrase "by its own majesty" (*svamāhātmyena*), he shows that the object is the cause of the cognition.

Since consciousness was produced by an object through its own capacity to be apprehended, it is therefore the apprehender of that object. How could such a thing [be established] by the power of conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*), which is not of the nature of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), because conceptualization itself lacks the status of valid cognition? Consequently, the power [of that cognition] is also of the nature of non-validity. Thus, having cast aside the true nature of the object and rendered it distorted, [the conceptual cognition] grasps it. (The reading *upagṛhya* occurs in some manuscripts; even there, the meaning is the same. Those who deny this very point would be persons whose words are to be trusted.

The intended meaning here is as follows: the two reasons—the necessity of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) and cognizability (*vedyatva*)—are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because their exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful. To explain: regarding the form of cognition, those qualities which appear as externality and grossness in respect to the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) cannot exist within cognition itself. For instance, grossness consists in pervading multiple locations, and externality consists in occupying distinct locations. Now, it is not possible for a single cognition to possess either pervasion of multiple locations or occupation of distinct locations.

Because it is impossible for the association of contradictory properties—characterized by occupying that location and not occupying that location—to exist in a single [entity], or else it would follow that the three worlds are one. If it is argued that, for this very reason, there must be a difference between cognitions, then alas! From whence comes this appearance of grossness in those cognitions which have extremely subtle objects as their domain, which are ignorant of each other's news, and which are wakeful only toward their own respective objects? Furthermore, this cannot be the domain of conceptual construction, because of the absence of verbal association and because of its vivid manifestation.

Nor has the gross [object] been perceived, such that there could be clarity for a subsequent cognition conditioned by it. Furthermore, unlike non-conceptual [cognition], conceptual cognition also has only its own internal form as its object; and since that [internal form] is not gross, it cannot have the gross as its object. Therefore, because a gross external object is impossible within an external cognition, this [gross object] must be accepted as false. Nor is the false non-different from consciousness, for if it were, consciousness would likewise entail the consequence of being insubstantial (*tucchatva*).

And thus, since being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*) does not possess the property of being pervaded by non-difference, how could it serve as an opponent to difference? Furthermore, the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) will be established—just as in the case of existence and non-existence—either due to the very nature of consciousness and its grossness, both of which exist, or due to some kind of causal obstruction. Therefore, because they are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), these two fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) produce nothing more than a mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) regarding the absence of external objects. Moreover, the majesty of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not set aside by a mere conceptual construction.

Therefore, it has been rightly asked: "How can [this be established] by the power of conceptual cognition, which is itself non-authoritative? By this, the proof for the lack of a real object (*nirālambanatva*)—which relies on the example of cognitions such as those in dreams—is also refuted. Furthermore, the alternative regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya-vikalpa*) has been answered by the establishment of the composite whole (*avayavin*). The detailed exposition should be followed in the *Nyāyakaṇikā*; thus, enough has been said here in detail. (4.14)
Since there is a difference in the minds even when the object is the same, the paths of the two are distinct. ||4.15||

Thus, having stated the reasoning for establishing [the self] as distinct from consciousness—which is contrary to the Sūtras—the author of the Bhāṣya introduces the reasoning based on the Sūtras with the words: "And why is this so? Because of the difference in minds despite the identity of the object, the path of these two is divided. That which is one while the other is manifold is absolutely distinct from it. For example, Caitra’s single cognition is distinct from the diverse cognitions of Devadatta, Viṣṇumitra, and Maitra."

Even though cognitions are diverse, the object does not differ; thus, it exists as something other than the cognitions. Furthermore, the non-difference of the object, despite the diversity of cognitions, is determined by the mutual recognition (*pratisaṃdhāna*) of knowers: for instance, when a single woman is being perceived, there is a recognition among those who are attached, those who are hostile, those who are deluded, and those who are neutral, such that "she who is seen by you is the very same one seen by me."

Therefore, since there is a difference in the minds and a difference in the cognitions despite the identity of the object, the path of those two—the object and the cognition—is divided; that is, the means for distinguishing their essential natures [is as follows]. For a lover, there is a cognition of pleasure regarding his beloved; for her rivals, there is a cognition of pain; but for Caitra, who does not possess her, there is a cognition of delusion, which is despondency. This might be so.

If it were the case that an object characterized as a "desirable woman," which is imagined by the mind of one person, colors the minds of others as well, then it would follow that [the object] is common [to all]. To this, he says: "And not another [mind]. If that were so, then when one person possesses the cognition of blue, everyone would possess the cognition of blue. [Objection: But even for those who maintain the existence of external objects (*arthavādin*), how can a single object be the cause of cognitions distinguished by differences such as pleasure and so forth?

For it is not logical that a difference in effects should arise from a cause that lacks distinguishing characteristics; therefore, he says: "In the Sāṃkhya position. It is possible for a single external object, which is a transformation of the three *guṇas*, to possess a threefold nature. Even so, [one might object] that everyone would have a consciousness consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion without distinction; therefore, he says: "Depending on causes such as merit (*dharma*), the *sattva* associated with *rajas*, depending upon merit, produces the cognition of pleasure."

"Sattva alone, when its rajas has dissolved and is dependent on knowledge, is the cognition of equanimity. Furthermore, those qualities such as dharma and so forth do not exist in every person at all times; rather, some exist in some persons. Thus, the established order is logically justified. On this point, certain teachers say: "The object is indeed co-existent with the cognition, because it is an object of experience, like pleasure and the rest."

This is what is meant: let it be granted that the object is distinct from cognition; nevertheless, because it is insentient (*jaḍa*), it cannot be apprehended without cognition. It must, however, be manifested by cognition. Thus, it exists only at the very time of cognition and not at any other time, due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*) refutes this, which deviates from the Sūtra, with the words: "These [objects], by means of this door..."

Indeed, the object is experienced by worldly investigators as being common to all cognitions, carried along by a succession of many moments, and consisting of transformation. If that [object] were to exist together with consciousness, then surely it would be exactly of such a nature; and if this is so, what is this insistence regarding the "this-portion" (idamaṃśa) such that even it should not be denied? This is the meaning. ||4.15||
And since an object does not depend on a single mind, what would become of that object at a time when it is not being cognized? (4.16)

Or, let there be no denial of this objective component; let the object simply coexist with the cognition. To that, he replies: "An entity is not dependent on a single mind; otherwise, what would it be when that [mind] is not a means of valid cognition? For when the mind apprehending a jar is occupied with the substance of a cloth, it does not function with respect to the jar."

Alternatively, if that very object which was the domain of discrimination enters into cessation (*nirodha*), then—due to the absence of either the cognition of the jar or the cognition of the discrimination—the discrimination or the jar would indeed be destroyed, since they exist solely as long as the distinction in cognition persists. Thus he says: "by a single mind" (*ekacitta*). The meaning is: what would that [object] be, or would it not be? Furthermore, from where would that object—whether it be the discrimination or the jar—arise when it is no longer connected with the mind?

For effects, which conform to the positive and negative concomitance of their fixed causes, are not capable of arising from other causes by overstepping their own cause; otherwise, their occasional occurrence would be contradicted if they were causeless. Nor is it reasonable to claim that being the cause of the cognition of an object is itself the cause of the object, for this would lead to the absurd consequence that a sweetmeat merely imagined in one's hope and one actually consumed would be identical in terms of their taste, potency, post-digestive effect, and so forth. Therefore, it has been rightly said: "or again, [the object] being connected with the mind."

Furthermore, whatever constitutes the near part (arvāgbhāga) is entirely pervaded by the middle and far parts. If the existence [of the object] were dependent upon cognition, then because it is not being experienced [at that time], the middle and far parts would not exist; thus, due to the absence of the pervader (vyāpaka), the near part would also not exist. Therefore, since the object would be non-existent, how could there be an object coexisting with the cognition? To this he says: "And those which... (*ye cāsya*). "Unpresent" means unknown. He concludes: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*). The remainder is easy to understand. 4.16.
Because the mind depends upon the coloring by that [object], the object is either known or unknown. 4.17.

It might be argued that if the object were independent, and its nature were insentient (*jaḍa*), it would never be manifest. Or, if it were manifest, its insentience would have to depart, and consequently the object itself would cease to exist; for an entity can never persist by abandoning its own nature. Nor is it tenable to say that the property of manifestation belongs to an insentient object through the influence of the sense organs and so forth.

If the object were the nature of the thing-in-itself (*dharman*), then like blueness and so forth, it would be common to all persons; thus, according to one [interpretation] of the meaning of the scripture, everyone would be omniscient, and there would be no one at all who is ignorant. Furthermore, it is not logical for the past and future to have a present nature. Therefore, the notion that the independent object is the domain of apprehension is merely a wishful thought. To this, he says: "Because the mind depends upon the coloring by that [object], the thing is known or unknown."

Even though an object is insentient by nature, it colors the mind through the medium of the sense organs. Thus, the power of consciousness (citi-śakti), having its reflection transferred to the mirror-like mind that has become such, experiences the object as the mind perceives itself colored by the object; however, it does not impart any quality such as "manifestness" to the object. Nor is it unrelated to the mind, since it has been stated that the reflection of the object is transferred to it.

And although there is no direct connection between the object and the all-pervading mind or the sense organ derived from the ego (ahaṃkārika), nevertheless, the objects are connected with that body wherein the active mind resides; thus it is said that they are like a magnet. The mind possesses properties similar to iron. Through the channel of the senses, [the objects] come into contact and color [the mind]. For this very reason, he says that the mind is subject to transformation—"of the thing"—[in verse 4.17].
The fluctuations of the mind are always known by their master, the Puruṣa, because of his unchangeability. 4.18.

Thus, having established the object as distinct from the mind, and in order to demonstrate the Self as distinct from those [objects] which are subject to transformation, and to state its dissimilarity to them—namely, its non-transformative nature—he completes the aphorism and recites it: "But for him for whom that very mind is the object, the fluctuations of the mind are always known, because the Puruṣa, who is their master, is non-transformative."

The mind—whether in states of distraction, delusion, agitation, one-pointedness, or steadiness—is always experienced by the Puruṣa as possessing fluctuations until its cessation. For what reason? Because the Puruṣa is unchanging; if he were subject to change like the mind, the Puruṣa too would have objects both known and unknown. However, his objects are only ever known; therefore, he is unchanging. And for that reason, he is distinct from those things which undergo transformation. This is what is stated [in the verse]: "If [he were] like the mind..."

The constant state of being known, however, belongs to that mind together with its modifications; he who is the master, the owner, or—in other words—the enjoyer of that [mind], is the Puruṣa. This [fact] leads one to infer the unchangeability of that master, the Puruṣa. Thus, the sense is that there is a distinction between that unchanging Puruṣa and the changing citta. ||4.18||
That [consciousness] does not possess its own appearance, because it is an object of perception. 4.19.

Here, he raises the objection of the Nihilist (Vaināśika): "There might be this doubt," and so forth. The meaning is as follows: this would be so if the mind were an object of the Self; however, since this [mind] is self-luminous and arises in dependence upon a preceding mind that appears as an object, how could there be for the Person (puruṣa) the state of having objects that are always known, or, even more so, the distinction from the changing mind by virtue of being unchanging? [The reply is: That [mind] does not manifest itself, because it is an object of perception (dṛśyatvāt).

This might be so if the mind were self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*), but that is not the case. For, due to its nature as a transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), it is pervaded by experience just like blue and other objects; and that which is pervaded by experience cannot be self-manifesting, because there is a contradiction in [the same thing] acting upon itself. Indeed, the very same thing cannot be both the action and the object-agent (*karmakāraka*). For cooking is not cooked, nor is cutting cut. But the *puruṣa*, being unchanging (*apariṇāmī*), is not the object of experience; therefore, self-luminosity is not untenable in his case.

For its self-luminosity consists in having a manifestation that is not dependent on another; it does not consist in being an object of experience. Therefore, because it is an object of vision, the mind is not self-manifesting, but rather an object of perception. The point is that the objects of the mind's modifications are manifested only by being reflected in the light of the Self. Now, one might object: "Fire is both visible and self-luminous; for fire is not manifested by another fire in the same way that jars and other things are manifested by fire. To this, he says: "And fire is not [the case] here. Why? Because... [he says]: "For... [and so forth].

The meaning is that there is no deviation [from the rule]: fire may indeed be manifested by another fire, but it is manifested through cognition; thus, it is not the case that it is not self-manifesting. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and this manifestation": the word "this" distinguishes manifestation from the nature of the person (*puruṣa*), meaning that manifestation is of the nature of an action (*kriyā*). This is what is being said: whatever action there is, all of it is observed to be connected with an agent, an instrument, and an object.

Just as cooking is observed through the relation between Caitra, fire, and rice, or likewise illumination; and since illumination is also an action, it must likewise [be understood] by that [same logic]. Furthermore, the meaning of the statement is that a relation depends upon difference and is not possible where there is non-difference. Moreover, the meaning of the words "the mind is self-luminous" is that it is simply not an object of apprehension for anyone. This might be so: let the mind not be an object of apprehension.

For the cessation of the mind does not follow from the cessation of that which is not its cause and which does not pervade it; therefore, he says: "by one's own cognition" (*svabuddhi*). "Cognition" (*buddhi*) means the mind (*citta*); "movements" (*pracāra*) mean activities; "beings" (*sattva*) mean living creatures; and the "variations of the mind's activity" (*cittasya vṛttibhedāḥ*) refer to anger, greed, and so forth. The meaning is that these, being experienced individually by each person along with their own substratum—the mind—and their respective objects, refute the mind's state of being ungraspable. He clarifies this very experience of the movements of one's own cognition with the words: "I am angry. (4.19)
And at one time, there is no determination of both. 4.20.

Furthermore, there can be no simultaneous determination of both [the self and the object]. One who asserts that "the mind appears as itself and appears as the object" cannot maintain that it determines the self by the very same activity by which it determines the object; for an activity that is not distinct [in its nature] is incapable of producing different effects. Therefore, a distinction between activities must be admitted. Yet for the Nihilists (Vaināśikas), there is no activity other than the difference in the arising [of moments].

Furthermore, it is not possible for a difference in effects to arise from the production of a single thing that lacks distinguishing characteristics, for that would entail the fallacy of such difference being accidental (*ākasmikatva*). Nor is it possible for a single entity to have two modes of production. Therefore, the determination of the object and the form of the cognition do not occur at one and the same time. This is stated in the Commentary: "Nor [can they occur] in a single moment. And thus it has been said by the Nihilists (*vaināśika*):
"For those [who hold this view], origination itself is the action, and that very same thing is called the agent."
Therefore, it is established that this constant objectivity of the mind, by removing its own inherent luminosity, reveals both the seer and the unchanging nature of the seer. 4.20.
If one cognition were perceived by another cognition, there would be an infinite regress, as well as a confusion of memories. (4.21)

Furthermore, he raises the objection of the Nihilist (Vaināśika): "It might be thought: 'Let it be that self-cognition does not exist as an object of perception; even so, the Self is not established. The meaning is this: because the final moment of consciousness (*cittakṣaṇa*) existing within one's own continuum (*svasaṃtāna*) perceives its own generative moment of consciousness, which has ceased through its own inherent nature (*svarasa*). [The opponent replies: "That [final moment] is 'immediately preceding' (*samanantara*) because it is equal in being a cognition (*jñānatva*) and because it is immediate in being uninterrupted (*avyavahitatva*). If [consciousness] were perceivable by another consciousness, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the cognition of a cognition, as well as a confusion of memory (*smṛtisaṃkara*)."

"Buddhi" means "citta. A final cognition that has not been apprehended is not capable of apprehending a preceding cognition; for a preceding cognition cannot be known if it is not connected with a [subsequent] cognition. Indeed, one who has not apprehended a staff cannot understand the bearer of the staff. Therefore, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). The aggregates (*skandhas*) are consciousness, sensation, perception, form, and mental formations.

Regarding the phrase "doctrines such as Sāṃkhya and Yoga": Sāṃkhya and Yoga are the first among those doctrines, such as Vaiśeṣika and others; thus they are called "doctrines such as Sāṃkhya and Yoga. The rest is easy to understand. (4.21)
To cite [the example]: when one falls into a state having that form without transition, there is the self-awareness of one's own intellect. 4.22.

It might be argued as follows: "If the mind does not manifest itself and is not cognizable by another mind, how will the self experience the mind? Indeed, for the self—which is self-luminous—there is no action whatsoever; and without such action, it cannot be an agent. Furthermore, it cannot be the experiencer of that object (the mind) if it were unconnected to it, for that would lead to an over-extension (of the definition of agency). With this intention, he asks: "How? He provides the answer in the aphorism: "The self's cognition of its own intellect occurs when the non-transmigrating consciousness assumes the form of that [intellect]."

That which was stated as "the conformity of the modification to [the seer] in other cases" has arisen from this: namely, the consciousness of one's own intellect by the consciousness, when the intellect assumes that form and thereby becomes a receptacle for the reflection of consciousness, attaining its very nature.

Just as water that is free from impurities, even without the activity of the moon, reflects the image of the moon and makes the moon—which is actually motionless—appear as if moving and as if curved within its own basin, so too the mind, even without the operation of consciousness (*citi*), reflects the image of consciousness. By means of its own inherent activity, it makes the power of consciousness—which is itself unattached—appear as if it possessed activity and as if it were attached; thus, by assuming the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*), it brings about for that power the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). This is the meaning of the aphorism.

Since this meaning has been explained repeatedly in various places in the *Bhāṣya*, it is not explained here. To provide scriptural authority for the fact that the modification of knowledge (*jñāna-vṛtti*) is not distinct from the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), he cites the following: "And so it has been said: 'Not Pātāla... They understand the cave to be the mental modification itself, which has taken on the reflection of consciousness (*cit-chāyāpannā*), belonging to the eternal, auspicious Brahman of pure nature; because it has taken on the reflection of consciousness, it is non-distinct from consciousness itself.
In that very cave is that secret Brahman; but upon its removal, it shines forth for the Blessed One in his final body—self-luminous, unobstructed, and free from affliction. ||4.22||
The mind, colored by both the seer and the seen, has all things as its object. 4.23.

Thus, since the mind is subject to transformation by virtue of being an object of perception, the Puruṣa has been established as distinct from it and characterized by the quality of non-transformation. Now, he provides even worldly perception as proof for this—namely, "And therefore this... The meaning is: "This must necessarily be so. The mind, colored by both the seer and the seen, is the knower of all objects.

For just as a mind colored by blue or other objects establishes that object—blue and so forth—through direct perception itself, so too, through the reflection of the seer, the mind colored by that [seer] establishes the seer as well through direct perception. Indeed, cognition possesses a threefold form: "I am now cognizing blue. Therefore, just like the object of knowledge, the knower of it is also established by direct perception; yet he is not established in a distinct manner, like the reflection of the moon in water. However, this much does not mean that he is not perceived directly.

And it is not the case that because this [reflection] resides in water it is invalid; therefore, it must also be invalid with respect to the form of the moon itself. Consequently, although a mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) has consciousness as its object by virtue of being a reflection in the mind, it does not have consciousness as its object [in the primary sense]. Thus, this is the "capacity for all objects" of the mind. This is what he says: "For the mind... Not only is the mind colored by the object to be thought through the assumption of its form, but it is so also by itself.

The particle *ca* (and) is displaced; it should be understood immediately after the word *puruṣeṇa*. The "falling of its reflection" is the modification (*vṛtti*) of the Puruṣa. And this "falling of the reflection of consciousness" into the mind must be accepted by the Nihilists (*vaināśika*). Otherwise, how could they have superimposed consciousness upon the mind? To this he says: "Therefore, by this... Some Nihilists are proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), while others are proponents of consciousness-only (*vijñānamātravādin*).
Now, if it is the mind alone that is experienced in the form of the seer and the form of the seen, then alas, the seer and the seen must indeed be non-different from the mind! As they have said:

"For although the nature of the intellect is non-dual, it is perceived by those of perverted vision as if it possessed the distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and the act of cognition."

How, then, are these people to be pitied? To this he says: "In the wisdom born of meditative concentration" (*samādhiprajñā*). Indeed, even though they have accepted a Puruṣa distinct from the mind through the aforementioned arguments, they must be awakened by being introduced to the wisdom born of meditative concentration which has the Self as its object, by means of instruction in the eight-limbed yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*). For example: in the wisdom born of meditative concentration, the object to be known—the Self—appears as a reflection; why is it other [than the mind]? Because that Self has become the objective support (*ālambana*) for it.

Now, if one should say out of impudence—even though it has been established through reasoning—that the object is not non-different from the mind, he states the reason for that: "If that object, which is of the nature of the self, were merely mind and not distinct from it, then how could the form of wisdom be apprehended by wisdom itself? For there is a contradiction in [an action] operating upon its own self. He concludes with: "Therefore. He says "Thus" to show that they have been moved by compassion through this correct instruction; the meaning is "by birth," that is, by their very nature. (4.23)
Therefore, although it is variegated by innumerable latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), it acts for the sake of others because it functions through collective effort. ||4.24||

He introduces another reason for the existence of a self distinct from the mind with the words, "And why? [The mind], although variegated by innumerable latent impressions (*vāsanā*), exists for the sake of another because it functions through combination. Even though the innumerable latent impressions of karma and the latent impressions of afflictions reside only in the mind and not in the *puruṣa*.

And thus, since the results (vipākas) are dependent on latent impressions (vāsanās) and have the mind as their substratum, they bring about the state of being an enjoyer for the mind; and since that which is to be enjoyed exists for the sake of the enjoyer, it follows that everything is for the sake of the mind. Nevertheless, even though that mind is variegated by innumerable latent impressions, it is for the sake of another. Why? Because it acts through combination—this is the meaning of the aphorism. He explains this with the words "This very... (tad etad).

Someone might say: "Let this mind act in combination and yet achieve its own purpose; what contradiction is there? To such a person, he replies: "By that which acts in combination. The term "pleasurable mind" indicates experience (*bhoga*); by this, the "painful mind" is also to be understood. By "knowledge," liberation (*apavarga*) is meant. This is what is being said: pleasure and pain, being by nature respectively agreeable and disagreeable, cannot exist within the Self, because it is a contradiction for [opposites] to reside in one's own self.

Nor can any other agent who acts through a combination [of causes], whether directly or indirectly, be one who is to be favored or opposed by pleasure and pain while producing them. Therefore, only that which does not operate toward pleasure and pain either directly or indirectly is the one to be favored or opposed by these two. And that is the eternally indifferent *puruṣa* alone; he is thus liberated by that knowledge, for even that knowledge is dependent upon an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself, knowledge cannot have itself as its purpose.

Liberation cannot arise from this external object, because liberation is impossible for those who are merged in the bodyless [state] or merged in primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Therefore, even that knowledge has the person (*puruṣa*) as its sole purpose; it is not for its own sake, nor is it for the sake of another alone. And since there would be the consequence of an infinite regress if it were for the sake of another through a composite [entity], it is established that it is for the sake of another who is non-composite. 4.24.
For one who perceives the distinction, there is the cessation of the cultivation of self-existence. 4.25.

Having thus explained the vision of the Self, which consists of reasoning and is the fundamental seed of isolation (*kaivalya*), he describes the person qualified for that instruction as distinguished from other unqualified persons: "For one who perceives the distinction, the cultivation of the sense of self-identity ceases. For one who possesses the cultivation of the sense of self-identity, as they practice the eightfold yoga based on its instruction, through the ripening of that practice and by perceiving the distinction between the *sattva* of the mind and the Puruṣa, the cultivation of the sense of self-identity comes to an end.

The meaning of the Sūtra is this: for that nihilist (*nāstika*) who lacks even the cultivation of the existence of a self (*ātmabhāvabhāvanā*), and who is thus ineligible for instruction—being one who has not ascertained the nature of the self or the existence of another world—there is neither instruction, nor the vision of distinction, nor the cessation of the cultivation of the existence of a self. Now, one might ask: "From what is the cultivation of the existence of a self, which resides in the mind, known? To this he says: "Just as in the rainy season... and so forth.

It is inferred that there exists a seed of the vision of reality from a previous birth, conducive to liberation, which has been brought forth by the practice of the eightfold yoga or even its partial practice. And the cultivation of the self-nature (*ātmabhāvabhāvanā*) of that [seed] necessarily proceeds spontaneously, even without the repeated practice of objects. He shows, by means of the words of the Āgamas, one who lacks qualification: "Because of the absence of which, this... and so forth.

The prima facie view is that there is no fruit of action because of the absence of one who goes to the next world, and thus there is no next world; in this regard, there is both attraction and aversion toward the determination concerning the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*). The cultivation of the sense of self has been explained previously. He states the reflection of one who perceives the distinction: "Of the mind alone," etc. For such a person, skilled in perceiving the distinction, the cultivation of the sense of self ceases. (4.25)
Then the mind is inclined toward discernment and tends toward isolation. 4.26.

Now, as to what kind of mind belongs to one who perceives the distinction, he says: "At that time, the mind is inclined toward discernment and tends toward isolation. This is explained by the words themselves. (4.26)
In those intervals, other conditions arise from the formative predispositions. 4.27.

It might be argued: "If the vision of distinction were firmly established in discernment (*viveka*), the mind would never again emerge from that state. Yet, we observe that even for one wandering for alms, the mind does emerge. To this he says: "In the gaps of that [vision], other cognitions arise from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Regarding the word "cognition" (*pratyaya*): that by which something is cognized is a cognition; it is the mental essence (*cittasattva*) from which discernment is distinguished.

By the phrase "I know," the direct perception of liberation is shown; by "I do not know," delusion is shown, as well as its roots—egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and possessiveness (*mamakāra*)—manifested either as "I am" or as "mine. The compound "and those seeds are being destroyed" refers to the destruction of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) arising from previous [worldly] tendencies. (4.27)
Furthermore, their abandonment is explained in the same manner as that of the afflictions. 4.28.

It might be argued: even when discriminative knowledge (*viveka-vijñāna*) exists, if the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence (*vyutthāna*) continue to produce other cognitions (*pratyaya*), what then is the cause for their abandonment, by which those other cognitions would no longer be produced? To this he says: "Their abandonment is said to be like that of the afflictions (*kleśa*). For one whose discriminative knowledge is not yet mature, the latent impressions of emergence—which have not been exhausted—produce other cognitions; however, for one whose discriminative knowledge is mature, these impressions, being exhausted, are no longer capable of producing other cognitions.

Just as afflictions, even when arising from a gap in isolation (*viveka*), do not produce further formative impressions (*saṃskāra*), for what reason? Because these afflictions have their seed-nature burnt by the fire of discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*). The same applies to the formative impressions of emergence (*vyutthāna*).

Now, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence must be suppressed by the latent impressions of discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*), and the latent impressions of discrimination must be suppressed by the latent impressions of cessation (*nirodha*). Since it has been shown that the latent impressions of cessation have no external object, the means for their cessation—which remains largely to be considered—is stated: "But the latent impressions of knowledge... This means the latent impressions of supreme detachment (*para-vairāgya*). (4.28)

For one who is not attached even to discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), there arises through the complete manifestation of discriminative discernment the *dharmamegha* (cloud of dharma) samādhi. 4.29.

Thus, having stated *prasaṃkhyāna* as the means for cessation upon emergence from meditation, the author of the Sūtras states the means for cessation through *prasaṃkhyāna*: "For one who is not even indifferent toward *prasaṃkhyāna*, there arises, due to discriminative discernment in every respect, the *dharmamegha* samādhi. Consequently, he does not seek anything—such as lordship over all beings—from that *prasaṃkhyāna*; on the contrary, becoming detached by perceiving the defect of changeability even in that state, he attains discriminative discernment in every respect."

He explains this very point with the words "even there": when there might be thoughts of emergence (*vyutthāna*), then this Brahmin would not have discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) in every respect; since no other thoughts arise for him, he possesses discriminative discernment in every respect. At that time, his samādhi becomes the "cloud of dharma" (*dharmamegha*). This is what is meant: one who is dispassionate toward even [the state of] higher knowledge (*prasaṃkhyāna*) and desires its cessation should practice the *dharmamegha* samādhi.
And through the practice of that [meditation], discriminative discernment arises in every respect; thus, one is able to restrain it. ||4.29||
From that follows the cessation of afflictions and karma. 4.30.

He states its purpose: "From that, there is the cessation of afflictions and karma. But why is the knower liberated while still living? The answer is: "Because... It is said that the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*), fueled by the impressions of afflictions and karma, is the cause of birth and so forth. And when the cause is absent, the effect cannot exist. As the venerable Akṣapāda has stated here: "Because one free from passion is not seen to be born again. (4.30)
Then, because the knowledge that is free from all veils and impurities is infinite, the knowable is small. (4.31)

Now, when the Cloud of Dharma (dharmamegha) has thus arisen, what is the nature of the mind? To this he says: "At that time, because the knowledge of that which is free from all stains of obscuration is infinite, the knowable is small. Obscurations (āvaraṇa) are those things by which the essence of the mind (cittasattva) is veiled; they are the stains, namely afflictions (kleśa) and karma. All these are the stains of obscuration, and being free from them, the knowledge of the essence of the mind is infinite—meaning immeasurable—by virtue of this etymology: "that by which something is known" (jñāyate 'nena). Because of its infinity, the knowable is small.

For just as in autumn, when the sun is freed from the mass of clouds and shines intensely on all sides, objects such as jars—which are small compared to the infinity of its light—are illuminated; so too, because of the infinity of the light of the *sattva* of the mind when *rajas* and *tamas* have departed, that which is to be illuminated is small. This is what he expresses with the words "by all" (*sarvaiḥ*). He clarifies this very point by way of contrast (*vyatirekamukhena*) with the phrase "overpowered by the obscuring *tamas*."

The meaning is that by means of the *rajas* characterized by activity (*kriyāśīla*), darkness (*tamas*)—which had been set in motion—is therefore opened up, that is, removed from its location. For this very reason, because it "sprinkles" or rains down (*mehati/varṣati*) all phenomena (*dharmas*) to be known through illumination, it is called the "Cloud of Dharma" (*dharmamegha*). Now, let this be the Cloud of Dharma samādhi, which is the cause for the pacification of the afflictions (*kleśas*), karmic latencies (*vāsanās*), and karmic impressions (*āśayas*); yet, even when this exists, why is it that a living being is not born again? To this, he says: "In this regard, it has been said..."

If an effect were produced even through the total destruction of its cause, then, alas! the piercing of gems and such would become perceptible by the blind and others. In that case, the worldly proverb whose meaning was previously considered untenable—"The blind man pierced the gem"—would instead become one whose meaning is established. "Āvayat" means he strung it; "grathitavān" means he tied it; "pratyamuñcat" means he fastened it; and "abhyapūjayat" means he praised it. (4.31)
Thereafter, for those who have achieved their purpose, there is the completion of the sequence of the transformation of the guṇas. ||4.32||

Now, one might object: "The ultimate limit of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*) is merely the clarity of knowledge and supreme dispassion, which utterly destroys the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of both emergent and meditative states along with the afflictions and karmic residues. Yet, since the *guṇas* are by their very nature prone to modification, why do they not initiate the body, senses, and so forth, even for such a person? To this he says: "Therefore, for those who have accomplished their purpose, there is a cessation of the sequence of transformation of the *guṇas*.
The meaning is that it is the inherent nature of the *guṇas* that they do not act toward one whom they have rendered purposeful. ||4.32||
Sequence is the counter-correlative of the moment, to be apprehended through the final limit of transformation. (4.33)

In this context, he asks about the sequence of transformation: "Now, what is this? A sequence is that which has moments as its counterpart and is apprehended through the final limit of transformation. That which has moments as its counterpart—that is, for which the moment is the related correlate—is thus described. The meaning is that it is based on an accumulation of moments. Indeed, a sequence can never be defined without something possessing sequence. Furthermore, there is no sequence belonging to a single moment alone. Therefore, it remains established that [sequence] is based on an accumulation of moments.

This is what he says: "immediately following the moment" (*kṣaṇānantarya*). He states the proof for the sequence of transformation (*pariṇāma*) with the words: "of transformation" (*pariṇāmasya*). For even in the case of a new garment that has been carefully preserved with effort, its state of oldness is observed after a long time. This is the "final limit" (*aparānta*), that is, the culmination of transformation; by means of this, the sequence of transformation is established. Even prior to that [culmination], the temporal succession of the various stages of oldness—namely, the subtle, subtler, subtlest, gross, grosser, and grossest—is inferred.

He demonstrates this very point by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "for not" (*na hi*). That which has not experienced—that is, has not attained—a sequential moment is described as such. Now, one might object that this sequence is not possible for *pradhāna* because it is eternal; therefore, he says: "And even in the case of eternal things. By means of the plural number, he asserts that sequence pervades all eternal entities. Having shown the different types among eternal things, he establishes the pervasion of sequence by them with the words: "It is twofold" (*dvayī*).

Now, one might object: let that which is immutable (*kūṭastha*) be eternal because it does not deviate from its own nature; but how can that which is transformative (*pariṇāmin*), always deviating from its essential form, be eternal? To this he says: "In which... The properties, characteristics, and states possess the nature of arising and passing away, whereas for the substrate (*dharmin*), there is indeed no impairment of its reality. Furthermore, is it the case that sequence is everywhere apprehended through the final limit of transformation? No; to this he says: "In that regard, among the qualities and their properties, such as intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth."

Since the sequence of transformation for the *pradhāna* has not reached its ultimate limit—unlike that of the *dharmas*, which reaches an end through their destruction—one might object: "Granted that there is a sequence of transformation for the *pradhāna* because it transforms into the form of *dharmas*; but how can there be a sequence of transformation for the *puruṣa*, who is unchanging? To this, he says: "immutable" (*kūṭastha*). In that regard, for those who are bound, because of the conceit of non-difference from the mind, there is a superimposition of transformation due to the transformation of that [mind].

And for liberated beings, based on the act of affirmation (*astikriyā*), even a non-real transformation imagined through delusion occurs; because the word precedes, the conceptual construction following it takes up that act of affirmation. It has been stated that the sequence of transformations finds no final rest within the qualities (*guṇas*). Not accepting this, he asks: "Now" (*atha*). "By persistence" refers to the state of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*); "by movement" refers to creation (*sṛṣṭi*).

This is what is meant: if, due to its infinity, there is no completion of the transformation of *saṃsāra*, then alas, how could the *saṃsāra* of all selves be suddenly cut off at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), and how could it arise all at once at the beginning of creation? Therefore, since all are liberated through the sequential liberation of each individual self, the cessation of *saṃsāra* for all occurs gradually; thus, there is a completion of the sequence of the transformation of primordial matter (*pradhāna*).

And in this way, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even the *pradhāna* is impermanent. Nor is the manifestation of a previously non-existent entity admitted, which would lead to its being infinite. For if that were the case, its beginninglessness would be contradicted, resulting in the collapse of the entire meaning of the treatise; such is the sense. He states the reply: "This is not to be spoken of (*avacanīya*), for it does not merit an answer. To demonstrate that this is absolutely not to be spoken of, he shows a question that is absolutely answerable by saying, "There is a question."

The answer to the question, "Will everyone who is born die? is: "O, yes. This means, "Truly, O, yes. Having stated that which is to be answered categorically (*avibhajya-vacanīya*), he poses a question regarding that which is to be answered analytically (*pravibhajya-vacanīya*): "Then, all... He states the nature of that which is to be answered analytically: "Analytically... He states another question, which is likewise to be answered analytically, for the sake of clarity: "Likewise, a human being... However, this [question] is absolutely not to be answered (*avacanīya*).

For it is not possible to state categorically, in general terms, whether the saṃsāra of virtuous or non-virtuous persons has an end or is infinite; just as it is not possible to determine categorically whether the welfare or non-welfare of living beings in general is certain, or just as death is certain for one who has been born. However, it can be determined with certainty once distinctions are made; thus he says: "Of the virtuous... and so forth.

The underlying intention is as follows: the inference that "because all [beings] attain liberation through a gradual process, saṃsāra will eventually be annihilated" relies upon liberation as established by scripture (āgama). Thus, how could one who accepts the authority of the very scripture that teaches liberation then treat that same scripture as non-authoritative regarding the permanence of the transformation of primordial matter (pradhāna)? Therefore, this inference has a subject contradicted by scripture and is not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

For it is heard in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas that the succession of creation and re-creation is both beginningless and endless. Moreover, the simultaneous cessation of the cycle of transmigration for all individual selves is not possible; for even for those of learned character, the establishment of discriminative discernment—which is to be achieved through the diligent practice over a succession of many births—is difficult to attain. How much less, then, could it happen all at once and by chance for every living being, whether stationary or moving?

Furthermore, it is not logical that there should be a simultaneity of effects when there is no simultaneity of causes. However, if discriminative discernment occurs sequentially, then through the sequential liberation of an infinite number of beings, there is no annihilation of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), because living beings are infinite and incalculable; thus, everything is perfectly clear. ||4.33||
Isolation is the reversion of the guṇas, which are devoid of the purpose of the Puruṣa; or it is the power of consciousness established in its own nature. (4.34)
(Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Kaivalyapāda, in the Yoga Sūtras composed by the venerable Patañjali.

He states the intermediate connection for the sūtra which defines the nature of isolation (kaivalya): "The withdrawal of the guṇas whose purpose has been fulfilled," and "Isolation is the re-establishment in one's own nature, or the power of consciousness."

The re-absorption of those qualities—which consist of both cause and effect—into their own cause, the *pradhāna*, because they have accomplished their task and are devoid of any further purpose for the Spirit; this dissolution of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence, meditative absorption, and restraint back into the mind, of the mind into the I-consciousness (*asmitā*), of the I-consciousness into the subtle body (*liṅga*), and of the subtle body into the unmanifest (*aliṅga*)—this very re-creation of the qualities consisting of cause and effect is *kaivalya*.

Regarding any person whatsoever, he states that the liberation of *pradhāna* or the establishment of the self-nature (*svarūpa*) of the *puruṣa* constitutes the liberation of the *puruṣa*—this is expressed by the words "establishment of self-nature" (*svarūpa*). For indeed, even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) remains established in its own nature; yet this is not considered liberation. Therefore, he says "again" (*punar*). The word "iti" in the sūtra marks the conclusion of the treatise. 4.34.

In this chapter, the mind worthy of liberation, the next world, the knowledge for the sake of accomplishing the goal, the concentration that is the mass of Dharma, and the twofold liberation have been set forth; other matters have also been mentioned as incidental. (1) The cause of the afflictions has been declared, and then the afflictions themselves along with their eight limbs; the two types of yoga have also been established here. The path to liberation has been made, the distinction between the qualities (*guṇa*) and the self (*puruṣa*) has been made very clear, and isolation (*kaivalya*)—the consciousness from which the afflictions have fallen away—has been distinguished. (2)
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Kaivalyapāda, in this commentary on the Pātañjala Bhāṣya composed by the venerable Vācaspatimiśra. ||4||
This Pātañjala Yoga-śāstra, together with its commentary and sub-commentary, is hereby completed.
